label: PW101
name: Answer all of these conceptual questions:
desc: Answer all of these conceptual questions: a) Which is more likely to knock something over: being hit by a rubber bullet (that bounces off) or being hit by a metal bullet (that gets stuck) or being hit by a piercing bullet (that goes through)? All three bullets have the same mass…
statement:
Answer all of these conceptual questions:

a) Which is more likely to knock something over: being hit by a rubber bullet (that bounces off) or being hit by a metal bullet (that gets stuck) or being hit by a piercing bullet (that goes through)? All three bullets have the same mass and initial speed.

b) In a standard physics demo, the instructor lies on the floor holding an anvil on their chest. A volunteer swings a sledgehammer and hits the anvil hard enough to severely injure the instructor if there were no anvil. But with the anvil, the instructor is safe. Why?

c) Which is more dangerous: to slam into a parked car identical to yours at 30 mph, or to have a head-on collision with a car identical to yours, both going 15 mph? (Ignore any interactions with the road.)

d) You are on an airplane going 250 m/s. A cat weighing $$4 \, \mathrm{kg}$$ escapes from its carrier and runs up the aisle at $$3 \, \mathrm{m/s}.$$ From your point of view, the cat increased its kinetic energy by $$\frac12 4\, \mathrm{kg}\times(3 \, \mathrm{m/s})^2 = 18 \,\mathrm{J}.$$ From the ground's point of view, the cat increased its kinetic energy by $$\frac12 4\,\mathrm{kg}\times(253^2 - 250^2)\,(\mathrm{m/s})^2 = 3018 \,\mathrm{J}.$$ The cat's muscles only had to output one of these two amounts of work. Which one and why? If it's the lower amount, where did the extra energy come from in the ground frame? If it's the higher amount, where did all that energy go in your frame?

e) A golfer wants to hit golf balls further. Would it be better to use a club head 10% heavier and swing it the same speed, or keep the club head the same and swing it 10% faster?

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors

name: Treat this as a one-dimensional problem.
desc: Treat this as a one-dimensional problem. Newton's cradle consists of five balls of identical size and mass in a line and touching. A cue ball (identical to the other balls) comes in from the left with velocity $$v$$ and collides with the ball at $$x=0.$$ Collisions are assumed…
statement:
Treat this as a one-dimensional problem.

Newton's cradle consists of five balls of identical size and mass in a line and touching. A cue ball (identical to the other balls) comes in from the left with velocity $$v$$ and collides with the ball at $$x=0.$$

Collisions are assumed to conserve momentum and energy. One way to conserve energy and momentum is that the cue ball comes to a dead stop, the first four balls don't move, and the last ball in the row shoots out with velocity $$v.$$ Find another solution that conserves both momentum and kinetic energy.

Suppose there are three spheres of masses $$m_a, m_b, \text{ and } m_c$$ such that \begin{aligned} m_a & = 2m_b. \\ m_a & = m_c. \end{aligned} Spheres $$b$$ and $$c$$ are initially stationary. Sphere $$a$$ approaches from the left with speed $$v$$ and collides with sphere $$b.$$ Sphere $$b$$ and sphere $$c$$ are initially separated by a distance $$l.$$ All the masses are in a line and all collisions are head on and perfectly elastic.

Find the time between the first and second collisions of spheres $$a$$ and $$b.$$

statement: Two small blocks, each of mass $$1\,\mathrm{kg}$$ (and negligible size) are in contact with a tiny explosive charge between them. If the blocks begin at rest on a frictionless surface, exploding the charge will cause them to separate with a relative velocity of $$8\,\mathrm{m/s}.$$ The blocks are confined to a smooth frictionless valley with walls that reach a height $$21 \, \mathrm{m}$$ above the bottom. The speed of the blocks at the bottom of the valley is $$20\,\mathrm{m/s}.$$ If you can control the timing of the explosion, calculate the maximum kinetic energy a block can have while leaving the valley.

desc: A ball is shot out of a vertical tube. It normally reaches a height of $$25 x$$ above the top of the tube. A soft lid is left on the top of the tube. When the ball collides with the lid, they stick together and fly upwards a height $$9x.$$ Then a hard lid is left on the top of…
statement:
A ball is shot out of a vertical tube. It normally reaches a height of $$25 x$$ above the top of the tube.

A soft lid is left on the top of the tube. When the ball collides with the lid, they stick together and fly upwards a height $$9x.$$

Then a hard lid is left on the top of the tube. The hard lid has the same mass as the soft lid, but collisions with it are perfectly elastic. Find the height above the top of the tube that the hard lid rises after the collision.

statement:
A bullet of mass $$4 \,\mathrm{g}$$ is fired vertically into the center of a cubical wooden block of mass $$100\,\mathrm{g}$$ and side length $$5 \, \mathrm{cm}.$$ The center of mass of the block/bullet system rises $$2\,\mathrm{m}$$ into the air.

The experiment is repeated with exactly the same parameters, but the bullet is fired $$2 \, \mathrm{cm}$$ off-center. How high does the center of mass of the block/bullet system rise in this case?

desc: A projectile of mass $$M = 100 \, \mathrm{kg}$$ was fired from a cannon. At some point of its trajectory, the projectile exploded and split into two fragments with initial momenta $$p_1 = 36 \cdot 10^3\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$$ and $$p_2 = 24\cdot 10^3 \…
statement: A projectile of mass $$M = 100 \, \mathrm{kg}$$ was fired from a cannon. At some point of its trajectory, the projectile exploded and split into two fragments with initial momenta $$p_1 = 36 \cdot 10^3\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$$ and $$p_2 = 24\cdot 10^3 \, \mathrm{kg}\cdot\mathrm{m/s}.$$ The angle between the momenta was $$\theta = 60^\circ.$$ Determine the ratio of masses of the fragments which minimizes the change $$\Delta E$$ of the kinetic energy due to the explosion.

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: Suppose a rocket, along with its fuel, has mass $$M.$$ Everything but the fuel has mass…
desc: Suppose a rocket, along with its fuel, has mass $$M.$$ Everything but the fuel has mass $$m.$$ Before time $$t=0,$$ the rocket and fuel are at rest. At time $$t=0,$$ the rocket begins to fire fuel out of its engines at speed $$v_0$$ (relative to the rocket). The fuel is fired at…
statement:
Suppose a rocket, along with its fuel, has mass $$M.$$ Everything but the fuel has mass $$m.$$ Before time $$t=0,$$ the rocket and fuel are at rest. At time $$t=0,$$ the rocket begins to fire fuel out of its engines at speed $$v_0$$ (relative to the rocket). The fuel is fired at a continuous rate of $$f$$ (this is the mass of fuel burned per unit time).

a) Write an equation for all the momentum of the system of the rocket and its fuel at time $$t < \frac{M-m}{f}.$$

b) Find the velocity of the rocket as a function of time.

c) Find the maximum velocity of the rocket.

d) Suppose the rocket driver person, who is in the rocket, wants to accelerate up to $$v_0,$$ drift for a while, turn around and return at speed $$v_0,$$ and stop where they began. If the rocket driver person and the rest of the rocket together weigh $$1000 \, \mathrm{kg}$$ (without fuel), what is the minimum amount of fuel required for them to do this?

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: Suppose a stationary box releases a photon of momentum $$p$$. An observer is moving…
desc: Suppose a stationary box releases a photon of momentum $$p$$. An observer is moving towards the box at speed $$v = \beta c$$ with $$c$$ the speed of light. From the observer's point of view, they are stationary, and the box is moving towards them. If the photon is released…
statement:
Suppose a stationary box releases a photon of momentum $$p$$. An observer is moving towards the box at speed $$v = \beta c$$ with $$c$$ the speed of light. From the observer's point of view, they are stationary, and the box is moving towards them. If the photon is released directly towards the observer, the special theory of relativity says the observer will measure the photon to have momentum $$p'_{\text{towards}} = p\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\frac{1}{1-\beta}.$$

If the photon is shot directly away from the observer, the sign of $$\beta$$ is reversed. This is the **Relativistic Doppler Shift**.

Suppose the box releases two photons simultaneously - one to the left and one to the right. The photons have equal magnitude of momentum. Momentum is conserved in relativity.

a) What is the change in the velocity of the box?

Now boost into a frame where the box moves to the right at speed $$v$$ and view the same photon emission event.

b) What is the net momentum of the photons in this frame?

c) The momentum of the box in this frame is $$\frac{mv}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}.$$ What is the change in the mass of the box in this frame from before the photons are fired to after?

d) The energy of a photon is $$E = pc.$$ What is the total energy of the photons in the frame where the box is stationary, expressed in terms of the change in the mass of the box?

__Note to problem solvers: You haven't encountered the Relativistic Doppler Shift, or any relativity, in WOOT so far. However, the fundamental principle you need to solve this problem is conservation of momentum, which you have studied. IPhO and USAPhO will often give questions on topics outside the scope of the official IPhO syllabus, so long as they can be solved with knowledge of topics in the syllabus. For example, IPhO 2018 involved gravitational waves, muon decays, and the Hagen-Poiseuille equation for viscous flow through a cylinder. None of these are on the official IPhO syllabus, but the test gave enough knowledge to work with them to solve the questions. That's something we're practicing here.__

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: The Marble Launcher on an Incline — A cart rolls horizontally at constant velocity. A small spring-loaded cup…
desc: A cart rolls horizontally at constant velocity. A small spring-loaded cup on the cart shoots a marble straight up (from the cart's own point of view). The marble flies up while the cart keeps moving, and the marble falls right back into the cup — a classic demonstration: Now the…
statement:
A cart rolls horizontally at constant velocity. A small spring-loaded cup on the cart shoots a marble straight up (from the cart's own point of view). The marble flies up while the cart keeps moving, and the marble falls right back into the cup — a classic demonstration:

Now the cart is taken to a __frictionless__ incline of constant slope angle $$\theta.$$ While moving freely on the incline (no motor, no friction — it simply accelerates under gravity), the cart fires the marble from the cup as before: "straight up" as seen from the cart, which on the incline means perpendicular to the incline's surface. Where does the marble land relative to the cup — ahead of it (downhill), behind it (uphill), or back inside it?

__(a)__ While the marble is in flight, what is its acceleration? Separately, find the magnitude and direction of the cart's acceleration, and explain where it comes from in terms of the two forces acting on the cart (gravity and the normal force from the incline).

__(b)__ Choosing the right __representation__ is often the hardest part of a problem. Here, tilt the coordinates: let the $$x$$ axis point down the slope and the $$y$$ axis point along the normal to the incline. Write the components of the marble's acceleration and of the cart's acceleration in these tilted coordinates.

__(c)__ Compare the $$x$$-components you found. Where does the marble land?

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: Acceleration Along a Cycloid — A bicycle rides in a straight line at constant speed $$v.$$ A point on the…
desc: A bicycle rides in a straight line at constant speed $$v.$$ A point on the edge of its wheel (radius $$r$$) traces out a shape called a __cycloid__: Here is a cleaner animation of a cycloid (the red curve) traced by a point on a rolling wheel: At what point of the cycloid is the…
statement:
A bicycle rides in a straight line at constant speed $$v.$$ A point on the edge of its wheel (radius $$r$$) traces out a shape called a __cycloid__:

Here is a cleaner animation of a cycloid (the red curve) traced by a point on a rolling wheel:

At what point of the cycloid is the magnitude of the point's acceleration greatest — at the top of each arch, at the "corners" where the point touches the ground, or somewhere in between?

__(a)__ The point's motion is a combination of two simpler motions that you already understand. Write a vector equation expressing the velocity $$\vec{v}_{\mathrm{point}}$$ of the point in terms of those two motions, then differentiate it with respect to time to get the corresponding equation for the acceleration $$\vec{a}_{\mathrm{point}}.$$

__(b)__ Evaluate each term in your acceleration equation. (Useful fact: an object in uniform circular motion at angular frequency $$\omega$$ and radius $$r$$ has acceleration $$-\omega^2 r\,\hat{r},$$ where $$\hat{r}$$ points away from the center; the magnitude can also be written $$v^2/r.$$)

__(c)__ Answer the original question.

__(d)__ Re-derive your answer with no equations at all, by viewing the motion from a well-chosen moving reference frame.

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: A Heavy Ball Strikes a Light Ball — A very light ball (mass $$m$$) is stationary. A very heavy ball (mass $$M…
desc: A very light ball (mass $$m$$) is stationary. A very heavy ball (mass $$M \gg m$$) moving at speed $$v$$ hits it head-on. What is the maximum possible speed of the light ball after the collision? Rather than grinding through collision equations, solve this by changing reference…
statement:
A very light ball (mass $$m$$) is stationary. A very heavy ball (mass $$M \gg m$$) moving at speed $$v$$ hits it head-on. What is the maximum possible speed of the light ball after the collision?

Rather than grinding through collision equations, solve this by changing reference frames. (The __principle of relativity__: adding the same constant velocity $$\vec{v}_{\mathrm{boost}}$$ to every object leaves all forces and accelerations — and hence all the physics — unchanged.)

__(a)__ Boost into the reference frame in which the heavy ball is stationary just before the collision. What are the velocities of the two balls in this frame?

__(b)__ In this frame, the collision is like a ball bouncing off a massive wall. What is the maximum possible speed of the light ball after the collision in this frame, and under what physical conditions is that maximum approached?

__(c)__ Boost back to the original frame. What are the final velocities of the two balls, and what is the answer to the original question?

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: Weighing an Exoplanet — The spectrum of a distant star is Doppler shifted depending on the star's __radial…
desc: The spectrum of a distant star is Doppler shifted depending on the star's __radial velocity__ — the speed at which it moves toward or away from Earth. When a planet orbits the star, the planet's gravity accelerates the star, so the star's radial velocity varies sinusoidally in…
statement:
The spectrum of a distant star is Doppler shifted depending on the star's __radial velocity__ — the speed at which it moves toward or away from Earth. When a planet orbits the star, the planet's gravity accelerates the star, so the star's radial velocity varies sinusoidally in time. Detecting these variations in stellar spectra is how most extrasolar planets are found.

Suppose the star has mass $$M,$$ the observed period of the radial-velocity variation is $$T,$$ and its amplitude is $$v.$$ The planet (unknown mass $$m$$) moves in a circular orbit at distance $$d$$ from the star, and the plane of the orbit contains the line of sight to Earth.

__(a)__ The star and planet both orbit the system's __center of mass__, located at $$\vec{r}_{\mathrm{com}} = \dfrac{m\vec{r}_{\mathrm{planet}} + M\vec{r}_{\mathrm{star}}}{m+M}.$$ Assuming the center of mass is at rest, differentiate this to get a relation between the velocities of the star and the planet, and explain why that relation is just conservation of momentum. (In general, $$\vec{p}_{\mathrm{system}} = M_{\mathrm{system}}\vec{v}_{\mathrm{com}}$$ — the total momentum of a system is its total mass times the velocity of its center of mass.)

__(b)__ The planet's orbit is a circle around the center of mass, not around the star. Find the radius $$x$$ of the planet's orbit (the distance from the planet to the center of mass) in terms of $$d,$$ $$m,$$ and $$M.$$ Then write the planet's maximum radial velocity in terms of $$d,$$ $$m,$$ $$M,$$ and $$T.$$

__(c)__ Combine your results to express the planet's mass in terms of the measured quantities: show that $$m = \dfrac{MvT}{2\pi d - Tv}.$$

__(d)__ Below is the actual radial-velocity data for 51 Pegasi, the first exoplanet detection around a main-sequence star (Mayor and Queloz, 1995). The horizontal axis $$\phi$$ is the orbital phase — the number of complete revolutions, not time.

The measured period is $$T = 4.2293\;\mathrm{d} \approx 3.65\times 10^5\;\mathrm{s},$$ the star's mass is about $$1.1$$ solar masses $$\approx 2.2\times 10^{30}\;\mathrm{kg},$$ the planet orbits about $$d = 8\times 10^9\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the star, and the velocity amplitude read off the plot is about $$v \approx 59\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Estimate the planet's mass, and compare it to the mass of Jupiter ($$1.9\times 10^{27}\;\mathrm{kg}$$).

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: Blimp the Spherical Dog in the Rain — It's raining. The raindrops fall straight down at speed $$v$$ and have…
desc: It's raining. The raindrops fall straight down at speed $$v$$ and have __number density__ $$n$$ (number of drops per unit volume); each drop has mass $$m.$$ Blimp the spherical dog (radius $$r$$) runs horizontally at speed $$s,$$ eating or absorbing with his fur every raindrop…
statement:
It's raining. The raindrops fall straight down at speed $$v$$ and have __number density__ $$n$$ (number of drops per unit volume); each drop has mass $$m.$$ Blimp the spherical dog (radius $$r$$) runs horizontally at speed $$s,$$ eating or absorbing with his fur every raindrop that touches him. Find the time-averaged force the raindrops exert on Blimp, as a function of his running speed $$s.$$

It's often helpful to solve a simpler problem first.

__(a)__ Simpler problem: a sphere of radius $$r$$ moves in a straight line at speed $$s$$ through __stationary__ drops (mass $$m,$$ number density $$n$$), absorbing every drop it touches. Use $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{p}}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ — force is the rate of change of momentum. Find the momentum change per absorbed drop, find the rate at which drops are absorbed, and combine them to get the force on the sphere.

__(b)__ Your answer should have the same structure as the __drag equation__ $$F_{\mathrm{drag}} = \dfrac12 C_D \rho A v^2$$ for an object moving through a fluid of density $$\rho$$ with cross-sectional area $$A$$ ($$C_D$$ is the dimensionless drag coefficient). Identify $$\rho$$ and $$A$$ in your answer, and read off the value of $$C_D$$ for this absorbing sphere.

__(c)__ Now return to the original problem, where the drops fall vertically at speed $$v$$ while Blimp runs horizontally at speed $$s.$$ Change to a reference frame in which you already know the answer, and find the force on Blimp.

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: The Range of Possible Masses — Ball 1, with mass $$m_1,$$ moves to the right with speed $$v_i$$ and collides…
desc: Ball 1, with mass $$m_1,$$ moves to the right with speed $$v_i$$ and collides head-on with ball 2, which is stationary and has unknown mass $$m_2.$$ After the collision, ball 1 is still moving to the right, now with speed $$v_f$$ (with $$0 < v_f < v_i$$); the final speed of ball…
statement:
Ball 1, with mass $$m_1,$$ moves to the right with speed $$v_i$$ and collides head-on with ball 2, which is stationary and has unknown mass $$m_2.$$ After the collision, ball 1 is still moving to the right, now with speed $$v_f$$ (with $$0 < v_f < v_i$$); the final speed of ball 2 is not known. What is the range of possible values of $$m_2?$$

__(a)__ First reason physically, without algebra. The momentum that ball 1 transfers to ball 2 is fixed by the given data — what is it? The collision could be anywhere from perfectly "sticky" (the balls move together afterward) to perfectly "bouncy" (elastic). For a fixed target mass, does a bouncier collision transfer more or less momentum than a stickier one? And does a larger $$m_2$$ absorb more or less momentum? Use these trends to decide: does the sticky case give the largest or the smallest possible $$m_2,$$ and which does the elastic case give?

__(b)__ Analyze the perfectly sticky (perfectly inelastic) case with momentum conservation, and find the corresponding value of $$m_2$$ in terms of $$m_1,$$ $$v_i,$$ and $$v_f.$$

__(c)__ Now the perfectly elastic case. Momentum conservation alone, $$m_1 v_i = m_1 v_f + m_2 v_{f,2},$$ has two unknowns. Get a second relation by boosting to the __center of mass frame__ — the frame in which the total momentum is zero. In that frame, what must a perfectly elastic collision between the two balls do to their velocities? Use the fact that relative velocities are the same in every reference frame to conclude what $$v_{f,2}$$ is in the original (lab) frame, and find the corresponding $$m_2.$$

__(d)__ Check your part (c) result in the special case $$m_2 = m_1,$$ and state the full range of possible values of $$m_2.$$

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: Why Kinetic Energy Goes as the Square of Speed — This problem derives the velocity dependence of kinetic…
desc: This problem derives the velocity dependence of kinetic energy from scratch, using only momentum conservation, energy conservation, and a change of reference frame. Write $$T(v)$$ for the (unknown!) kinetic energy of one sphere of mass $$m$$ moving at speed $$v.$$ Assume $$T(0)…
statement:
This problem derives the velocity dependence of kinetic energy from scratch, using only momentum conservation, energy conservation, and a change of reference frame. Write $$T(v)$$ for the (unknown!) kinetic energy of one sphere of mass $$m$$ moving at speed $$v.$$ Assume $$T(0) = 0,$$ and assume the potential energy stored in a spring is the same in every reference frame.

Two identical spheres, each of mass $$m,$$ are attached to the two ends of a compressed spring that stores potential energy $$S.$$ Everything is initially at rest, and there is no gravity or friction. The spring is released and the spheres fly apart, with all of the spring's energy going into the spheres' kinetic energy.

__(a)__ In the original rest frame: use momentum conservation to relate the spheres' velocities after the release, calling their common final speed $$v.$$ Then write the energy conservation equation for the process in terms of $$S$$ and $$T(v).$$

__(b)__ Now view the same release from the reference frame in which the __left__ sphere ends up at rest. What are the velocities of both spheres in this frame before the release, and after? Write the energy conservation equation for the process as seen in this frame.

__(c)__ Combine your two equations to find how $$T(2v)$$ is related to $$T(v),$$ and conclude how kinetic energy depends on speed. (The full formula, fixing the constant of proportionality, is $$T = \dfrac12 mv^2.$$)

__(d)__ Application: a point-like mass slides on a frictionless surface, bouncing back and forth between two walls, with initial kinetic energy $$E.$$ With every collision with a wall, the mass loses $$\dfrac12$$ of its kinetic energy to thermal energy. How many collisions are needed before the __speed__ of the mass (not its kinetic energy) is reduced by a factor of $$8?$$

lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: Identical Balls Bounce at Right Angles — Two identical balls: ball 2 is stationary, and ball 1 moves at…
desc: Two identical balls: ball 2 is stationary, and ball 1 moves at constant velocity and strikes it. The collision is __perfectly elastic__ but __not necessarily head-on__. Find the angle between the velocities of the two balls after the collision. Off-center collisions are…
statement:
Two identical balls: ball 2 is stationary, and ball 1 moves at constant velocity and strikes it. The collision is __perfectly elastic__ but __not necessarily head-on__. Find the angle between the velocities of the two balls after the collision.

Off-center collisions are characterized by the __impact parameter__ $$b$$ — the closest distance between the balls' centers if they could pass freely through each other and continue in straight lines:

Show that the answer is the same no matter the impact parameter.

__(a)__ Calling the initial velocity of ball 1 $$\vec{v}_{i,1}$$ and the final velocities $$\vec{v}_{f,1}$$ and $$\vec{v}_{f,2},$$ write down the conservation laws that apply: conservation of momentum (which all collisions obey) and conservation of kinetic energy (which perfectly elastic collisions obey). Use the fact that the masses are equal to eliminate the mass from both equations.

__(b)__ One of your equations is a vector equation and the other is a scalar equation. Square the vector equation — take the dot product of each side with itself — and combine it with the scalar equation to find $$\vec{v}_{f,1}\cdot\vec{v}_{f,2}.$$ Conclude the angle between the final velocities. (Recall $$\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = ab\cos\theta.$$)

__(c)__ Now suppose ball 2 is initially __moving__. We can always boost into the frame where ball 2 is at rest, and by the result above the balls separate at right angles in that frame. Does it follow that they separate at right angles in the original frame? Justify your answer by considering an ordinary billiards collision viewed from a frame moving at $$10\,000\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ relative to the table.

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus

statement:
A child of mass $$m$$ is running on a large frozen lake with velocity $$v$$ to the north. Due to friction, the child is able to exert a maximum horizontal force of $$\alpha$$ times their own weight on the ice.

a) What is the minimum time necessary for the child to change directions so that he moves east at $$v?$$

b) What is the shape of the optimal trajectory called?

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: a) Let $$f(x) = u(x)v(x)w(x).$$ Show that $$\dfrac{f'}{f} = \left(\dfrac{u'}{u} +…
desc: a) Let $$f(x) = u(x)v(x)w(x).$$ Show that $$\dfrac{f'}{f} = \left(\dfrac{u'}{u} + \dfrac{v'}{v} + \dfrac{w'}{w}\right).$$ b) Find the analogous expression for $$\dfrac{f'}{f}$$ when $$f(x) = u(x)^a v(x)^b w(x)^c.$$ c) The volume of an ideal gas is given by $$V =…
statement:
a) Let $$f(x) = u(x)v(x)w(x).$$ Show that $$\dfrac{f'}{f} = \left(\dfrac{u'}{u} + \dfrac{v'}{v} + \dfrac{w'}{w}\right).$$

b) Find the analogous expression for $$\dfrac{f'}{f}$$ when $$f(x) = u(x)^a v(x)^b w(x)^c.$$

c) The volume of an ideal gas is given by $$V = \dfrac{Nk_BT}{P}.$$ All of $$N,$$ $$T,$$ and $$P$$ are subject to change based on applied external conditions. Find an equation for small changes in the volume, $$\mathrm{d}V,$$ in terms of $$V, N, T, P, \mathrm{d}N, \mathrm{d}T,\mathrm{d}P.$$

d) What does this result say about the change in $$f$$ when you change $$u, v, \text{ or } w$$ by a small percentage?.

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: You can ignore gravity in this problem.
desc: You can ignore gravity in this problem. In class we saw $$F\propto v^2$$ for drag forces in a fluid. For very small spheres moving through fluid at low speeds the resistive force is dominated by the fluid viscosity. The viscosity is a resistance to sliding layers of fluid past…
statement:
You can ignore gravity in this problem.

In class we saw $$F\propto v^2$$ for drag forces in a fluid. For very small spheres moving through fluid at low speeds the resistive force is dominated by the fluid viscosity. The viscosity is a resistance to sliding layers of fluid past each other, which happens as the objects move through the fluid.

The viscous resistance for a sphere is given by the **Stokes Formula** \ where $$\mu$$ is the fluid viscosity, a property of the fluid that depends on temperature. The force acts in the direction opposite the motion.

a) If a small sphere has initial velocity $$v_0,$$ mass $$m,$$ and radius $$r,$$ find the total distance it travels before stopping, assuming viscous resistance.

b) Find a relevant time scale on which the sphere stops in terms of the other quantities in the problem.

c) Imagine a model where a sphere feels both the viscous resistance force and the drag force $$F_d = \dfrac12 C_d \rho A v^2.$$ Find a dimensionless combination of variables which, when large compared $$1,$$ indicates that the drag force is much larger than the viscous force. You can throw out small constant factors. The result you find is called the **Reynolds Number**.

name: A dumbbell is above a planet like this:
desc: A dumbbell is above a planet like this: You can model the dumbell as two points, one located $$x-\Delta x$$ from the planet center and the other $$x+\Delta x$$ from the planet center, rigidly connected by a massless rod. a) Does the dumbbell accelerate towards the planet with…
statement:
A dumbbell is above a planet like this:

You can model the dumbell as two points, one located $$x-\Delta x$$ from the planet center and the other $$x+\Delta x$$ from the planet center, rigidly connected by a massless rod.

a) Does the dumbbell accelerate towards the planet with greater, the same, or less acceleration than a point mass at the center of the dumbbell would? Answer qualitatively with justification.

b) Calculate the difference in acceleration you thought about in part (a) to "leading order" in $$\Delta x$$. I.E. approximate it with as many terms as are necessary to get something that isn't zero.

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: In a lens system, light goes from the object (source of light) to the lens, then to the…
desc: In a lens system, light goes from the object (source of light) to the lens, then to the image. The distance from the object to the lens is $$o$$ and the distance from the lens to the image is $$i.$$ The light goes via a variety of paths, a few of which are shown here as dashed…
statement:
In a lens system, light goes from the object (source of light) to the lens, then to the image.

The distance from the object to the lens is $$o$$ and the distance from the lens to the image is $$i.$$

The light goes via a variety of paths, a few of which are shown here as dashed lines:

**Fermat's Principle**, applied to a lens, says that the time for each path from object to image is the same.

Consider just two partial paths: one the object to the center of the lens, the other from the object to a point $$h$$ higher on the lens.

a) Assuming $$h\ll o$$, estimate the time difference in light's travel along these two paths to leading order in $$h.$$

b) What shape should the lens take, according to your answer to (a)?

c) Comment on your answer's relation to the lens equation, $$\dfrac{1}{i} + \dfrac{1}{o} = \dfrac{1}{f}.$$ The focal length $$f$$ is defined as a length long enough that light rays approaching the lens parallel all converge to a point $$f$$ away from the lens.

statement:
Suppose the limiting factor for an accelerating race car is its horsepower, $$P$$. The car always accelerates such that the car's kinetic energy increases at a constant rate.

The car is racing a drag race of length $$l.$$ Find the speed of the car at the end of the race in terms of the car's mass $$m$$ and power $$P.$$

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: The Lennard-Jones potential is a model for the potential energy of a system of two atoms…
desc: The Lennard-Jones potential is a model for the potential energy of a system of two atoms as a function of the distance $$r$$ between the atoms. The Lennard-Jones potential is given by $$ V_{LJ} = 4\epsilon\left[\left(\dfrac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} -…
statement:
The Lennard-Jones potential is a model for the potential energy of a system of two atoms as a function of the distance $$r$$ between the atoms.

The Lennard-Jones potential is given by

$$ V_{LJ} = 4\epsilon\left[\left(\dfrac{\sigma}{r}\right)^{12} - \left(\dfrac{\sigma}{r}\right)^6 \right]. $$

a) Find $$r$$ at which the system is at equilibrium.

b) Suppose the first molecule is held fixed and the second is displaced slightly away from the equilibrium point by a small amount $$\Delta r.$$ Find the force on the second atom from the first atom (to first order in $$\Delta r).$$

c) Suppose the Lennard-Jones potential is describing the potential energy when two atoms, one of mass $$m_1$$ and one of mass $$m_2$$, are separated by a distance $$r.$$ What would the angular frequency of oscillations of the atoms be? In your answer, use the variable $$k$$, where the solution to the previous problem is $$F \approx -k \Delta r.$$

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: Near a stable equilibrium, we usually have oscillations and the differential equation $$…
desc: Near a stable equilibrium, we usually have oscillations and the differential equation $$ \ddot{x} = -\omega^2 x.$$ The solutions are sinusoidal oscillations, $$x = A\sin(\omega t) + B \cos(\omega t).$$ However, consider a pendulum that is inverted (pointing straight up) and…
statement:
Near a stable equilibrium, we usually have oscillations and the differential equation $$ \ddot{x} = -\omega^2 x.$$ The solutions are sinusoidal oscillations, $$x = A\sin(\omega t) + B \cos(\omega t).$$

However, consider a pendulum that is inverted (pointing straight up) and rigid. It is balanced in equilibrium, but any small misalignment or any small push will set it falling out away from equilibrium.

a) Suppose the pendulum has length $$l$$ and mass $$m$$, and all the mass is at the end of the pendulum. Find a differential equation for the motion of the pendulum.

b) Approximate the trigonometric terms in the differential equation from part (a) for small deviations from vertical.

c) Find a solution such that the initial angle is $$0$$ and the initial velocity is $$v_0$$. Write the solution in terms of the **hyperbolic sine**, $$\text{sinh}$$ function, defined by $$\mathrm{sinh}(x) = \dfrac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}.$$

d) Find a solution such that the initial velocity is zero and the initial angle is $$\theta_0$$. Also write the solution in terms of the **hyperbolic cosine** , $$\text{cosh}$$ function, defined by $$\mathrm{cosh}(x) = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}.$$

e) In class, we found the velocity of an object falling under gravity and experiencing $$v^2$$ drag to be \ Rewrite this in terms of hyperbolic trig functions.
tags: kinematics and techniques of single-variable calculus

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: A certain gas is made from $$N_1$$ molecules of $$X_2$$, $$N_2$$ molecules of $$Y_2,$$…
desc: A certain gas is made from $$N_1$$ molecules of $$X_2$$, $$N_2$$ molecules of $$Y_2,$$ and $$N_3$$ molecules of $$X_2Y.$$ The only possible chemical reaction is $$2X_2 + Y_2 \leftrightarrow 2X_2Y.$$ The rate of the forward reaction is proportional to…
statement:
A certain gas is made from $$N_1$$ molecules of $$X_2$$, $$N_2$$ molecules of $$Y_2,$$ and $$N_3$$ molecules of $$X_2Y.$$

The only possible chemical reaction is

$$2X_2 + Y_2 \leftrightarrow 2X_2Y.$$

The rate of the forward reaction is proportional to $$\left(\dfrac{N_1}{V}\right)^2\left(\dfrac{N_2}{V}\right)$$ and the rate of the backwards reaction is proportional to $$\left(\dfrac{N_3}{V}\right)^2.$$

The gas is at equilibrium at some pressure $$P,$$ temperature $$T,$$ and volume $$V,$$ meaning that these macroscopic variables are not changing and the reaction is not proceeding either direction on net. These variables are related by the ideal gas law, $$PV = Nk_BT$$ with $$N$$ the total number of molecules and $$k_B$$ Boltzmann's constant.

The pressure is given a slight increase, $$\mathrm{d}P$$ while the temperature is held fixed.

Find the change in volume of the gas, $$\mathrm{d}V,$$ in terms of $$\mathrm{d}P$$ and the other quantities given in the problem.
tags: kinematics and techniques of single-variable calculus

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: A Bead Sliding Down a Helix — A small bead slides from rest along a wire that is shaped like a vertical…
desc: A small bead slides from rest along a wire that is shaped like a vertical uniform helix (a spring held with its axis vertical, so the wire winds downward around a cylinder at a constant pitch angle $$\theta$$). Which of the graphs below shows the magnitude of the bead's…
statement:
A small bead slides from rest along a wire that is shaped like a vertical uniform helix (a spring held with its axis vertical, so the wire winds downward around a cylinder at a constant pitch angle $$\theta$$). Which of the graphs below shows the magnitude of the bead's acceleration $$a$$ as a function of time? (2016 F=ma exam. Assume the bead slides freely, without friction.)

Useful facts: an object sliding freely down a straight incline at angle $$\theta$$ has constant acceleration $$g\sin\theta$$ directed along the incline, and an object moving at speed $$v$$ around a circle of radius $$r$$ has centripetal acceleration $$\dfrac{v^2}{r}$$ directed toward the center of the circle.

On a multiple-choice graph question you rarely need the exact formula. Instead, identify __key features__ that the correct graph must have, and eliminate choices feature by feature.

__(a)__ Should the $$y$$-intercept of the graph — the acceleration at $$t = 0$$ — be zero or positive? Be careful to distinguish the initial velocity from the initial acceleration. Which choices does this eliminate?

__(b)__ The bead's acceleration has two pieces: a __tangential__ piece directed along the wire, and a __centripetal__ piece pointing toward the axis of the helix, caused by the bead circling the axis. Is the magnitude of the total acceleration constant in time, or changing? Which choice does this eliminate?

__(c)__ The bead's speed grows in proportion to $$t,$$ just as on a straight incline. Use this to decide whether the graph of $$a$$ versus $$t$$ rises along a straight line or curves upward, and choose the answer.

__(d)__ The tangential and centripetal accelerations are perpendicular to each other. Write an expression for the magnitude $$a$$ of the total acceleration in terms of the tangential piece $$a_t$$ and the centripetal piece $$a_c.$$
tags: kinematics and techniques of single-variable calculus

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: Zero Acceleration on an Accelerating Wheel — A disk rolls without slipping along level ground, accelerating…
desc: A disk rolls without slipping along level ground, accelerating to the right. Label the quadrants of the disk as in the figure: I is upper right, II upper left, III lower left, and IV lower right. In which quadrant, if any, is there a point of the disk whose total acceleration is…
statement:
A disk rolls without slipping along level ground, accelerating to the right. Label the quadrants of the disk as in the figure: I is upper right, II upper left, III lower left, and IV lower right. In which quadrant, if any, is there a point of the disk whose total acceleration is __zero__? (Slightly modified from the 2017 F=ma exam.)

Facts about rotation you may use: a point at distance $$\rho$$ from the center of a disk spinning with angular speed $$\omega$$ and angular acceleration $$\alpha$$ has, relative to the center, a __centripetal__ acceleration of magnitude $$a_c = \omega^2\rho$$ pointing toward the center, and a __tangential__ acceleration of magnitude $$a_t = \alpha\rho$$ pointing perpendicular to the radius, in the direction the spin carries the point. For a disk rolling to the right and speeding up, the spin is clockwise (as drawn) and the spin rate is increasing.

__(a)__ Explain why the acceleration of any point of the disk can be written as the vector sum of three pieces, $$\vec{a}_{\rm point} = \vec{a}_{\rm disk} + \vec{a}_c + \vec{a}_t,$$ where $$\vec{a}_{\rm disk}$$ is the acceleration of the disk's center, and describe the direction of each piece for the point drawn in quadrant I.

__(b)__ Using only the $$y$$ (vertical) components of the three pieces, rule out quadrants I and III.

__(c)__ Using the $$x$$ (horizontal) components, rule out quadrant II.

__(d)__ It remains to show that a zero-acceleration point really exists in quadrant IV. First show that the points where the $$y$$-component of the total acceleration vanishes form a line segment running from the center of the disk out to the rim, at one particular angle in quadrant IV. (Hint: how do $$a_c$$ and $$a_t$$ each depend on $$\rho?$$)

__(e)__ Compare the total acceleration at the two ends of that segment — the center of the disk and the point on the rim. Use rolling without slipping to find $$a_t$$ at the rim, and conclude that somewhere along the segment the acceleration is exactly zero.
tags: kinematics and techniques of single-variable calculus

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: Tidus, Fundy, and the Roche Limit — The distant planet Tidus is a sphere of radius $$R$$ and mass $$M.$$ Its…
desc: The distant planet Tidus is a sphere of radius $$R$$ and mass $$M.$$ Its moon Fundy is a sphere of radius $$r$$ and mass $$m.$$ Both are made of very stiff, strong material and do not deform due to the tidal forces of each other. Fundy moves in a circular orbit so close to Tidus…
statement:
The distant planet Tidus is a sphere of radius $$R$$ and mass $$M.$$ Its moon Fundy is a sphere of radius $$r$$ and mass $$m.$$ Both are made of very stiff, strong material and do not deform due to the tidal forces of each other. Fundy moves in a circular orbit so close to Tidus that an astronaut standing on the surface of Fundy, at the point where Tidus is directly overhead, feels __weightless__. Find the distance $$x$$ between the center of Tidus and the center of Fundy. (This critical orbital distance is called the __Roche limit__ of the planet-moon system.)

Background facts you may use: (i) two bodies in circular orbit each circle their common __center of mass__, which lies a distance $$x\dfrac{M}{M+m}$$ from the center of Fundy (equivalently, $$x\dfrac{m}{M+m}$$ from the center of Tidus); (ii) in a reference frame rotating with angular velocity $$\omega,$$ a body of mass $$\mu$$ at distance $$d$$ from the rotation axis feels a __centrifugal force__ of magnitude $$\mu\omega^2 d$$ directed away from the axis (in the rotating frame the orbiting bodies are stationary, which often simplifies the analysis); (iii) the gravitational acceleration toward a mass $$M$$ at distance $$d$$ is $$\dfrac{GM}{d^2};$$ (iv) the first-order (tangent line) approximation: for $$\Delta x$$ small, $$f(x_0 + \Delta x) \approx f(x_0) + f'(x_0)\,\Delta x.$$

__(a)__ Work in the frame rotating with the orbit, so that Tidus, Fundy, and the astronaut are all stationary. Using the fact that the astronaut is weightless (so the normal force on them is zero), show that the accelerations acting on the astronaut balance according to $$\omega^2\left(x\dfrac{M}{M+m} - r\right) + \dfrac{Gm}{r^2} = \dfrac{GM}{(x-r)^2}.$$

__(b)__ Apply Newton's second law to Fundy as a whole, which moves in a circle of radius $$x\dfrac{M}{M+m}$$ about the center of mass, to show $$\omega^2 = \dfrac{G(M+m)}{x^3}.$$ (This is __Kepler's third law__.)

__(c)__ Substituting (b) into (a) gives an equation that is a quintic (fifth-degree) polynomial in $$x$$ — hopeless to solve exactly by hand. Instead, work in the approximation that Fundy is small compared to the orbital distance, $$r \ll x.$$ Apply the tangent-line approximation to the function $$a(d) = \dfrac{GM}{d^2}$$ about $$d = x,$$ with $$\Delta d = -r,$$ to show $$\dfrac{GM}{(x-r)^2} \approx \dfrac{GM}{x^2} + \dfrac{2GM}{x^3}r.$$ Why does the correction enter with a plus sign even though the derivative is negative?

__(d)__ Substitute everything into the balance equation from (a) and simplify to show $$x \approx r\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{M}{m}\left(3 + \dfrac{m}{M}\right)},$$ which for $$m \ll M$$ becomes the standard form $$x \approx r\sqrt[3]{3\dfrac{M}{m}}.$$

__(e)__ Could you have predicted, before doing any algebra, that $$G$$ would cancel out of the final answer? Explain using dimensions. ($$G$$ has dimensions $$^3^{-1}^{-2}.$$)

__(f)__ Real moons that are large enough to be round are held together mainly by their own gravity — rock simply isn't strong enough at that scale. What happens to such a moon if it ends up orbiting inside the Roche limit, and what famous feature of the outer planets does this explain?
tags: kinematics and techniques of single-variable calculus

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: Sanity-Checking a Relativistic Rocket Formula — You look up an equation for the distance traveled by a rocket…
desc: You look up an equation for the distance traveled by a rocket with constant acceleration, including the effects of special relativity. If the rocket begins at position $$0$$ at $$t = 0$$ and accelerates at acceleration $$a,$$ the proposed equation for its position as a function…
statement:
You look up an equation for the distance traveled by a rocket with constant acceleration, including the effects of special relativity. If the rocket begins at position $$0$$ at $$t = 0$$ and accelerates at acceleration $$a,$$ the proposed equation for its position as a function of time is $$x = \dfrac{c^2}{a}\left(\sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{at}{c}\right)^2} - 1\right),$$ where $$c$$ is the speed of light. (It's not vital to this question, but the exact meaning of "acceleration" here is: at any given time, someone flying alongside the rocket at the rocket's direction and speed, but not accelerating, would measure the rocket's acceleration to be $$a.$$) Without deriving the formula, test whether it is __plausible__ based on what you know about non-relativistic mechanics and about relativity.

A key tool: the first-order __binomial expansion__ $$(1+u)^n \approx 1 + nu,$$ valid when $$|nu| \ll 1.$$ This expansion comes up constantly in olympiad problem solving.

__(a)__ Check the easiest known value first: what does the formula give at $$t = 0,$$ and is that correct?

__(b)__ Expand the formula for short times using the binomial expansion, and show that it reduces to a familiar result from non-relativistic mechanics.

__(c)__ For roughly what range of times is the approximation in (b) good? State the condition on $$t$$ and interpret it physically: why should relativistic corrections be small for exactly those times?

__(d)__ Find the approximate behavior of $$x$$ at very long times, $$\dfrac{at}{c} \gg 1,$$ and explain why the result makes sense.
tags: kinematics and techniques of single-variable calculus

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: Guess the Solution: A Mass on a Spring — The force on an object of mass $$m$$ moving along the $$x$$-axis is…
desc: The force on an object of mass $$m$$ moving along the $$x$$-axis is $$F = -kx,$$ where $$x$$ is the object's position and $$k$$ is a positive constant (the force law of an ideal spring). Find the position of the object at all times. Background: a __differential equation__ is an…
statement:
The force on an object of mass $$m$$ moving along the $$x$$-axis is $$F = -kx,$$ where $$x$$ is the object's position and $$k$$ is a positive constant (the force law of an ideal spring). Find the position of the object at all times.

Background: a __differential equation__ is an equation that relates a quantity to its own derivatives; its __order__ is the order of the highest derivative that appears. Differential equations on USAPhO and IPhO can usually be solved by __guessing__ a familiar function and checking it. Useful derivatives: $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\sin(\omega t) = \omega\cos(\omega t)$$ and $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\cos(\omega t) = -\omega\sin(\omega t).$$

__(a)__ Use Newton's second law to write a differential equation for $$x(t).$$ What is its order?

__(b)__ What familiar functions return themselves with a minus sign after two derivatives? Guess $$x = \sin(\omega t)$$ and substitute it into your equation: what must $$\omega$$ be for the guess to work? Then point out what is dimensionally wrong with this solution, and fix it.

__(c)__ Write the most general solution. (A fact worth remembering: a second-order differential equation has __two__ independent solutions, so the general solution carries two arbitrary constants; a first-order equation has just one.)

__(d)__ The two constants are fixed by __boundary conditions__ — for example, initial conditions. Suppose the initial position is $$x(0) = x_0$$ and the initial velocity is $$v(0) = v_0.$$ Determine both constants.
tags: kinematics and techniques of single-variable calculus

lesson: PW102: Kinematics and Techniques of Single-Variable Calculus
label: PW102
name: Falling with Quadratic Drag — A sphere of mass $$m$$ and cross-sectional area $$A$$ is dropped from rest and…
desc: A sphere of mass $$m$$ and cross-sectional area $$A$$ is dropped from rest and falls under gravity through air of density $$\rho.$$ The air exerts a drag force of magnitude $$F_a = \dfrac12 C_D\rho A v^2$$ directed opposite the motion, where $$C_D$$ is a dimensionless drag…
statement:
A sphere of mass $$m$$ and cross-sectional area $$A$$ is dropped from rest and falls under gravity through air of density $$\rho.$$ The air exerts a drag force of magnitude $$F_a = \dfrac12 C_D\rho A v^2$$ directed opposite the motion, where $$C_D$$ is a dimensionless drag coefficient (typically of order $$1$$) and $$v$$ is the sphere's speed. Take upward as the positive direction with $$g > 0,$$ so the falling sphere's velocity is negative. Find the velocity of the sphere as a function of time.

You may use this integral, which can be derived by partial fractions: $$\int\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{1-u^2} = \dfrac12\ln\left(\dfrac{1+u}{1-u}\right) + C.$$ Also useful: the first-order expansion $$e^u \approx 1 + u$$ for $$|u| \ll 1.$$ (On USAPhO and IPhO you are expected to differentiate and integrate polynomials, trig functions, and exponentials; less standard integrals like the one above are typically supplied to you.)

__(a)__ Start with the long-time behavior: the sphere speeds up until drag balances gravity and it reaches a __terminal velocity__. Find the terminal speed $$v_t.$$

__(b)__ Write Newton's second law for the falling sphere as a first-order differential equation for $$v,$$ and show it can be put in the dimensionless form $$-1 + \left(\dfrac{v}{v_t}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{g}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}.$$ (Putting equations in dimensionless form is a listed skill on the IPhO syllabus.) Read the short-time and long-time behavior directly off this equation.

__(c)__ The equation in (b) is __separable__: everything involving $$v$$ can be moved to one side and everything involving $$t$$ to the other. Separate variables, integrate both sides using the supplied integral, fix the constant of integration with the initial condition $$v(0) = 0,$$ and solve for $$v$$ to show $$v = v_t\left(\dfrac{e^{-2gt/v_t} - 1}{1 + e^{-2gt/v_t}}\right).$$

__(d)__ Check the result by expanding it for small $$t$$ using $$e^u \approx 1 + u,$$ and interpret what you find. In the expansion you should keep the exponential to first order in the __numerator__ but only zeroth order in the __denominator__ — explain why that is the right thing to do.

__(e)__ For what times is the free-fall approximation from (d) good? Show that the condition can be rewritten (dropping constant factors of order $$1,$$ including $$C_D$$) as $$\rho A x_d \ll m,$$ where $$x_d \sim gt^2$$ is the distance fallen, and interpret this condition physically.
tags: kinematics and techniques of single-variable calculus
