label: PW103
name: A slinky (massive spring of approximately zero rest length) is held by its top and…
desc: A slinky (massive spring of approximately zero rest length) is held by its top and allowed to come to equilibrium while suspended. The bottom of the slinky is $$1\,\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground and the top of the slinky is $$2.5\,\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground. When the slinky…
statement:
A slinky (massive spring of approximately zero rest length) is held by its top and allowed to come to equilibrium while suspended. The bottom of the slinky is $$1\,\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground and the top of the slinky is $$2.5\,\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground.

When the slinky collapses, the coils collide inelastically. The entire slinky has collapsed before it hits the ground.

How long after the top coil is released does the slinky hit the ground?

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: One rope sits stationary in a pile next to a hole with a small length $$x_0$$ hanging…
desc: One rope sits stationary in a pile next to a hole with a small length $$x_0$$ hanging into the hole. Another rope lies stationary in a long laid out line next to a hole, again with a small amount $$x_0$$ hanging into the hole. Both ropes are on a frictionless table and are…
statement:
One rope sits stationary in a pile next to a hole with a small length $$x_0$$ hanging into the hole. Another rope lies stationary in a long laid out line next to a hole, again with a small amount $$x_0$$ hanging into the hole. Both ropes are on a frictionless table and are themselves frictionless. The ropes both have length $$l.$$

a) Find the position versus time for the laid-out rope as it falls through the hole.

b) Find the speed of the laid-out rope when the entire thing has fallen through the hole. (Assume no whipping up off the table, take the limit $$x_0 \to 0.$$)

c) Find the position versus time for the coiled-up rope as it falls through the hole. (When you encounter a differential equation, you can try guessing a solution of the form $$x = \alpha t^2.)$$

d) Find the speed of the coiled-up rope when the entire thing has fallen through the hole.

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: A rope of length $$l$$ is held by its end at the top of a frictionless sphere of radius…
desc: A rope of length $$l$$ is held by its end at the top of a frictionless sphere of radius $$r.$$ You can assume $$l<\dfrac{\pi r}{2}.$$ Then the rope is released. a) What is the acceleration of the rope right after it is released? b) At what point on the rope is the tension at its…
statement:
A rope of length $$l$$ is held by its end at the top of a frictionless sphere of radius $$r.$$ You can assume $$l<\dfrac{\pi r}{2}.$$ Then the rope is released.

a) What is the acceleration of the rope right after it is released?

b) At what point on the rope is the tension at its maximum right after release?

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: A space elevator is a hypothetical long wire that goes from the Earth's surface into…
desc: A space elevator is a hypothetical long wire that goes from the Earth's surface into outer space. Imagine a satellite in orbit, then imagine a rope hanging from the bottom of the satellite. Make the rope longer and longer until it eventually touches Earth's surface. This is a…
statement:
A space elevator is a hypothetical long wire that goes from the Earth's surface into outer space. Imagine a satellite in orbit, then imagine a rope hanging from the bottom of the satellite. Make the rope longer and longer until it eventually touches Earth's surface. This is a space elevator.

a) Suppose the space elevator will be anchored to an asteroid much more massive than the space elevator itself. Find the height above the surface of the Earth that the asteroid must orbit. You can use that the radius of the Earth is $$\approx 6400 \,\mathrm{km}$$ and that a low-Earth orbit (one just above the surface of Earth) takes about $$90 \, \mathrm{min}.$$ You can give your answer in terms of Earth radii.

b) Suppose the space elevator has a constant cross-section $$A$$ and density $$\rho,$$ and that the bottom of the space elevator is under no tension. Find the tension in the space elevator as a function of height above the surface of the Earth.

c) Here is some data on tensile strengths and densities of materials. The tensile strength is given in megapascals, $$MPa,$$ the maximum tension supported per unit cross-sectional area of the cable.

$$\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|} \hline Material & Tensile strength (MPa) & Density $$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{g}}{cm^3}\right)$$ \\ steel & 500 & 7.8 \\ human skin & 15 & 2 \\ glass & 33 & 2.53 \\ carbon fiber & 4000 & 1.75 \\ spider silk & 1000 & 1.3 \\ Kevlar & 4000 & 1.44 \\ diamond & 2800 & 3.5\\ carbon nanotube & $$50\,000$$ & 0.55 \\ theoretical limit of carbon nanotubes & $$300\,000$$ & 0.037\\ \hline \end{tabular}$$

Could any of these materials allow for the construction of a space elevator?

d) We can reduce the demand on the material properties by tapering the elevator, making it thinner at the base and thicker higher up. Find the optimal shape for a space elevator that supports some minimum tension $$T_0$$ at its base.

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: Three Quick Conceptual Problems — Here are three short conceptual problems. Each one can be settled with a…
desc: Here are three short conceptual problems. Each one can be settled with a clean Newton's-laws argument and essentially no algebra. __(a)__ A mass sits on a table, connected to a rope that runs over a pulley at the edge of the table. Hanging from the other end of the rope is a…
statement:
Here are three short conceptual problems. Each one can be settled with a clean Newton's-laws argument and essentially no algebra.

__(a)__ A mass sits on a table, connected to a rope that runs over a pulley at the edge of the table. Hanging from the other end of the rope is a weight that weighs $$10$$ pounds; gravity accelerates both masses (setup 1). Now remove the $$10$$-pound weight, grab the rope where the weight used to be, and pull straight down with a steady force of $$10$$ pounds (setup 2). Compared with setup 1, does the mass on the table accelerate the same amount, more, or less?

__(b)__ A fly sits on your dinner inside an airplane in level flight. You shoo it away, and it takes off and buzzes around the cabin. The cabin is airtight. While the fly is in the air, is the plane lighter — that is, can the wings generate less lift and still keep the plane flying level?

__(c)__ A rod of length $$l$$ and mass $$m$$ is held with one end touching a frictionless table, inclined at an angle $$\theta_0$$ above the horizontal. The rod is released from rest and falls. Find the horizontal displacement of the center of the rod between the moment it is released and the moment it lands flat on the table.

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: A Mass on the Table, a Mass Through the Hole — A mass $$m$$ sits on a frictionless table. It is connected to…
desc: A mass $$m$$ sits on a frictionless table. It is connected to a massless rope that passes through a thin hole in the table; a mass $$M$$ hangs from the rope beneath the table. __(a)__ A student attacks the problem like this: "Let $$T$$ be the tension and $$a$$ the acceleration…
statement:
A mass $$m$$ sits on a frictionless table. It is connected to a massless rope that passes through a thin hole in the table; a mass $$M$$ hangs from the rope beneath the table.

__(a)__ A student attacks the problem like this: "Let $$T$$ be the tension and $$a$$ the acceleration. For the mass on the table (taking 'toward the hole' as positive), $$ma = T.$$ For the hanging mass (taking 'up' as positive), $$Ma = T - Mg.$$ Substituting the first equation into the second gives $$Ma = ma - Mg,$$ so $$a = \dfrac{Mg}{m-M}.$$" This answer is clearly wrong — it predicts infinite acceleration when $$m = M.$$ Yet neither of the two starting equations is false by itself. What exactly went wrong?

__(b)__ Fix the mistake and find the acceleration of the mass on the table.

__(c)__ Now the mass on the table is set moving in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around the hole, with the rope's tension supplying the inward force, while the hanging mass hangs at rest. Work in an inertial frame, where an object in uniform circular motion has acceleration $$a = \omega^2 r$$ toward the center ($$\omega$$ is the angular frequency of the orbit, and the period is $$\tau = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$$). Find the period of the orbit.

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: Tension in a Rotating Space Station — A classic science-fiction design is a circular space station that…
desc: A classic science-fiction design is a circular space station that rotates to create artificial gravity. Suppose a thin circular loop of radius $$r$$ and mass $$m$$ floats in deep space and spins about its center with angular frequency $$\omega,$$ fast enough that a small object…
statement:
A classic science-fiction design is a circular space station that rotates to create artificial gravity. Suppose a thin circular loop of radius $$r$$ and mass $$m$$ floats in deep space and spins about its center with angular frequency $$\omega,$$ fast enough that a small object on the rim experiences artificial gravity $$a = \omega^2 r.$$ Find the tension in the loop.

A free body diagram of the whole loop is empty — there are no external forces on it at all. The forces we are after are __internal__: each piece of the loop pulls on its neighbors with tension. Cutting the loop in half exposes them: the half-loop has a tension force $$T$$ pulling inward at each cut end, so Newton's second law for the half-loop reads $$2T = \dfrac{1}{2}m\,a_{\mathrm{cm}}$$ — but this is stuck, because we don't know where the half-loop's center of mass is. Instead, use the technique of analyzing an __infinitesimal segment__.

__(a)__ Consider a small segment of the loop subtending an angle $$\theta$$ at the center. Find the segment's mass. Then show that the two tension forces at its ends produce a net force of magnitude $$2T\sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) \approx T\theta$$ pointing toward the center of the loop. (Each end tension makes an angle $$\phi = \dfrac{\theta}{2}$$ with the segment's overall tangent direction, since the loop bends by $$\theta$$ across the segment; use the small-angle approximation $$\sin x \approx x.$$)

__(b)__ Apply Newton's second law to the segment. Because the segment is small, its center of mass sits a distance $$\approx r$$ from the center, so its acceleration is $$\approx \omega^2 r.$$ Solve for the tension $$T,$$ and express it in terms of the artificial gravity $$a.$$

__(c)__ The derivation used two approximations: $$\sin x \approx x$$ and $$a_{\mathrm{cm}} \approx \omega^2 r.$$ Is your formula for $$T$$ therefore only approximate? Explain.

__(d)__ Combine your tension result with the stuck half-loop equation $$2T = \dfrac{1}{2}m\,a_{\mathrm{cm}}$$ to find the location of the center of mass of a uniform half-circle of radius $$r.$$

__(e)__ Your tension formula does not depend on $$r.$$ Does that mean we could build an arbitrarily large rotating space station out of any given material? Explain.

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: A Block on a Sliding Wedge — A block of mass $$m$$ sits on the inclined face of a wedge of mass $$M$$ and…
desc: A block of mass $$m$$ sits on the inclined face of a wedge of mass $$M$$ and angle $$\theta.$$ The wedge sits on a flat table. There is no friction between the block and the wedge, or between the wedge and the table. Both objects are released from rest: the block slides down the…
statement:
A block of mass $$m$$ sits on the inclined face of a wedge of mass $$M$$ and angle $$\theta.$$ The wedge sits on a flat table. There is no friction between the block and the wedge, or between the wedge and the table. Both objects are released from rest: the block slides down the incline while the wedge scoots backward. Find the acceleration of the wedge.

Set up coordinates with $$x$$ horizontal (positive in the direction the block slides, toward the bottom of the incline) and $$y$$ vertical (positive up). Write $$a_{bx}, a_{by}$$ for the block's acceleration components, $$a_{wx}$$ for the wedge's horizontal acceleration, and $$N$$ for the normal force between the block and the wedge.

__(a)__ Explain why the vertical forces on the wedge can be ignored. Then write Newton's second law for the wedge in the $$x$$ direction, and for the block in both the $$x$$ and $$y$$ directions. You should get three equations in the four unknowns $$N, a_{bx}, a_{by}, a_{wx}.$$

__(b)__ The missing fourth equation expresses the fact that the block stays on the surface of the wedge. The kinematics is simplest in a reference frame moving with the wedge. (This step is pure kinematics — no force equations — so no fictitious forces are needed.) In that frame, what is the block's horizontal acceleration? Write the equation stating that the block's acceleration in this frame points down along the incline.

__(c)__ Solve the four equations for $$a_{wx}.$$ Competition advice: the algebra here is exactly the kind where sign errors creep in, and many students lose contest points to it — push through carefully.

__(d)__ Check the limit $$M \gg m.$$ In that limit the wedge barely moves, so the block slides as on a fixed incline, with acceleration $$g\sin\theta$$ directed along the plane. Use momentum conservation in the $$x$$ direction, $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(mv_{bx} + Mv_{wx}\right) = 0,$$ to predict the wedge's acceleration in this limit, and confirm that your formula from part (c) agrees.

__(e)__ Check the limit $$m \gg M.$$ What should happen physically, and does your formula agree?

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: The Double Atwood Machine — The figure shows a "double Atwood's machine," a classic problem that also appears…
desc: The figure shows a "double Atwood's machine," a classic problem that also appears in Morin's __Introduction to Classical Mechanics__. The circles are frictionless, massless pulleys; the lines are massless ropes; the dots are masses. The top pulley is held fixed. A rope over the…
statement:
The figure shows a "double Atwood's machine," a classic problem that also appears in Morin's __Introduction to Classical Mechanics__. The circles are frictionless, massless pulleys; the lines are massless ropes; the dots are masses. The top pulley is held fixed. A rope over the top pulley connects mass $$m_1$$ on one side to the axle of the bottom pulley on the other side; the bottom pulley is free to move, but only vertically. A second rope over the bottom pulley connects masses $$m_2$$ and $$m_3.$$ Find the acceleration of mass $$m_1.$$

Take "up" as positive for everything. Let $$a_1, a_2, a_3$$ be the accelerations of the three masses, $$T_1$$ the tension in the top rope, and $$T_2$$ the tension in the bottom rope. (The tension is the same everywhere within one massless rope, even where it passes over a frictionless pulley.)

__(a)__ There are five unknowns ($$a_1, a_2, a_3, T_1, T_2$$), so we need five equations. Write Newton's second law for each of the three masses. Then get a fourth equation by considering the net force on the massless bottom pulley.

__(b)__ The fifth equation is the constraint from the bottom rope. A tempting guess is $$a_2 = -a_3,$$ but it is wrong: if $$m_2 = m_3,$$ the whole lower assembly can accelerate as a unit (while $$m_1$$ accelerates the other way), giving $$a_2 = a_3 \ne 0.$$ The quantities that are truly opposite are the accelerations measured __relative to the bottom pulley__, which itself accelerates at $$-a_1$$ (the top rope makes it move opposite to $$m_1$$). Write the correct constraint.

__(c)__ Solve the five equations for $$a_1.$$ Express your answer using the __reduced mass__ of $$m_2$$ and $$m_3,$$ defined by $$\mu_{23} = \dfrac{m_2 m_3}{m_2+m_3}.$$

__(d)__ Check special cases: (i) $$m_2 = m_3$$ with $$m_1 = m_2 + m_3$$ (note that when $$m_2 = m_3,$$ the reduced mass is $$\mu_{23} = \dfrac{m_2}{2}$$); (ii) $$m_2 = m_3 = 0$$; (iii) $$m_1 = 0.$$ Does your formula behave sensibly in each?

__(e)__ Now find $$a_2$$ — the clever way. Background fact: in an ordinary Atwood machine whose pulley is __fixed__, the acceleration of $$m_2$$ is $$a_2 = -g\,\dfrac{m_2-m_3}{m_2+m_3}.$$ In the reference frame of the accelerating bottom pulley, every object feels an extra inertial (fictitious) force proportional to its own mass — exactly like gravity. Show that in this frame the lower machine is a fixed-pulley Atwood machine with gravity $$g - a_1,$$ and use that to write down $$a_2$$ in the original frame.

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: A Spring Inside a Falling Box — A mass $$m$$ hangs from a massless spring of spring constant $$k$$ attached…
desc: A mass $$m$$ hangs from a massless spring of spring constant $$k$$ attached to the roof of a box of mass $$M.$$ While the box is held stationary, the mass oscillates vertically on the spring with angular frequency $$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}.$$ The box is then dropped and…
statement:
A mass $$m$$ hangs from a massless spring of spring constant $$k$$ attached to the roof of a box of mass $$M.$$ While the box is held stationary, the mass oscillates vertically on the spring with angular frequency $$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}}.$$ The box is then dropped and falls freely under gravity. What is the angular frequency of the oscillations during the fall?

__(a)__ First examine what gravity does to a spring oscillator. With the box held fixed, let $$x$$ be the stretch of the spring beyond its rest length, with signs chosen so the equation of motion (Newton's second law written as a differential equation) is $$m\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2x}{\mathrm{d}t^2} = -kx + mg.$$ Substitute $$\tilde{x} = x - \dfrac{mg}{k}$$ and interpret the result: what does gravity actually change about the motion?

__(b)__ A free-falling reference frame behaves exactly as if gravity were turned off. By part (a), turning gravity off does not change the oscillation frequency — and yet the frequency __does__ change when the box is dropped. What else is different about the dropped box? In the falling frame, no external forces act on the box-plus-mass system, so its center of mass stays put. If the spring is stretched a distance $$x$$ beyond its equilibrium length, find how far the mass $$m$$ is displaced from its own equilibrium position.

__(c)__ The spring force on the mass has magnitude $$kx,$$ but by part (b) the mass itself moves only a fraction of $$x.$$ Find the effective spring constant felt by the mass and the new angular frequency of oscillation. Are the oscillations faster or slower than before the drop?

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: Shaping a Wire for a Spinning Bead — A bead of mass $$m$$ is threaded onto a rigid, frictionless wire. The…
desc: A bead of mass $$m$$ is threaded onto a rigid, frictionless wire. The wire is bent into a shape $$y(x)$$ (symmetric about the $$y$$ axis) and spun around the $$y$$ axis with angular frequency $$\omega.$$ The design goal: the bead's equilibrium distance from the axis should be…
statement:
A bead of mass $$m$$ is threaded onto a rigid, frictionless wire. The wire is bent into a shape $$y(x)$$ (symmetric about the $$y$$ axis) and spun around the $$y$$ axis with angular frequency $$\omega.$$ The design goal: the bead's equilibrium distance from the axis should be $$x_{\mathrm{eq}}(\omega) = x_0\,\dfrac{\omega}{\omega_0}$$ for given constants $$x_0$$ and $$\omega_0.$$ Find the shape of the wire.

Work in the reference frame rotating with the wire. In that frame the bead sits at rest, and every object feels an outward __centrifugal force__ of magnitude $$m\omega^2 d,$$ where $$d$$ is its distance from the rotation axis. For the bead, $$d = x$$ — it is the distance from the axis that counts, not the distance along the wire.

__(a)__ Three forces act on the bead in the rotating frame: gravity $$mg$$ downward, the centrifugal force $$m\omega^2 x$$ outward, and the normal force $$\vec{N}$$ from the wire, which is perpendicular to the wire. For the bead to be in equilibrium, the forces must sum to zero. Using the perpendicularity condition $$-\dfrac{N_x}{N_y} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x},$$ show that equilibrium at position $$x$$ requires $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\omega^2 x}{g}.$$

__(b)__ Suppose we treat $$\omega$$ as a fixed constant and integrate the equation from part (a), getting $$y = \dfrac{\omega^2 x^2}{2g} + y_0.$$ This parabola is __not__ the answer to the problem — but it means something. What physical situation does it describe, and what does it have to do with telescopes?

__(c)__ The shape of the wire cannot depend on $$\omega$$ — it is one bent piece of metal that must work at every spin rate. Use the design goal $$x_{\mathrm{eq}}(\omega) = x_0\,\dfrac{\omega}{\omega_0}$$ to eliminate $$\omega$$ from the equilibrium condition, then integrate to find the shape $$y(x).$$

__(d)__ Interpret your answer: why should $$g$$ appear in the denominator, and why must the wire steepen faster than a parabola ($$y \propto x^4$$ rather than $$x^2$$)?

lesson: PW103: Newton's Laws
label: PW103
name: Pulling a Pulley Across Stacked Blocks — A block of mass $$m$$ sits on top of a block of mass $$2m,$$ which…
desc: A block of mass $$m$$ sits on top of a block of mass $$2m,$$ which sits on a table. The coefficients of friction, both static and kinetic, between all surfaces (block on block, and block on table) are $$\mu_s = \mu_k = 1.$$ A string runs horizontally from the top block, wraps…
statement:
A block of mass $$m$$ sits on top of a block of mass $$2m,$$ which sits on a table. The coefficients of friction, both static and kinetic, between all surfaces (block on block, and block on table) are $$\mu_s = \mu_k = 1.$$ A string runs horizontally from the top block, wraps halfway around a massless pulley, and runs back horizontally to the bottom block, as shown. You pull the pulley horizontally, away from the blocks, with a force of $$6mg.$$ Find the acceleration of the pulley. (Adapted from a problem by David Morin.)

Friction warning: the formula $$F = \mu N$$ is __not__ the general friction law. For static friction the correct statement is the inequality $$F \le \mu_s N$$; friction equals $$\mu_k N$$ only when the surfaces are actually sliding against each other. So before plugging in any friction values, you must determine which surfaces slip.

__(a)__ The pulley is massless, so the net force on it must be zero. Find the tension in the string.

__(b)__ Show that it is impossible for everything to remain stationary.

__(c)__ Show that it is also impossible for the two blocks to slide along the table together as a unit, with the top block not slipping on the bottom one.

__(d)__ Both contact surfaces therefore slip. Find the kinetic friction force between the blocks and the kinetic friction force from the table, and use them to find the acceleration of each block.

__(e)__ The string is inextensible, so the pulley's position is tied to the blocks' positions. Find that relationship, and use it to find the acceleration of the pulley.

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: Imagine two scenarios:, 1) There is a star of mass $$M$$ and a planet of mass $$m.$$ They…
desc: Imagine two scenarios: 1) There is a star of mass $$M$$ and a planet of mass $$m.$$ They are in a circular orbit, and the distance from the center of the planet to the center of the star is $$r.$$ 2) The same scenario, but with a "counter planet" that is located on the opposite…
statement:
Imagine two scenarios:

1) There is a star of mass $$M$$ and a planet of mass $$m.$$ They are in a circular orbit, and the distance from the center of the planet to the center of the star is $$r.$$

2) The same scenario, but with a "counter planet" that is located on the opposite side of the star, with the same mass as the planet. The distance from either the center of the planet or the center of the counter-planet to the center of the star is $$r,$$ and the distance between the centers of the planet and counter-planet is $$2r.$$ Each planet has a circular orbit.

In which scenario is the period of the orbit longer? By how much? If the star is about $$3 \times 10^5$$ times as massive as either planet, evaluate this numerically in terms of the period of the orbit.

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: a) What are the dimensions of Newton's gravitational constant, $$G$$?
desc: a) What are the dimensions of Newton's gravitational constant, $$G$$? b) To within a constant factor, what is the period of oscillations driven by gravity of a planet of constant density $$\rho$$ and radius $$r$$? c) What is this period for Earth? Use $$G = 6.7\times 10^{-11}…
statement:
a) What are the dimensions of Newton's gravitational constant, $$G$$?

b) To within a constant factor, what is the period of oscillations driven by gravity of a planet of constant density $$\rho$$ and radius $$r$$?

c) What is this period for Earth? Use $$G = 6.7\times 10^{-11} \mathrm{N} \,\mathrm{kg}^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}^2$$ and $$M_{\mathrm{Earth}} = 6\times 10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}.$$

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: a) Suppose a very light object approaches a sphere in deep space with speed $$v$$. The…
desc: a) Suppose a very light object approaches a sphere in deep space with speed $$v$$. The mass of the sphere is $$m.$$ The object has impact parameter $$b.$$ Estimate the angle by which the light object is deflected as it passes the sphere. You may assume the deflection angle is…
statement:
a) Suppose a very light object approaches a sphere in deep space with speed $$v$$. The mass of the sphere is $$m.$$ The object has impact parameter $$b.$$ Estimate the angle by which the light object is deflected as it passes the sphere. You may assume the deflection angle is small.

b) A distant galaxy (called the **image galaxy**) is behind another galaxy, called the **lens galaxy**, as viewed from Earth. Light from the distant galaxy is bent by the gravity of the lens galaxy and arrives at Earth.

What would the source galaxy look like in the sky, as seen from Earth?

c) This is a figure from the first announcement of an **Einstein Ring**, the phenomenon described in (b). The numbers on the vertical axis of the figure measure angles in the night sky in **arcseconds**. One arcsecond is one sixtieth of an **arcminute**. One arcminute is one sixtieth of a degree.

Hewitt, J. N., et al. "Unusual radio source MG1131+ 0456: a possible Einstein ring." Nature 333.6173 (1988): 537.

Suppose the distance from Earth to the source galaxy is about 11 billion light years and the distance from Earth to the lens galaxy is 7 billion light years. Estimate the mass of the lens galaxy.

(This is very approximate, because we need to use cosmology and general relativity to understand the expanding universe and the bending of light in a more accurate way; this problem is just a first approach.)

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: In a Hohmann transfer orbit, a rocket begins in a circular orbit, fires its engines to…
desc: In a Hohmann transfer orbit, a rocket begins in a circular orbit, fires its engines to enter an elliptical orbit, continues in the elliptical orbit until it reaches apogee, then fires its engines again to enter a new circular orbit. In this problem, assume that Earth and Mars…
statement:
In a Hohmann transfer orbit, a rocket begins in a circular orbit, fires its engines to enter an elliptical orbit, continues in the elliptical orbit until it reaches apogee, then fires its engines again to enter a new circular orbit. In this problem, assume that Earth and Mars have circular orbits around the sun.

a) Does the rocket speed up or slow down, from the point of view of the sun, in order to enter a circular orbit at the end of a Hohmann transfer orbit from Earth to Mars?

b) Mars is $$1.37\,\mathrm{au}$$ from the Sun. How long does it take a rocket to get from Earth to Mars via a Hohmann transfer?

c) Suppose today is an ideal day to send a rocket to Mars. How long will you have to wait for the next ideal day?

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: In cosmology, the concept of **dark energy** is sometimes modeled by a **cosmological…
desc: In cosmology, the concept of **dark energy** is sometimes modeled by a **cosmological constant** $$\Lambda,$$ a parameter in the equations of general relativity. In the Newtonian limit, of general relativity with a cosmological constant, the force from a star on an orbiting…
statement:
In cosmology, the concept of **dark energy** is sometimes modeled by a **cosmological constant** $$\Lambda,$$ a parameter in the equations of general relativity. In the Newtonian limit, of general relativity with a cosmological constant, the force from a star on an orbiting planet is $$F = -\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} + \dfrac{\Lambda m r}{3} .$$

a) Show that for $$\Lambda > 0,$$ the cosmological term is equivalent to putting uniform negative mass density over a very large spherical volume centered on the star. Find the value of the mass density in terms of $$\Lambda$$ and $$G.$$

b) Cosmological observations limit the value of $$\Lambda$$ to be less than or equal to $$10^{-35}\mathrm{s}^{-2}.$$ By how much would such a cosmological constant affect the period of Earth's orbit around the sun?

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: Suppose an object is dropped from rest (in an inertial frame comoving with Earth) from a…
desc: Suppose an object is dropped from rest (in an inertial frame comoving with Earth) from a distance of 1 Earth radius above the surface of Earth. How long would it take to fall to the surface of Earth? You can give your answer as a fraction of $$\tau$$, the time to complete one…
statement: Suppose an object is dropped from rest (in an inertial frame comoving with Earth) from a distance of 1 Earth radius above the surface of Earth. How long would it take to fall to the surface of Earth? You can give your answer as a fraction of $$\tau$$, the time to complete one low-earth orbit.

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: A rocket is launched from a pole of the Earth with the speed that would be necessary for…
desc: A rocket is launched from a pole of the Earth with the speed that would be necessary for a low-Earth orbit (but due to the angle of its launch, it doesn't go into this orbit). The rocket lands at the equator. You can use the fact that the energy of an elliptical orbit with…
statement:
A rocket is launched from a pole of the Earth with the speed that would be necessary for a low-Earth orbit (but due to the angle of its launch, it doesn't go into this orbit). The rocket lands at the equator.

You can use the fact that the energy of an elliptical orbit with semi-major axis $$a$$ is $$E = \dfrac{-GMm}{2a}.$$

a) Find the semi-major axis of the rocket's orbit.

b) What is the maximal height of the rocket's orbit in terms of Earth's radius?

c) What is the rocket's time of flight?

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: In distant galaxies, we can measure the speed of stars' orbits around the center of their…
desc: In distant galaxies, we can measure the speed of stars' orbits around the center of their own galaxy, $$v$$, as a function of the stars' distance from the center of the galaxy, $$r$$. The function $$v(r)$$ is called a **rotation curve**. a) Suppose almost all the mass of a…
statement:
In distant galaxies, we can measure the speed of stars' orbits around the center of their own galaxy, $$v$$, as a function of the stars' distance from the center of the galaxy, $$r$$. The function $$v(r)$$ is called a **rotation curve**.

a) Suppose almost all the mass of a galaxy was located in a very small volume at the center of the galaxy, but there were still some stars at higher radii we could use to measure the rotation curve. What would the rotation curve be in this case?

b) Imagine the galaxy's mass distribution to be spherically-symmetric, but to vary with $$r$$, so the density $$\rho$$ is a function of $$r$$. For many observed galaxies $$v(r) = v_0.$$ Find $$\rho(r)$$ in this case.

c) Show that for a spherically-symmetric mass distribution, $$\rho(r) = \dfrac{v(r)^2}{4\pi G r^2}\left(1 + 2\dfrac{\mathrm{d}(\ln v(r))}{\mathrm{d}(\ln r)}\right).$$

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: a) Find the force from a circle of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r$$ on a particle of mass…
desc: a) Find the force from a circle of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r$$ on a particle of mass $$m'$$ on the axis of the circle, a distance $$l$$ from the center of the circle. b) By thinking of a spherical shell of radius $$R$$ as a series of circles (of different radii) stacked on top…
statement:
a) Find the force from a circle of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r$$ on a particle of mass $$m'$$ on the axis of the circle, a distance $$l$$ from the center of the circle.

b) By thinking of a spherical shell of radius $$R$$ as a series of circles (of different radii) stacked on top of each other, prove the shell theorem. You may use the integral $$ \int \dfrac{1-x}{(1-2x+a^2)^{3/2}}\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{x-a^2}{\sqrt{a^2 - 2x + 1}} +c.$$

If you want to do the integral over the shell by a different method than the one in this problem, feel free to do that instead.

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: Suppose there is a star of mass $$M$$ at point $$S.$$ A missile is fired from a launching…
desc: Suppose there is a star of mass $$M$$ at point $$S.$$ A missile is fired from a launching pad at point $$P.$$ The launching pad is at rest with respect to the star. The distance $$|SP| = R.$$ The initial speed of the missile is $$v_0.$$ Throughout this problem, if you find the…
statement:
Suppose there is a star of mass $$M$$ at point $$S.$$ A missile is fired from a launching pad at point $$P.$$ The launching pad is at rest with respect to the star. The distance $$|SP| = R.$$ The initial speed of the missile is $$v_0.$$ Throughout this problem, if you find the semi-major axis of an orbit to be $$a,$$ you can give your answers to the questions in terms of $$a.$$

a) What is the period of the missile's orbit?

b) The orbit of the missile is an ellipse with the sun at one focus. The position of the other focus, $$F,$$ depends on the launch angle of the missile; as the launch angle is varied, the position of the second focus travels along a curve. What curve is it?

c) At some point $$Q$$ on the missile's trajectory, the distance from the star to the missile is $$|SQ| = r.$$ What is the distance $$|QF|?$$

d) The position of $$Q$$ depends on the launching angle. For a fixed $$r,$$ what is the largest possible distance value of $$|PQ|?$$

e) For questions (c) and (d), we thought of $$r$$ as having a fixed value. If we think of $$r$$ as a free parameter, the position of point $$Q$$ is a function of both $$r$$ and the launch angle. What is the boundary of the region of space to which $$Q$$ can belong?

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: A Binary Star's Equation of Motion — Two stars of masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2$$ sit at positions $$\vec{r}_1$$…
desc: Two stars of masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2$$ sit at positions $$\vec{r}_1$$ and $$\vec{r}_2,$$ interacting only through gravity. The system's center of mass is at the origin. Newton's law of universal gravitation says the force on one point mass from another is $$\vec{F} =…
statement:
Two stars of masses $$m_1$$ and $$m_2$$ sit at positions $$\vec{r}_1$$ and $$\vec{r}_2,$$ interacting only through gravity. The system's center of mass is at the origin. Newton's law of universal gravitation says the force on one point mass from another is $$\vec{F} = -\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}\hat{r},$$ where $$r$$ is the distance __between the two masses__ and $$\hat{r}$$ is the unit vector pointing away from the attracting mass. The first question of IPhO 2018 writes the acceleration of mass $$m_1$$ in the form $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2\vec{r}_1}{\mathrm{d}t^2} = -\alpha\,\dfrac{\vec{r}_1}{r_1^n}.$$ Find $$\alpha$$ and $$n$$ in terms of $$G,$$ $$m_1,$$ and $$m_2.$$

__(a)__ A tempting quick answer is $$n = 2$$ and $$\alpha = Gm_2,$$ found by matching the given form against $$\vec{a} = -\dfrac{GM}{r^2}\hat{r}.$$ Both are wrong. First explain why $$n \neq 2$$: the given formula contains the position vector $$\vec{r}_1,$$ not a unit vector. How is a position vector related to the unit vector pointing the same way, and what does that suggest $$n$$ should be?

__(b)__ The $$r$$ in Newton's law is the distance between the stars, but the given formula uses $$r_1,$$ the distance from $$m_1$$ to the center of mass. Use the center-of-mass condition $$m_1\vec{r}_1 + m_2\vec{r}_2 = 0$$ to express $$r_1$$ in terms of the separation $$r = r_1 + r_2.$$

__(c)__ Combine the two results to find $$n$$ and $$\alpha.$$

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: Gravity from a Uniform Rod — A thin uniform beam has mass $$m$$ and length $$l.$$ A particle of mass $$m'$$…
desc: A thin uniform beam has mass $$m$$ and length $$l.$$ A particle of mass $$m'$$ sits a distance $$r$$ from the center of the beam, on the perpendicular bisector of the beam (see the figure). Find the gravitational force the beam exerts on the particle. You may use the integral…
statement:
A thin uniform beam has mass $$m$$ and length $$l.$$ A particle of mass $$m'$$ sits a distance $$r$$ from the center of the beam, on the perpendicular bisector of the beam (see the figure). Find the gravitational force the beam exerts on the particle. You may use the integral $$\int \dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{(a^2+x^2)^{3/2}} = \dfrac{x}{a^2\sqrt{a^2+x^2}} + C.$$

__(a)__ Before integrating anything: in which direction does the net force on the particle point, and why? Is its magnitude larger than, smaller than, or equal to $$\dfrac{Gmm'}{r^2},$$ the force the beam would exert if all of its mass sat at its center?

__(b)__ Consider a small piece of the beam at height $$y$$ (measured from the beam's center) with height $$\mathrm{d}y.$$ Write down the mass $$\mathrm{d}m$$ of the piece, the distance $$s$$ from the piece to the particle, and the magnitude $$\mathrm{d}F$$ of the gravitational attraction between the piece and the particle. Then explain why integrating these magnitudes over the whole beam would give the wrong total force.

__(c)__ Using similar triangles (no need to introduce an angle variable), write the component $$\mathrm{d}F_x$$ of the piece's pull along the line from the particle to the beam's center, and integrate over the beam to find the total force $$F.$$

__(d)__ Check the result two ways. Verify that the limit $$l = 0$$ recovers a familiar formula. Then show that as $$l \to \infty$$ the force approaches $$F = \dfrac{2Gm'\lambda}{r},$$ where $$\lambda = \dfrac{m}{l}$$ is the beam's __linear mass density__. (Hint: before taking the limit, factor $$l$$ out of the square root so that one term visibly goes to zero. Compare the result to the field of an infinite line of charge in electrostatics, which also falls off as $$\dfrac{1}{r}.$$)

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: The Suddenly Expanding Dust Cloud — A spherical cloud of dust in space has a uniform density $$\rho_0$$ and a…
desc: A spherical cloud of dust in space has a uniform density $$\rho_0$$ and a radius $$R_0.$$ The gravitational acceleration of free fall at the surface of the cloud, due to the mass of the cloud, is $$g_0.$$ A process (heat expansion) causes the cloud to suddenly grow to a radius…
statement:
A spherical cloud of dust in space has a uniform density $$\rho_0$$ and a radius $$R_0.$$ The gravitational acceleration of free fall at the surface of the cloud, due to the mass of the cloud, is $$g_0.$$ A process (heat expansion) causes the cloud to suddenly grow to a radius $$2R_0$$ while its density remains uniform, though smaller than before. (2014 F=ma exam.)

Use the __shell theorem__: for a spherically symmetric mass distribution, (1) at any point outside the distribution, the gravitational force is the same as if all the mass were concentrated at the center, and (2) a uniform spherical shell exerts __no__ gravitational force anywhere in its hollow interior — even just inside the shell, all the pulls cancel. Consequently, at a radius $$r$$ inside a spherically symmetric body, only the mass at radii smaller than $$r$$ contributes to gravity, and it acts as if it were at the center.

__(a)__ After the expansion, what is the gravitational acceleration of free fall at a point a distance $$R_0$$ from the center of the cloud, in terms of $$g_0?$$

__(b)__ After the expansion, what is the gravitational acceleration of free fall at the edge of the cloud (a distance $$2R_0$$ from the center), in terms of $$g_0?$$

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: Orbital Energies, the Virial Theorem, and Stirring a Galaxy — An object of mass $$m$$ moves in a circular…
desc: An object of mass $$m$$ moves in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around a star of mass $$M.$$ The gravitational potential energy of two point masses a distance $$r$$ apart is $$PE = -\dfrac{GMm}{r},$$ where the zero of potential energy is taken at infinite separation. (The…
statement:
An object of mass $$m$$ moves in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around a star of mass $$M.$$ The gravitational potential energy of two point masses a distance $$r$$ apart is $$PE = -\dfrac{GMm}{r},$$ where the zero of potential energy is taken at infinite separation. (The energy is negative because the masses sit in a __potential well__: they would need to gain energy just to climb up to zero energy and escape each other.)

__(a)__ In a circular orbit, the gravitational acceleration $$\dfrac{GM}{r^2}$$ equals the centripetal acceleration $$\dfrac{v^2}{r}.$$ Use this to find the ratio of the object's kinetic energy to its potential energy.

__(b)__ Your result is a special case of the __virial theorem__: for any self-gravitating system in which nothing flies off to infinity — a planet and star, a star cluster, an entire galaxy — the time-averaged kinetic energy is $$-\dfrac12$$ times the potential energy. Use the virial theorem to express the total energy $$E = KE + PE$$ of such a system in terms of its kinetic energy alone.

__(c)__ Suppose a giant stirs a galaxy with an enormous spoon until they have added total energy $$Q,$$ after which the galaxy settles back into a state obeying the virial theorem. The temperature of a collection of stars, like that of a gas, is proportional to the average kinetic energy. Does the galaxy end up hotter or colder than before? Explain physically what happens to the stars.

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: Speed at Perigee — A planet orbits a star $$S$$ on an ellipse of semi-major axis $$a.$$ The perigee — the…
desc: A planet orbits a star $$S$$ on an ellipse of semi-major axis $$a.$$ The perigee — the shortest distance between the planet and the star — is $$0.5a.$$ When the planet passes the point $$P,$$ which lies on the line through the star perpendicular to the major axis, its speed is…
statement:
A planet orbits a star $$S$$ on an ellipse of semi-major axis $$a.$$ The perigee — the shortest distance between the planet and the star — is $$0.5a.$$ When the planet passes the point $$P,$$ which lies on the line through the star perpendicular to the major axis, its speed is $$v_1.$$ Find its speed $$v_2$$ when it passes the perigee, in terms of $$v_1.$$ (2017 F=ma exam — about the hardest level of F=ma problem.)

You may use the following facts. The star sits at one focus of the ellipse; call the other (empty) focus $$F.$$ For any point on an ellipse, the sum of the distances to the two foci is $$2a.$$ The total energy of an elliptical orbit is $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a},$$ where $$M$$ is the star's mass and $$m$$ the planet's, and the gravitational potential energy at distance $$r$$ from the star is $$-\dfrac{GMm}{r}.$$

__(a)__ Explain why $$|SF| = a,$$ then use the focal-sum property and the right triangle $$SPF$$ to show that $$|SP| = \dfrac{3a}{4}.$$

__(b)__ Write the total energy of the orbit as evaluated at $$P,$$ and again as evaluated at the perigee.

__(c)__ Combine these with $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a}$$ to find $$v_2$$ in terms of $$v_1.$$

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: How Long to Fall into the Sun? — An object starts at rest a distance $$R = 1\,\mathrm{au}$$ from the sun and…
desc: An object starts at rest a distance $$R = 1\,\mathrm{au}$$ from the sun and falls straight in. Treating the sun as a point of zero size, how long does the object take to reach the sun, in years? You may use $$M_{\odot} \approx 2\times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg},$$ $$G \approx 7\times…
statement:
An object starts at rest a distance $$R = 1\,\mathrm{au}$$ from the sun and falls straight in. Treating the sun as a point of zero size, how long does the object take to reach the sun, in years? You may use $$M_{\odot} \approx 2\times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg},$$ $$G \approx 7\times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}},$$ and $$R \approx 1.5\times 10^8\,\mathrm{km},$$ along with the definite integral $$\int_0^1 \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{1-x}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$$ and the fact that one year is the period of Earth's (nearly circular) orbit, $$2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R^3}{GM_{\odot}}}.$$

__(a)__ Use conservation of energy (the gravitational potential energy at distance $$x$$ from the sun is $$-\dfrac{GM_{\odot}m}{x}$$) to find the object's velocity $$v(x)$$ at distance $$x.$$ Choose the sign of the square root deliberately.

__(b)__ You can't integrate the velocity over time directly, because the end time is exactly what you're solving for. Instead, rewrite $$v = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ as $$\mathrm{d}t = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{v}$$ and integrate over the positions the object passes through to find the total fall time.

__(c)__ Evaluate the fall time numerically, in years.

__(d)__ Now re-derive the answer with no integral at all. The straight-line fall is the limiting case of an extremely eccentric elliptical orbit, as in the figure below — note that the sun sits at a __focus__ of the thin ellipse, which for a nearly degenerate ellipse is all the way out at one end, not at the center. Use Kepler's third law, $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{a^3}{GM}}$$ with $$a$$ the semi-major axis, to find the exact fall time as a fraction of a year, and check that it matches part (c).

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: Ranking Speeds on Two Orbits — Two bodies orbit the sun, as shown below. Orbit P is circular with radius…
desc: Two bodies orbit the sun, as shown below. Orbit P is circular with radius $$R.$$ Orbit Q is elliptical: its farthest point $$b$$ is between $$2R$$ and $$3R$$ from the sun, and its nearest point $$a$$ is between $$R/3$$ and $$R/2$$ from the sun. Let $$v_c$$ be the speed of the…
statement:
Two bodies orbit the sun, as shown below. Orbit P is circular with radius $$R.$$ Orbit Q is elliptical: its farthest point $$b$$ is between $$2R$$ and $$3R$$ from the sun, and its nearest point $$a$$ is between $$R/3$$ and $$R/2$$ from the sun. Let $$v_c$$ be the speed of the body on the circular orbit, and let $$v_a$$ and $$v_b$$ be the speeds of the comet on orbit Q at the nearest and farthest points. Which of the following rankings is correct? (2012 F=ma exam.)

(A) $$v_b > v_c > 2v_a$$

(B) $$2v_c > v_b > v_a$$

(C) $$10v_b > v_a > v_c$$

(D) $$v_c > v_a > 4v_b$$

(E) $$2v_a > \sqrt{2}\,v_b > v_c$$

Useful facts: Kepler's second law (the line from the sun to an orbiting body sweeps out area at a constant rate) implies $$v_a r_a = v_b r_b$$ for the nearest and farthest points of an orbit. The total energy of an orbit with semi-major axis $$a_e$$ is $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a_e},$$ the potential energy at distance $$r$$ is $$-\dfrac{GMm}{r},$$ and the speed of a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ satisfies $$v^2 = \dfrac{GM}{r}.$$

__(a)__ Use Kepler's second law to compare $$v_a$$ and $$v_b,$$ and rule out two of the choices.

__(b)__ The points $$a$$ and $$c$$ lie on different orbits, so a sweeping-area argument doesn't directly compare $$v_a$$ and $$v_c.$$ Make an __energy__ argument instead: compare the semi-major axes of the two orbits, then compare kinetic energies at the same distance scale to decide whether $$v_a > v_c.$$ Rule out another choice.

__(c)__ Verify the remaining claim of choice (C): show that $$10v_b > v_a$$ no matter where in their allowed ranges $$r_a$$ and $$r_b$$ fall.

__(d)__ Finally, rule out choice (E) by deciding whether $$\sqrt{2}\,v_b > v_c$$ can ever hold. (Hint: what kind of orbit has the constant speed $$\dfrac{v_c}{\sqrt{2}}?$$) Conclude which ranking is correct.

lesson: PW104: Gravity and Kepler's Laws
label: PW104
name: Three Stars Rotating as a Rigid Body — Three non-collinear point masses $$m_1,$$ $$m_2,$$ and $$m_3$$ at…
desc: Three non-collinear point masses $$m_1,$$ $$m_2,$$ and $$m_3$$ at points $$P_1, P_2, P_3$$ interact with one another through their mutual gravitational forces only. Let $$\sigma$$ be the axis through the center of mass of the three masses, perpendicular to the plane of triangle…
statement:
Three non-collinear point masses $$m_1,$$ $$m_2,$$ and $$m_3$$ at points $$P_1, P_2, P_3$$ interact with one another through their mutual gravitational forces only. Let $$\sigma$$ be the axis through the center of mass of the three masses, perpendicular to the plane of triangle $$P_1P_2P_3.$$ Suppose the system rotates about $$\sigma$$ as a rigid body with angular frequency $$\omega.$$ What conditions must the distances $$a_{12}, a_{13}, a_{23}$$ between the bodies and the frequency $$\omega$$ satisfy? (It is not obvious that a rigid rotation is possible for arbitrary starting positions — the side lengths may need to satisfy special relationships.)

__(a)__ Work in the frame rotating with the system. There, each mass is in equilibrium under gravity plus a __centrifugal force__ of magnitude $$m r \omega^2$$ directed away from the rotation axis, where $$r$$ is the mass's distance from the axis. Measuring all positions $$\vec{r}_i$$ from the center of mass (so that $$m_1\vec{r}_1 + m_2\vec{r}_2 + m_3\vec{r}_3 = 0$$), show that the centrifugal force on $$m_1$$ can be written $$\vec{F}_{c;1} = \omega^2\,\dfrac{m_1\left(m_2(\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2) + m_3(\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_3)\right)}{M},$$ where $$M = m_1 + m_2 + m_3.$$

__(b)__ For equilibrium, this centrifugal force must be balanced by the gravitational pull of the other two masses, $$\vec{F}_{g;1} = -Gm_1\left(\dfrac{m_2}{a_{12}^3}(\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2) + \dfrac{m_3}{a_{13}^3}(\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_3)\right)$$ (inverse-square forces written with position vectors, hence the cubes). Find a solution of the balance equation by matching the terms proportional to $$\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2$$ and to $$\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_3$$ separately, and use the symmetry of the setup under relabeling the masses. What does the solution say about the shape of the triangle, and what is $$\omega?$$

__(c)__ Part (b) found __a__ solution by matching terms; show it is the __only__ one. Prove that if $$\alpha\vec{a} + \beta\vec{b} = \gamma\vec{a} + \delta\vec{b}$$ for vectors $$\vec{a}$$ and $$\vec{b}$$ that point in different directions, then $$\alpha = \gamma$$ and $$\beta = \delta.$$ (Hint: take the dot product of both sides with a vector perpendicular to $$\vec{a}.$$) Explain why this applies here.

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys

name: Answer all the following conceptual questions:

statement:
Answer all the following conceptual questions:

a) Suppose you hang some laundry on a laundry line. It will sag in the middle. The tighter you hang the line, the less sag. How tight does the line need to be so that there's no sag at all?

b) A heavy chain of flexible links hangs from the ceiling. If we pull down on the lowest link, increasing our pulling force slowly, the chain eventually breaks. If we grab the lowest link and yank down, the chain also breaks, but a different link in the chain breaks. Explain why. Is the chain broken with the yank closer or further from the yanking hand than the chain broken with the slow pull?

c) A monkey hangs on one side of a massless rope that goes over a frictionless pulley. The other side of the rope is connected to a bunch of bananas that weighs exactly the same as the monkey. What happens when the monkey tries to climb the rope?

d) A pendulum swings back and forth. Draw the acceleration of the pendulum at various points in its swing.

statement:
Suppose a planet has uniform density $$\rho,$$ and radius $$r.$$ The planet does not spin. You dig a hole straight through the planet from one side to the other, through the center. There is no air resistance in the hole.

a) Suppose you drop something in the hole. Find the time for it to return back to its starting point.

b) Show that the time you found in (a) is the same for a circular orbit around the planet at $$r$$ and explain why.

c) Suppose a hole is drilled straight through the planet, but off-center. Find the time to fall through such a hole.

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: We might model a steel bar as a bunch of small springs, each with a cross-sectional area…
desc: We might model a steel bar as a bunch of small springs, each with a cross-sectional area $$a,$$ a rest length $$l,$$ and a spring constant $$k.$$ In order to make a steel bar of cross-sectional area $$A$$ and length $$L,$$ we would need $$\dfrac{AL}{al}$$ small springs. a) The…
statement:
We might model a steel bar as a bunch of small springs, each with a cross-sectional area $$a,$$ a rest length $$l,$$ and a spring constant $$k.$$ In order to make a steel bar of cross-sectional area $$A$$ and length $$L,$$ we would need $$\dfrac{AL}{al}$$ small springs.

a) The spring constant of a steel bar is $$K = \dfrac{YA}{L}.$$ Find $$Y$$ in terms of $$a,l,\text{ and } k.$$ $$Y$$ is called the **Young's Modulus**.

b) Suppose a pressure $$P$$ is applied to the end of an steel bar. You measure the contraction of the bar, $$\Delta L,$$ the pressure $$P,$$ and the length $$L.$$ What is the Young's modulus? The quantity $$\dfrac{\Delta L}{L}$$ is called the **strain** of the steel bar and the pressure applied can be called the **stress**. The equation you find here is a **stress-strain relationship.**
