desc: A long board of mass $$m_1$$ lies at rest on a frictionless horizontal surface of a table; a box of a mass $$m_2$$ is put on the right end of the board. The box is tethered to a wall by a light uncompressed spring with a spring coefficient $$k.$$ A weight of a mass $$M$$ is…
statement:
A long board of mass $$m_1$$ lies at rest on a frictionless horizontal surface of a table; a box of a mass $$m_2$$ is put on the right end of the board. The box is tethered to a wall by a light uncompressed spring with a spring coefficient $$k.$$ A weight of a mass $$M$$ is attached to the board via a light inextensible cord threaded through a pulley. Initially the system is at rest. There is static friction between the box and the board with coefficient of friction $$\mu.$$ The board length and initial distance between the pulley and the board are large enough that the board doesn't slam into anything.

How far will the box travel before it starts sliding on the board?

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: In this problem you will analyze the longitudinal motion of a linear molecule, i.e., the…
desc: In this problem you will analyze the longitudinal motion of a linear molecule, i.e., the motion along the molecular axis. The rotational motion and the bending of the molecule are not considered. The molecule is assumed to consist of $$N$$ atoms of mass $$m_1, m_2, \ldots,m_N,$$…
statement:
In this problem you will analyze the longitudinal motion of a linear molecule, i.e., the motion along the molecular axis. The rotational motion and the bending of the molecule are not considered. The molecule is assumed to consist of $$N$$ atoms of mass $$m_1, m_2, \ldots,m_N,$$ respectively. Each atom is assumed to be connected to its neighbors by a chemical bond. Each bond is approximated by a massless spring which obeys Hooke's law with spring constant $$k_1, k_2, \ldots , k_{N-1}.$$ The molecule is shown below:

Use the following facts when solving this problem: The longitudinal vibrational motion of a linear molecule consists of a superposition of separate vibrational motions called normal vibrations, or normal modes. In a normal mode, all atoms vibrate in simple harmonic motion with the same frequency and pass through their equilibrium positions simultaneously.

a) Let $$x_i$$ be the displacement of atom $$i$$ from its equilibrium position. Express the force $$F_i$$ acting on each atom $$i$$ as a function of the displacements $$x_1, x_2, \ldots , x_N$$ and the spring constant $$k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_{N-1}.$$ What relationship is there among the forces $$F_1, F_2, \ldots F_N?$$ Using this relationship, derive a relationship between the displacements $$x_1, x_2, \ldots , x_N$$ and give a physical interpretation of this relationship.

b) Analyze the motion of a diatomic molecule $$AB$$ shown below.

The value of the spring constant is $$k$$. Derive an expression for the forces acting on atoms $$A$$ and $$B.$$ Find the frequency of the normal mode. Explain how it is possible for the atoms to vibrate with the same frequency even though their masses are not the same.

c) Analyze the motion of the triatomic molecule $$BA_2$$ shown below.

Find the two normal modes of the molecule and the corresponding vibrational frequencies.

d) The frequencies of the two longitudinal modes of vibration of the $$CO_2$$ molecule are $$3.998\times 10^{13} \, \mathrm{Hz}$$ and $$7.042 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm{Hz},$$ respectively. Determine a numerical value for the spring constant of the $$CO$$ bond.

How well do you think this approximation for the bond structure of the molecule describes the vibrational motion of the real molecule?

The atomic mass of the carbon atom is $$12\,\mathrm{amu}$$ and that of the oxygen atom is $$16\,\mathrm{amu}.$$ The atomic mass unit is $$1\,\mathrm{amu} = 1.660 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}.$$

This was IPhO 1992 Problem 2.

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: Pulling a Rope Wrapped Around a Pole (the Capstan Equation) — A massless rope is wrapped through an angle…
desc: A massless rope is wrapped through an angle $$\theta_1$$ around a fixed circular pole of radius $$R.$$ The coefficient of friction between the rope and the pole is $$\mu.$$ One end of the rope is pulled with force $$F.$$ Find the maximum force with which you can pull the other…
statement:
A massless rope is wrapped through an angle $$\theta_1$$ around a fixed circular pole of radius $$R.$$ The coefficient of friction between the rope and the pole is $$\mu.$$ One end of the rope is pulled with force $$F.$$ Find the maximum force with which you can pull the other end of the rope without the rope slipping.

Friction acts all along the region of contact, so there is no single friction force and no single tension: both change gradually along the rope. The standard technique for a continuously varying tension is to draw a free body diagram of an __infinitesimal__ piece of rope, derive a differential equation, and integrate it.

__(a)__ Consider a generic small piece of rope in contact with the pole, subtending an angle $$\mathrm{d}\theta.$$ The tension is $$T$$ on one side of the piece and $$T + \mathrm{d}T$$ on the other, and the pole exerts a small normal force $$\mathrm{d}N$$ and a small friction force $$\mathrm{d}F_\mu$$ on it. Balance forces perpendicular to the rope, using the small-angle approximation $$\sin x \approx x$$ and keeping only first-order infinitesimals (so a product like $$\mathrm{d}T\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$ is negligible), to show that $$\mathrm{d}N = T\,\mathrm{d}\theta.$$

__(b)__ The rope is on the verge of slipping, so the friction on each piece is at its maximum value $$\mathrm{d}F_\mu = \mu\,\mathrm{d}N.$$ Balance forces along the rope (the tangential direction, where $$\cos\left(\mathrm{d}\theta/2\right) \approx 1$$) to find an equation relating $$\mathrm{d}T$$ and $$\mathrm{d}\theta.$$

__(c)__ Separate variables and integrate your equation. (Useful antiderivative: $$\int \dfrac{\mathrm{d}T}{T} = \ln T + c.$$) Use the boundary condition $$T = F$$ at $$\theta = 0$$ to find the tension $$T(\theta)$$ at wrap angle $$\theta,$$ and hence the maximum pull $$F_{\mathrm{max}}.$$

__(d)__ A practical payoff: you throw a rope over a tree branch with $$\mu = 0.7.$$ Compare two cases — the rope simply goes over the branch (half a turn, $$\theta_1 = \pi$$), and the rope is looped one full turn plus a half turn ($$\theta_1 = 3\pi$$). In each case, how many times larger can the force on one side be than the force you hold on the other side?

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: The Shape of a Hanging Rope (the Catenary) — A uniform rope with mass per unit length $$\lambda$$ hangs…
desc: A uniform rope with mass per unit length $$\lambda$$ hangs between two tall towers, with both ends attached at equal heights. Let $$x$$ be the horizontal direction, $$y$$ the vertical direction, and $$x = 0$$ at the center (lowest point) of the rope. Find the shape $$y(x)$$ of…
statement:
A uniform rope with mass per unit length $$\lambda$$ hangs between two tall towers, with both ends attached at equal heights. Let $$x$$ be the horizontal direction, $$y$$ the vertical direction, and $$x = 0$$ at the center (lowest point) of the rope. Find the shape $$y(x)$$ of the hanging rope. This is a classic — everyone should solve it once!

What's new compared with massless-rope problems is that gravity acts on the rope itself, so the tension varies along the rope. Analyze a small piece of rope extending from $$x$$ to $$x + \mathrm{d}x,$$ with tension components $$T_x$$ (horizontal) and $$T_y$$ (vertical) pulling on each end. Write $$y' = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$$ for the slope of the rope.

__(a)__ Balance forces on the piece in the horizontal direction. What does this tell you about $$T_x?$$ Call its constant value $$T_{x0}.$$

__(b)__ The length of the piece is $$\sqrt{\mathrm{d}x^2 + \mathrm{d}y^2}.$$ Find the mass $$\mathrm{d}m$$ of the piece in terms of $$\lambda,$$ $$\mathrm{d}x,$$ and $$y',$$ and show that vertical force balance gives $$\mathrm{d}T_y = g\lambda\,\mathrm{d}x\sqrt{1 + (y')^2}.$$

__(c)__ That equation alone has too many unknowns. Use one more fact about ropes — the tension always points along the rope's tangent — to relate $$T_y,$$ $$T_x,$$ and $$y',$$ and derive the differential equation $$y'' = \dfrac{g\lambda}{T_{x0}}\sqrt{1 + (y')^2}.$$

__(d)__ Substitute $$u = y',$$ separate variables, and integrate to find $$y(x).$$ You may use $$\int \dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\sqrt{1+u^2}} = \operatorname{arcsinh}(u)$$ (the inverse of the hyperbolic sine) and $$\int \sinh(u)\,\mathrm{d}u = \cosh(u);$$ a USAPhO would likely hand you these. Use the symmetry of the rope to evaluate the first constant of integration.

__(e)__ Intuitively, should the __shape__ of the rope depend on $$\lambda?$$ On $$g?$$ (Hint: hanging two identical ropes side by side is the same as doubling $$\lambda.$$) Your formula appears to contain both — explain how to reconcile this with your intuition.

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: Two Spring Scales and a Pulley — A spring scale (scale 1) hangs from the ceiling. A rigid wire frame hangs…
desc: A spring scale (scale 1) hangs from the ceiling. A rigid wire frame hangs from scale 1, and a second spring scale (scale 2) hangs from the top bar of the frame. A small pulley is attached to the bottom of scale 2. A rope is tied to the bottom bar of the frame, runs up and over…
statement:
A spring scale (scale 1) hangs from the ceiling. A rigid wire frame hangs from scale 1, and a second spring scale (scale 2) hangs from the top bar of the frame. A small pulley is attached to the bottom of scale 2. A rope is tied to the bottom bar of the frame, runs up and over the pulley, and hangs back down, with its free end within reach. The rope is massless, the pulley is frictionless, and each scale reads the force pulling down on its hook. (This is a classic demonstration by Richard Berg.)

Initially nobody touches the rope, it hangs with no tension, and scale 1 reads $$5\,\mathrm{N}$$ (the total weight of everything hanging from it). Now you grab the free end of the rope and pull straight down until __scale 2 reads__ $$10\,\mathrm{N}.$$

__(a)__ Before calculating: the two most popular gut answers for the new reading on scale 1 are $$15\,\mathrm{N}$$ and $$10\,\mathrm{N}.$$ What reasoning leads to each?

__(b)__ When scale 2 reads $$10\,\mathrm{N},$$ what is the tension in the rope?

__(c)__ What does scale 1 read? (Think about which __external__ forces act on the collection of everything hanging below scale 1.)

__(d)__ The rope is not attached to the pulley — it only touches the pulley's surface, where the forces are normal forces (and there's no friction). Explain, by considering the system consisting of the pulley plus the small bit of rope in contact with it, why the rope nevertheless pushes down on the pulley with a force equal to twice the rope tension.

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: The Force on the Pulley in a Half-Atwood Machine — A block of mass $$m_1$$ lies on a frictionless horizontal…
desc: A block of mass $$m_1$$ lies on a frictionless horizontal table. A massless rope runs horizontally from the block to a small massless, frictionless pulley at the table's edge, turns $$90^\circ,$$ and runs straight down to a hanging block of mass $$m_2.$$ The table cannot move…
statement:
A block of mass $$m_1$$ lies on a frictionless horizontal table. A massless rope runs horizontally from the block to a small massless, frictionless pulley at the table's edge, turns $$90^\circ,$$ and runs straight down to a hanging block of mass $$m_2.$$ The table cannot move, and the system is released from rest.

__(a)__ Find the acceleration of the blocks and the tension $$T$$ in the rope.

__(b)__ Find the net force (magnitude and direction) that the __rope__ exerts on the __pulley__. The rope only touches the pulley — it isn't attached — so the force is transmitted by normal forces along the contact arc. Avoid analyzing those directly by using a system trick: treat the pulley plus the small bit of massless rope in contact with it as one system, so the only rope forces on the system are the two tensions where the straight segments are cut.

__(c)__ Find the acceleration of the __center of mass__ of the system consisting of the two blocks and the rope: give the horizontal component, the vertical component, and the magnitude. (Apply Newton's second law to the whole system; the pulley's force on the system is the reaction to your answer in (b).)

__(d)__ Each block individually accelerates with magnitude $$\dfrac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}g.$$ Why isn't that the magnitude of the center-of-mass acceleration?

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: Five Masses Hanging from One String — A single massless string is draped over four fixed pulleys hanging from…
desc: A single massless string is draped over four fixed pulleys hanging from the ceiling. Riding on the string between the fixed pulleys are three movable pulleys, each carrying a hanging mass $$m;$$ the two free ends of the string also each carry a mass $$m.$$ All five masses are…
statement:
A single massless string is draped over four fixed pulleys hanging from the ceiling. Riding on the string between the fixed pulleys are three movable pulleys, each carrying a hanging mass $$m;$$ the two free ends of the string also each carry a mass $$m.$$ All five masses are identical, and all pulleys are massless and frictionless. Find the acceleration of each mass. (Take upward as positive.)

__(a)__ Explain why the tension $$T$$ is the same everywhere in the string, then write Newton's second law for an end mass and for a middle mass (a movable pulley together with its hanging mass). Why must all three middle masses share one acceleration $$a_{\mathrm{mid}},$$ and the two end masses share one acceleration $$a_{\mathrm{end}}?$$

__(b)__ The equations of motion leave one more unknown than equation — the missing fact is that the string has fixed length. Suppose both end masses rise by $$1\,\mathrm{cm}.$$ How much extra string becomes available, how many string segments must absorb it, and what do the middle masses therefore do? Convert your conclusion into a __constraint__ relating $$a_{\mathrm{mid}}$$ and $$a_{\mathrm{end}}.$$

__(c)__ Solve the system for $$a_{\mathrm{end}}$$ and $$a_{\mathrm{mid}}.$$

__(d)__ Now generalize: with $$N$$ movable-pulley masses (and $$N+1$$ fixed pulleys), find $$a_{\mathrm{end}}$$ and $$a_{\mathrm{mid}}$$ in terms of $$N.$$ Check that your answer reproduces part (c) at $$N = 3.$$ (Olympiad tip: even a justified partial pattern — like the ratio of the accelerations — earns partial credit on USAPhO, and a plausible guess costs nothing.)

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: A Ring on a Circle with Two Zero-Rest-Length Springs — A small ring slides without friction along a fixed…
desc: A small ring slides without friction along a fixed circular wire of radius $$R$$ lying on a horizontal plane (so gravity plays no role). Two identical springs, each with spring constant $$k$$ and __zero rest length__, connect the ring to two points $$A$$ and $$B$$ fixed on the…
statement:
A small ring slides without friction along a fixed circular wire of radius $$R$$ lying on a horizontal plane (so gravity plays no role). Two identical springs, each with spring constant $$k$$ and __zero rest length__, connect the ring to two points $$A$$ and $$B$$ fixed on the circle $$180^\circ$$ apart. A zero-rest-length spring pulls with force proportional to its entire length: as a vector, $$\vec{F} = -k\vec{r},$$ where $$\vec{r}$$ runs from the anchored end to the object. Find the acceleration of the ring.

__(a)__ First, a special fact about zero-rest-length springs (false for ordinary springs): the component of the spring's force in any chosen direction is $$k$$ times the component of the spring's length in that direction — proportional to the spring's "shadow" along that direction. Explain why this follows from $$\vec{F} = -k\vec{r}.$$

__(b)__ The ring is confined to the circle, so only the __tangential__ direction matters. Using the fact from (a), compare the tangential force components from the two springs and find the ring's acceleration. (A clean geometric argument: write each chord vector, from anchor to ring, as a radius-to-center piece plus a center-to-anchor piece, and project each piece onto the tangent.)

__(c)__ The potential energy stored in a zero-rest-length spring of length $$l$$ is $$\dfrac12 k l^2.$$ Label the two spring lengths $$a$$ and $$b,$$ and let $$c$$ be the circle's diameter. Use your answer to (b) — and the fact that sliding the ring around the circle therefore does no work — to prove that $$a^2 + b^2 = c^2.$$ What famous theorem have you just proven, and why does it apply to every right triangle?

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: Unhooking Two Springs: Does the Mass Rise or Fall? — Two identical massless springs, each with rest length…
desc: Two identical massless springs, each with rest length $$l_0$$ and spring constant $$k,$$ hang in series from the ceiling: the upper spring (spring 1) is attached to the ceiling, its lower end is joined by a small hook to the upper end of the lower spring (spring 2), and a box of…
statement:
Two identical massless springs, each with rest length $$l_0$$ and spring constant $$k,$$ hang in series from the ceiling: the upper spring (spring 1) is attached to the ceiling, its lower end is joined by a small hook to the upper end of the lower spring (spring 2), and a box of mass $$m$$ hangs from the bottom of spring 2. There are also two ropes, which cannot stretch. Rope 1 connects the ceiling to the __top of spring 2__. Rope 2 connects the __bottom of spring 1__ to the box. Each rope has just enough slack that it carries no tension, but so little slack that it is almost taut. The system hangs in equilibrium. (This setup is a classic demonstration by Richard Berg; it is a mechanical analog of Braess's paradox.)

Now the hook is undone, separating the two springs. After everything settles into the new equilibrium, does the box hang __higher__, __lower__, or at the __same height__ as before?

__(a)__ Before unhooking: find the tension in each spring, and the total stretch of the two springs combined.

__(b)__ After unhooking, describe how the box is now supported, and find the tension in and the stretch of each spring.

__(c)__ Treating the slack in the ropes as negligibly small, determine whether the box rises or falls, and by how much.

lesson: PW105: Springs, Ropes, and Pulleys
label: PW105
name: Transverse versus Longitudinal Oscillations on a Stretched Spring — A thin, light spring obeys Hooke's law…
desc: A thin, light spring obeys Hooke's law (spring constant $$k$$) and has rest length $$l_0.$$ It is stretched by $$\Delta l$$ and its two ends are fixed to points $$A$$ and $$B$$ on a smooth horizontal table, so the spring's total length is $$l_0 + \Delta l.$$ A small weight of…
statement:
A thin, light spring obeys Hooke's law (spring constant $$k$$) and has rest length $$l_0.$$ It is stretched by $$\Delta l$$ and its two ends are fixed to points $$A$$ and $$B$$ on a smooth horizontal table, so the spring's total length is $$l_0 + \Delta l.$$ A small weight of mass $$m$$ is attached to the midpoint of the spring. The weight can oscillate __longitudinally__ (along the line $$AB$$) or __transversely__ (perpendicular to $$AB,$$ in the plane of the table). The transverse oscillation frequency is observed to be $$\dfrac14$$ of the longitudinal frequency. The spring is then stretched an additional $$3.5\,\mathrm{cm}$$ and re-fixed, and the transverse frequency becomes $$\dfrac13$$ of the longitudinal frequency. Determine $$l_0$$ and $$\Delta l.$$

For each kind of oscillation, find an __effective spring constant__ $$k_{\mathrm{eff}}$$ — the coefficient in the restoring force law $$F = -k_{\mathrm{eff}}\,x$$ for small displacements — and use $$\omega = \sqrt{k_{\mathrm{eff}}/m},$$ so that for the same mass the frequency ratio is $$\dfrac{\omega_t}{\omega_l} = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_t}{k_l}}.$$

__(a)__ Find $$k_l,$$ the effective spring constant for longitudinal oscillations. (Attaching the mass to the midpoint is equivalent to cutting the spring into two half-springs, one on each side. How does the spring constant of half a spring compare to that of the whole spring?)

__(b)__ Find $$k_t,$$ the effective spring constant for transverse oscillations. The tension in the spring is $$T \approx k\Delta l;$$ for a small transverse displacement $$y,$$ each half-spring pulls the mass back with the component of its tension along $$y.$$ Also explain why it is legitimate to ignore the extra stretching of the spring caused by the displacement $$y.$$

__(c)__ Form the ratio $$\dfrac{\omega_t}{\omega_l}$$ and write down the two equations corresponding to the two measurements.

__(d)__ Solve the equations for $$\Delta l$$ and $$l_0.$$

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: Answer these conceptual questions:
desc: Answer these conceptual questions: **a)** In the CGS system of units, everything is measured in centimeters, grams, and seconds. Coulomb's law takes the form $$F = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} $$ What are the units of charge in the CGS system? **b)** In the CGS system of units the unit…
statement:
Answer these conceptual questions:

**a)** In the CGS system of units, everything is measured in centimeters, grams, and seconds. Coulomb's law takes the form $$F = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} $$ What are the units of charge in the CGS system?

**b)** In the CGS system of units the unit for capacitance is the centimeter. Suppose you have some two conductors of arbitrary shape - they may be sheets, spheres, cones, lumpy blobs, etc. You think of these two conductors as a capacitor (capacitors don't have to be just two metal sheets). This means that for a given amount of charge on the conductors, there is a voltage difference between them given by $$\Delta V = \dfrac{Q}{C}.$$ If you scale the system up by a factor $$\alpha$$ so that all lengths are $$\alpha$$ times as much as they were originally, what happens to the capacitance?

**c)** If two physics quantities have the same dimensions, do they have to be the same? Do they have to be multiples of each other? If not, give a counterexample.

**d)** Design (or look up the details of) an experiment to measure $$G.$$ Suppose that in this experiment, you measured some masses, but your scale was miscalibrated by $$1\%.$$ All your mass readings were too large by $$1\%.$$ How far off would your measurement of $$G$$ be? What if your ruler was off by $$1\%$$ (independently of the scale)? What if your stopwatch was off by $$1\%$$ (independently of the other two)?

**e)** This is a series of open-ended questions for you to think about and discuss.

You know that dimensions of $$L^2$$ can refer to an area. But where is the area involved in the equation for the potential energy of a spring, $$U = \dfrac12 kx^2,$$ which involves squaring the length $$x?$$

The equation for the shape of a one-dimensional elastic beam is $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d^4\eta}}{\mathrm{d}x^4} = \dfrac{W}{D},$$ where $$D$$ is the stiffness of the beam (its **bending modulus**), $$W$$ is the beam's weight per unit length, and $$\eta$$ is the displacement of the beam (distance it moves in the $$y$$-direction from its equilibrium position, as a function of $$x$$). The fourth derivative with respect to space carries dimensions of $$L^{-4}.$$ But there are only three dimensions of space, so how can we have $$L^{-4}$$ in a formula?

In the formula $$E = mc^2,$$ the speed of light is squared, but what is the square of a speed?

In general, what does it mean to you to say that a formula has some given dimensions? Can you deduce from the dimensions the type of geometric object the formula is about?

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: In question 1e, we introduced the **bending modulus**, $$D,$$ of a one-dimensional beam.
desc: In question 1e, we introduced the **bending modulus**, $$D,$$ of a one-dimensional beam. Suppose you place a beam across two supports and push down in the middle. The beam will deflect an amount $$y.$$ a) Find a formula (up to a constant) for the amount of deflection, $$y.$$ b)…
statement:
In question 1e, we introduced the **bending modulus**, $$D,$$ of a one-dimensional beam.

Suppose you place a beam across two supports and push down in the middle. The beam will deflect an amount $$y.$$

a) Find a formula (up to a constant) for the amount of deflection, $$y.$$

b) The bending modulus is determined by the beam's Young's modulus $$Y$$ (see Homework 5, Short Problem 4), and the width $$w$$ and height $$h$$ of its cross-section. Find a formula for $$D$$ in terms of these variables.

c) Comment briefly on how your result in (b) relates to why I-beams are used in construction instead of solid square beams.

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: Suppose mass 1 with mass $$m$$ is sitting on a frictionless table. The mass is attached…
desc: Suppose mass 1 with mass $$m$$ is sitting on a frictionless table. The mass is attached to a string, which goes through a hole in the table and is connected to another mass 2 with mass $$M$$ which is hanging. This is the same scenario we analyzed near the beginning of class 3…
statement:
Suppose mass 1 with mass $$m$$ is sitting on a frictionless table. The mass is attached to a string, which goes through a hole in the table and is connected to another mass 2 with mass $$M$$ which is hanging. This is the same scenario we analyzed near the beginning of class 3.

There, we found the acceleration of $$m$$ assuming both masses begin at rest (with the string taught) and we found the period of a circular orbit of mass 1 to be $$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{Mg}{rm}}.$$

Suppose we give mass 1 a horizontal push, but push slightly too hard to send it into a perfect circular orbit. Then $$r$$, the distance between mass 1 and the hole in the table, will oscillate over time. Using dimensional analysis, what can you say about the frequency of these oscillations?

(Optional) For an extra challenge, find the frequency of small oscillations exactly (in the limit of small oscillations) with a direct analysis (not dimensional analysis).

label: PW106
name: Suppose there were tiny people about 3 inches tall, like those described in the…
desc: Suppose there were tiny people about 3 inches tall, like those described in the children's book __The Borrowers__. a) What would a comfortable walking speed be for such a person? b) How much weight could a tiny person lift? c) How high could a tiny person jump?

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: a) Suppose a sphere of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ moves through fluid with density…
desc: a) Suppose a sphere of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ moves through fluid with density $$\rho$$ and viscosity $$\mu$$ at speed $$v.$$ What does dimensional analysis tell you about the force on the sphere? Connect what you found to what you already know about the force on the sphere…
statement:
a) Suppose a sphere of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ moves through fluid with density $$\rho$$ and viscosity $$\mu$$ at speed $$v.$$

What does dimensional analysis tell you about the force on the sphere? Connect what you found to what you already know about the force on the sphere in these conditions.

b) In order to study the motion of flies, a lab at Caltech built a large mechanical version of a fly on which they could measure the forces.

__image: Dickinson lab__

Suppose the fly is in fluid 1000 times as dense as air and with viscosity $$10^5$$ times greater. The fly itself has a wingspan 50 times that of an actual fly.

If a real fly beats its wings 200 times per second, how many times per second should the model beat its wings to have fluid flow around the fly's wings in the same patterns?

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: A **Helmholtz resonator** is a roughly-spherical bottle with a "neck". A common household…
desc: A **Helmholtz resonator** is a roughly-spherical bottle with a "neck". A common household version is an empty glass bottle with a thinned neck at the top. You can blow across the opening horizontally to make a musical note. Helmholtz constructed resonators that look like this…
statement:
A **Helmholtz resonator** is a roughly-spherical bottle with a "neck". A common household version is an empty glass bottle with a thinned neck at the top. You can blow across the opening horizontally to make a musical note.

Helmholtz constructed resonators that look like this:

By Stephencdickson - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=67566287

When you blow across the neck, the air in the neck oscillates up and down, compressing and expanding the air in the spherical part of the bottle, which acts like a spring. The air in the neck acts like a mass on that spring. The frequency of oscillations is usually in the audible range, so these resonators each play a single note.

a) Assuming Helmholtz's cylinders were similar to each other but simply scaled up or down, how did the frequency depend on the scale factor $$\alpha?$$ (If $$\alpha = 2,$$ the sphere has twice the radius of a reference resonator.)

b) Suppose the sphere had radius $$r$$ and the neck was a cylinder of length $$l$$ and area $$A.$$ Try to find a formula for the frequency of the pitch generated by the oscillator. You will find that dimensional analysis alone cannot find the formula. What are at least two candidates?

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: a) Use dimensional analysis to estimate the speed of a gravity-driven water wave of…
desc: a) Use dimensional analysis to estimate the speed of a gravity-driven water wave of length $$\lambda$$ traveling through the ocean (very deep compared to $$\lambda.$$) b) Use dimensional analysis to estimate the speed of a short water wave with wavelength $$\lambda.$$ (Short…
statement:
a) Use dimensional analysis to estimate the speed of a gravity-driven water wave of length $$\lambda$$ traveling through the ocean (very deep compared to $$\lambda.$$)

b) Use dimensional analysis to estimate the speed of a short water wave with wavelength $$\lambda.$$ (Short compared to the characteristic length scale at which gravity and surface tension balance, discussed in class.)

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: In 1899, Max Planck suggested a system of units based on five physical constants: [*] The…
desc: In 1899, Max Planck suggested a system of units based on five physical constants: [*] The speed of light, $$c = 3\times10^8 \,\mathrm{m/s}$$ [*] Newton's gravitational constant, $$G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \,\mathrm{m^3 kg^{-1} s^{-2}}$$ [*] The reduced Planck's constant, $$\hbar…
statement:
In 1899, Max Planck suggested a system of units based on five physical constants: [*] The speed of light, $$c = 3\times10^8 \,\mathrm{m/s}$$ [*] Newton's gravitational constant, $$G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \,\mathrm{m^3 kg^{-1} s^{-2}}$$ [*] The reduced Planck's constant, $$\hbar = 1.054\times 10^{-34} \mathrm{J\cdot s}$$ [*] The Coulomb constant $$k_e = 8.988\times 10^9 \,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^3 s^{-2} C^{-2} }$$ [*] The Boltzmann constant $$k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\, \mathrm{J/K}$$

a) Planck found a unique length, the Planck length, that was a combination of these five fundamental constants. What combination gives the Planck length? What does the Planck length evaluate to in SI units?

b) Repeat (a) for the Planck time.

c) Repeat for the Planck mass.

d) Repeat for the Planck temperature.

e) Repeat for the Planck charge. You have now found a system of units called **Planck units** or **natural units**.

f) What is the speed of light in Planck units? What is $$G$$ in Planck units?

g) In his book __Fantastic Realities__, physicist Frank Wilczek wrote,

What do you think he meant by this, and how is it related to the work you did here?

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: The speed of sound in a material is set by the stiffness of the material and its density…
desc: The speed of sound in a material is set by the stiffness of the material and its density. The stiffness, in turn, depends on the energy involved in pushing the atoms of the material closer together. A good material to work with is a very pure diamond, since this consists of a…
statement:
The speed of sound in a material is set by the stiffness of the material and its density. The stiffness, in turn, depends on the energy involved in pushing the atoms of the material closer together.

A good material to work with is a very pure diamond, since this consists of a single atom in a lattice, a very simple material.

a) What fundamental constants do you expect to affect the sound speed in diamond?

b) How much can you learn about the sound speed from dimensional analysis alone?

c) Guess a formula for the sound speed in diamond in terms of fundamental constants. Justify the guess you made by appealing to other formulas you know or other physics knowledge.

d) Check your formula against the measured value of $$12\,000\,\mathrm{m/s}.$$ (You may look up any constants you need.)

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: A cubical crystal has density $$\rho,$$ side length $$s,$$ and **bulk modulus** $$B.$$…
desc: A cubical crystal has density $$\rho,$$ side length $$s,$$ and **bulk modulus** $$B.$$ The bulk modulus is the pressure needed to squeeze the crystal down to a significantly-smaller size. More precisely, if we subject the crystal to pressure, it will get smaller. The volume…
statement:
A cubical crystal has density $$\rho,$$ side length $$s,$$ and **bulk modulus** $$B.$$ The bulk modulus is the pressure needed to squeeze the crystal down to a significantly-smaller size. More precisely, if we subject the crystal to pressure, it will get smaller. The volume change obeys $$\Delta V = \dfrac{VP}{B}$$ for small pressures.

a) Find the frequency of oscillations of crystal (entire crystal grows and shrinks), up to a constant factor.

b) Quartz crystals for watches are designed to have a frequency of $$2^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}.$$ The bulk modulus of quartz is about $$38\,\mathrm{GPa}.$$ ($$1\,\mathrm{GPa}$$, or **gigapascal**, is $$10^9 \,\mathrm{N \, m^{-2}}.$$ Quartz is basically the same stuff as sand. About how large is the quartz crystal in a clock?

c) Estimate the speed of sound in quartz.

d) Review your work in (c) and compare it to your work from the problem on speed of sound in materials elsewhere on this problem set (solve that problem first.) Find a formula for the bulk modulus in terms of fundamental constants.

e) Use your formula from (d) to estimate the bulk modulus of quartz. How well does your answer agree with the value given in part (b)?

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: A Ball Orbiting in a Cone — A small solid ball of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r$$ rolls without slipping around…
desc: A small solid ball of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r$$ rolls without slipping around the inside of a cone whose axis is vertical and whose apex points down. The half-angle of the cone, measured from the axis to the wall, is $$\theta.$$ The ball circles the axis in a horizontal orbit…
statement:
A small solid ball of mass $$m$$ and radius $$r$$ rolls without slipping around the inside of a cone whose axis is vertical and whose apex points down. The half-angle of the cone, measured from the axis to the wall, is $$\theta.$$ The ball circles the axis in a horizontal orbit of radius $$R$$ (measured from the axis to the ball) with angular frequency $$\omega.$$

Solving this with a full mechanics analysis is fairly tough: friction both holds the ball up and supplies the torque that keeps it rolling, while a normal force provides centripetal acceleration. Instead, see how much __dimensional analysis__ alone can say. Write dimensions in brackets, using $$\mathrm{M}$$ (mass), $$\mathrm{L}$$ (length), and $$\mathrm{T}$$ (time); for example $$[\omega] = \mathrm{T}^{-1},$$ $$ = \mathrm{L\cdot T^{-2}},$$ and $$ = \mathrm{L}.$$

__(a)__ What are the dimensions of the angle $$\theta?$$ Then assume the answer has the form $$\omega = g^\alpha R^\beta \theta^\gamma,$$ substitute the dimensions of each variable into both sides, and match the powers of $$\mathrm{T}$$ and $$\mathrm{L}$$ to find $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta.$$

__(b)__ Explain why dimensional analysis can never determine $$\gamma$$ — and in fact why $$\theta$$ need not enter as a power law at all. Conclude that the most honest statement is $$\omega = c\,\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R}}\,f(\theta)$$ for some unknown dimensionless constant $$c$$ and unknown function $$f.$$

__(c)__ Why is it safe to leave the ball's mass $$m$$ out of the list of variables for $$\omega?$$ Name a physical quantity in this problem that __would__ have to depend on $$m,$$ and find its proportionality to $$m$$ without doing any further analysis.

__(d)__ Is leaving out the ball's radius $$r$$ justified on dimensional grounds? If not, write the fullest honest form of the answer using $$c,$$ $$f,$$ and the variables $$g,$$ $$R,$$ $$\theta,$$ and $$r.$$

__(e)__ Suppose the apparatus is a $$\dfrac{1}{20}$$-scale model of an upcoming art installation, and the full-size version scales every length up by a factor of $$20$$ while keeping all shapes (and $$\theta$$) the same. If the model's ball orbits at angular frequency $$\omega,$$ what is the angular frequency of the full-size version, even though $$c$$ and $$f$$ are unknown?

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: Toppling Dominoes on Another Planet — A row of toppling dominoes can be considered to have a propagation…
desc: A row of toppling dominoes can be considered to have a propagation speed equal to the spacing $$\ell$$ between adjacent dominoes divided by the time $$t$$ between successive collisions. When the first domino is given a minimal push, just large enough to topple it and start a…
statement:
A row of toppling dominoes can be considered to have a propagation speed equal to the spacing $$\ell$$ between adjacent dominoes divided by the time $$t$$ between successive collisions. When the first domino is given a minimal push, just large enough to topple it and start a chain reaction, the propagation speed increases with each domino but approaches an asymptotic speed $$v.$$ Now suppose there is a row of dominoes on another planet. These dominoes have the same density as the original ones but are twice as tall, twice as wide, and twice as thick, and they are placed with spacing $$2\ell.$$ This row topples with the __same__ asymptotic speed $$v.$$ What is the local gravitational acceleration on that planet? (Adapted from a USAPhO problem.)

A useful tool here is the __Buckingham Pi theorem__: if a situation involves $$N$$ variables and $$D$$ different dimensions are needed to describe them, then exactly $$N - D$$ independent dimensionless products can be formed from the variables. When there is just __one__ such product, it can be set equal to an unknown constant — there are no variables left over to put on the other side of the equation.

__(a)__ The candidate variables are the asymptotic speed $$v,$$ the spacing $$\ell,$$ the collision time $$t,$$ the dominoes' height, width, and thickness, their density $$\rho,$$ and the gravitational acceleration $$g.$$ Explain why $$t$$ and the three domino dimensions can all be dropped from the analysis.

__(b)__ The remaining variables have dimensions $$ = \mathrm{L\cdot T^{-1}},$$ $$[\ell] = \mathrm{L},$$ $$ = \mathrm{L\cdot T^{-2}},$$ and $$[\rho] = \mathrm{M\cdot L^{-3}}.$$ Which variable can be eliminated immediately, and why?

__(c)__ Apply the Buckingham Pi theorem to the variables that remain: how many independent dimensionless products are there? Find one, and explain why it may be set equal to a constant. (Also: why does writing a second equation like $$\dfrac{v^2}{\ell g} = c_1\,\dfrac{\ell g}{v^2}$$ add nothing new?)

__(d)__ Use your dimensionless product to find the gravitational acceleration on the other planet in terms of $$g,$$ the gravitational acceleration where the original dominoes were toppled.

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: Maxwell and the Viscosity of a Gas — James Clerk Maxwell was a founder of __kinetic theory__, the study of…
desc: James Clerk Maxwell was a founder of __kinetic theory__, the study of the motion of the individual molecules in a gas. From 1860 to 1866 he studied the __viscosity__ of gases — a fluid's resistance to having adjacent layers move at different speeds — both theoretically and…
statement:
James Clerk Maxwell was a founder of __kinetic theory__, the study of the motion of the individual molecules in a gas. From 1860 to 1866 he studied the __viscosity__ of gases — a fluid's resistance to having adjacent layers move at different speeds — both theoretically and experimentally, using a stack of plates suspended in gas:

A schematic version of such an experiment: two circular plates of radius $$R$$ are separated by a gap $$h$$ filled with gas. The bottom plate is stationary and the top plate spins at angular frequency $$\omega.$$ Gas right next to a surface sticks to it, so the gas at the bottom plate is at rest, the gas at the top plate rotates at $$\omega,$$ and in between the rotation rate increases with height — horizontal layers of gas slip past one another, resisted by viscosity.

Take as given that keeping the top plate spinning at $$\omega$$ requires a constant torque $$\tau = \dfrac{\pi \mu \omega R^4}{2h},$$ where $$\mu$$ is the viscosity of the gas.

__(a)__ Imagine supplying that torque by pushing with a force $$F$$ on the rim of the plate (so $$\tau = FR$$), and write $$A = \pi R^2$$ for the plate's area and $$v = \omega R$$ for the rim speed. Show that $$\dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{\mu v}{2h},$$ with no $$R$$ remaining. The viscous force per unit area is proportional to the slip speed, $$F_{\rm viscous} \propto v$$ — compare this with kinetic friction ($$F \propto v^0$$) and aerodynamic drag ($$F \propto v^2$$).

__(b)__ Use the relation from part (a) to find the dimensions of $$\mu$$ in terms of $$\mathrm{M},$$ $$\mathrm{L},$$ and $$\mathrm{T}.$$

__(c)__ Viscosity is a property of the gas itself, not of any one apparatus, so a formula for $$\mu$$ should use only __intensive__ variables — quantities describing the gas as a fluid, unchanged by having more or less of it. These are: $$m,$$ the mass per molecule ($$ = \mathrm{M}$$); $$n,$$ the number density of molecules ($$ = \mathrm{L^{-3}}$$); $$v,$$ the mean molecular speed ($$ = \mathrm{L\cdot T^{-1}}$$); and $$r,$$ the radius of a molecule ($$ = \mathrm{L}$$). The Buckingham Pi theorem says that $$N$$ variables built from $$D$$ dimensions admit $$N - D$$ independent dimensionless products. For the five variables $$\mu, m, n, v, r,$$ how many independent dimensionless products are there?

__(d)__ Find two independent dimensionless products $$\Pi_1$$ (containing $$\mu$$) and $$\Pi_2$$ (containing neither mass nor time). The most general relation between them is $$\Pi_1 = f(\Pi_2)$$ for an unknown function $$f.$$ Use this to write a formula for $$\mu,$$ specified as far as dimensional analysis allows.

__(e)__ Maxwell predicted theoretically — and then confirmed by experiment — the "curious result" that $$\mu \propto n^0$$: pumping gas into or out of the gap leaves the viscosity unchanged. Use this fact to finish the formula for $$\mu$$ up to a dimensionless constant. (Careful: you may not simply delete the $$n$$ inside $$f$$ and keep the rest of its argument.)

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: The Accidental Slow-Motion Video — You take videos of physics experiments, and you have taught a friend to…
desc: You take videos of physics experiments, and you have taught a friend to use tracking software to extract the acceleration of objects in your videos. One day you record a video in slow motion — played back at $$\dfrac{1}{10}$$ of normal speed — and send it to your friend, but…
statement:
You take videos of physics experiments, and you have taught a friend to use tracking software to extract the acceleration of objects in your videos. One day you record a video in slow motion — played back at $$\dfrac{1}{10}$$ of normal speed — and send it to your friend, but forget to mention that it is slow motion. The acceleration your friend reports will therefore be wrong. By what factor must you adjust their reported acceleration to recover the real-life acceleration?

For example, you might want to know how violently this toilet exploded:

__(a)__ Suppose you receive an unlabeled video like this and want to detect for yourself how slowed-down it is. Nothing in the video states the frame rate. What visible feature of such a video provides a known __time__ standard, and what provides a known __distance__ scale?

__(b)__ If the video plays at $$\dfrac{1}{10}$$ normal speed, by what factor are all the velocities your friend measures too large or too small?

__(c)__ By what factor is the reported acceleration off, and what factor should you multiply it by?

__(d)__ Generalize using the finite-difference estimate of acceleration: if an object is at positions $$y_1,$$ $$y_2,$$ $$y_3$$ at three moments separated by equal time steps $$\Delta t,$$ then $$a_y = \dfrac{y_3 - 2y_2 + y_1}{\Delta t^2}.$$ Show that if the time step used in the analysis is too large by a factor $$\alpha$$ (i.e. $$\Delta t' = \alpha\,\Delta t$$), the computed acceleration is wrong by the factor $$\alpha^{-2}$$ — and explain why __any__ formula for acceleration built from measured lengths and times must misbehave by exactly this factor. Connect this to the dimensions of acceleration.

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: Why the Log Eiffel Tower Collapses — You build a small model of the Eiffel Tower out of toothpicks and…
desc: You build a small model of the Eiffel Tower out of toothpicks and Elmer's glue, like this one: Encouraged by your success, you decide to build a life-size version out of giant logs and the same Elmer's glue, scaling everything up exactly: the logs have the same density and shape…
statement:
You build a small model of the Eiffel Tower out of toothpicks and Elmer's glue, like this one:

Encouraged by your success, you decide to build a life-size version out of giant logs and the same Elmer's glue, scaling everything up exactly: the logs have the same density and shape as the toothpicks, just bigger, and the glue is applied in the same proportions. Why does the life-size tower fall apart, when it is an exact scale-up of a tower that stands?

Model the glue as failing at a maximum __stress__ (force per unit area) of $$\sigma.$$ Imagine each log of mass $$m$$ as held up entirely by glue (the logs touch only glue, not each other), and let $$\rho$$ be the density of the wood.

__(a)__ Write the condition for a glued log not to break loose, in the form $$mg < \sigma A_{\rm glue}.$$ Then rewrite each side in terms of effective lengths: let $$\ell_g$$ be a length with $$A_{\rm glue} = \ell_g^2,$$ and let $$\ell_t$$ be a length with the log's volume equal to $$\ell_t^3.$$ What inequality results?

__(b)__ Both sides of your inequality are forces, with identical dimensions $$\mathrm{M\cdot L\cdot T^{-2}}.$$ Explain how they can nevertheless scale __differently__ as the whole tower is scaled up by a common factor, and why the tower must fail once it is big enough.

__(c)__ Show that the safety ratio $$\dfrac{F_{\rm glue}}{F_{\rm grav}}$$ scales as $$\dfrac{1}{\ell},$$ where $$\ell$$ is the size of a toothpick or log.

__(d)__ Combine $$\sigma,$$ $$\rho,$$ and $$g$$ into a quantity with dimensions of length — the natural length scale of glued wooden structures on Earth. Estimate it numerically using $$\sigma \approx 10^5\;\mathrm{Pa}$$ (a rough figure for white glue), $$\rho \approx 10^3\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$$ (wood floats, but not by much, so its density is near water's), and $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.$$ Use the result to explain the fates of the toothpick tower and of the $$300\;\mathrm{m}$$ life-size tower.

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: How Big Is a Water Drop? — The surface tension of water is $$\gamma \approx 0.1\;\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}$$ — an…
desc: The surface tension of water is $$\gamma \approx 0.1\;\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}$$ — an energy per unit area of water surface. Even without studying surface tension, dimensional analysis can answer: about how large does a drop of water get before it falls off a faucet? __(a)__ Besides…
statement:
The surface tension of water is $$\gamma \approx 0.1\;\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}$$ — an energy per unit area of water surface. Even without studying surface tension, dimensional analysis can answer: about how large does a drop of water get before it falls off a faucet?

__(a)__ Besides $$\gamma$$ and the drop radius $$r,$$ the relevant quantities are the water density $$\rho \approx 10^3\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$$ and the gravitational acceleration $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.$$ Argue that $$\rho$$ and $$g$$ can enter the answer only through the product $$w = \rho g$$ (the __specific weight__), so they may be treated as a single variable. (Hint: think about what doubling $$\rho$$ does to the weight of a drop, versus doubling $$g.$$)

__(b)__ The dimensions are $$ = \mathrm{M\cdot L^{-2}\cdot T^{-2}},$$ $$[\gamma] = \mathrm{M\cdot T^{-2}},$$ and $$ = \mathrm{L}.$$ The Buckingham Pi theorem says that $$N$$ variables requiring $$D$$ dimensions to describe them admit $$N - D$$ independent dimensionless products. Naively, $$N = 3$$ and $$D = 3$$ gives zero dimensionless products — which would leave dimensional analysis with nothing to say. Find the flaw in the naive count. (Hint: look at how mass and time appear in these variables, or try introducing force $$\mathrm{F}$$ as a base dimension.)

__(c)__ Find the one dimensionless product, set it equal to a constant $$c,$$ and solve for $$r.$$ Then estimate the size of a drop numerically by guessing $$c \approx 1.$$

__(d)__ Some insects stand on top of water, supported by surface tension. Using your result — and no new calculation — estimate how large such insects can be, and explain why a mouse could not stand on water this way. What does your analysis say, and not say, about basilisk lizards, which run across the surface of water?

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: The Natural Time Scale of a Planet — Find the natural time scale of gravitationally driven processes for a…
desc: Find the natural time scale of gravitationally driven processes for a planet of uniform density $$\rho$$ and radius $$r.$$ The relevant constant of nature is Newton's gravitational constant $$G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}},$$ with dimensions $$ =…
statement:
Find the natural time scale of gravitationally driven processes for a planet of uniform density $$\rho$$ and radius $$r.$$ The relevant constant of nature is Newton's gravitational constant $$G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}},$$ with dimensions $$ = \mathrm{M^{-1}\cdot L^3\cdot T^{-2}}.$$ The other dimensions are $$[\rho] = \mathrm{M\cdot L^{-3}}$$ and $$ = \mathrm{L}.$$

__(a)__ Build a quantity $$t$$ with dimensions of time from $$G,$$ $$\rho,$$ and $$r.$$ Show that the planet's radius drops out entirely.

__(b)__ Name some physical processes whose duration should be set (up to a dimensionless constant) by this time scale, and explain why such different-sounding processes share it.

__(c)__ Earth's mean density is about $$5.5\times 10^3\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}.$$ Evaluate your time scale for Earth, and compare it with the roughly $$90$$-minute period of a low Earth orbit. About how big is the dimensionless constant for that process?

lesson: PW106: Dimensional Analysis and Problem Solving
label: PW106
name: G. I. Taylor and the Trinity Test — Perhaps the most famous dimensional analysis ever was performed by G. I…
desc: Perhaps the most famous dimensional analysis ever was performed by G. I. Taylor, Great Britain's leading expert in fluid dynamics, who estimated the yield (energy released) of the Trinity test — the first atomic bomb explosion, in New Mexico on July 16, 1945 — using only…
statement:
Perhaps the most famous dimensional analysis ever was performed by G. I. Taylor, Great Britain's leading expert in fluid dynamics, who estimated the yield (energy released) of the Trinity test — the first atomic bomb explosion, in New Mexico on July 16, 1945 — using only photographs published in magazines. The military had released the photos not realizing anyone could extract the highly classified yield from them. (Taylor had in fact been asked by his government, years earlier, to develop a method for estimating bomb yields; his first attempts were far more complicated calculations, and the celebrated dimensional analysis came later.)

__(a)__ Here is a photograph of the blast:

Suppose you can establish the photo's distance scale from the power line silhouetted at the lower right, and you take the relevant mass scale to come from the density of the surrounding air, which the fireball shoves out of its way as it expands. What dimension needed for an energy estimate is still missing from a photo like this one?

__(b)__ The photos the government actually released were stamped with extra information, like this one:

The stamp gives the time after detonation, $$t = 0.025\;\mathrm{s},$$ and a $$100\;\mathrm{m}$$ scale bar showing the fireball's radius to be about $$r = 150\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Take the variables to be the blast energy $$E,$$ the density of air $$\rho,$$ the fireball radius $$r,$$ and the elapsed time $$t.$$ The Buckingham Pi theorem states that $$N$$ variables described by $$D$$ dimensions admit $$N - D$$ independent dimensionless products; when there is exactly one, it can be set equal to an unknown constant. How many independent dimensionless products are there here?

__(c)__ Using $$ = \mathrm{M\cdot L^2\cdot T^{-2}}$$ and $$[\rho] = \mathrm{M\cdot L^{-3}},$$ find the formula for $$E$$ in terms of $$\rho,$$ $$r,$$ and $$t,$$ up to a dimensionless constant $$c.$$

__(d)__ Guess $$c \approx 1$$ and use $$\rho = 1\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$$ for air to estimate the yield in joules, and convert to kilotons of TNT using $$1\;\mathrm{kiloton\ TNT} \approx 4.2\times 10^{12}\;\mathrm{J}.$$ The accepted yield of the Trinity test is about $$22$$ kilotons — how did dimensional analysis do?

lesson: PW107: Fluid Statics: Buoyancy and Surface Tension
label: PW107
name: Answer these conceptual questions:
desc: Answer these conceptual questions: **a)** A wooden block of volume $$1.2\;\mathrm{m}^3$$ has a density of $$0.8$$ times the density of water. What is the minimum amount of water necessary to float the block? **b)** You're in a canoe in a lake. In the canoe is a rock. You toss…
statement:
Answer these conceptual questions:

**a)** A wooden block of volume $$1.2\;\mathrm{m}^3$$ has a density of $$0.8$$ times the density of water. What is the minimum amount of water necessary to float the block?

**b)** You're in a canoe in a lake. In the canoe is a rock. You toss the rock overboard and it sinks to the bottom of the lake. Does the water level in the lake go up or down?

**c)** A beaker of water sits on a scale. You put your finger in the water without touching the beaker or the scale. Does the reading on the scale change?

**d)** You set up a rigid frame with some string in it, then put a soap film around the frame and string as shown.

source: UC Berkeley fluid mechanics demonstrations http://www.nhn.ou.edu/demo/fluid/fluid.html

What happens when you pop the central bit of film?

**e)** When you look at things that are very small - a bacterium, for instance, does surface tension play a larger or smaller role than for everyday, human-sized things?

lesson: PW107: Fluid Statics: Buoyancy and Surface Tension
label: PW107
name: **a)** Suppose a cylinder of density $$\rho_c$$, radius $$r,$$ and height $$h$$ floats…
desc: **a)** Suppose a cylinder of density $$\rho_c$$, radius $$r,$$ and height $$h$$ floats upright in a large vat of fluid of density $$\rho_f.$$ Suppose the cylinder is held down a distance $$x$$ below its equilibrium floating point. What is the buoyant force on the cylinder?…
statement:
**a)** Suppose a cylinder of density $$\rho_c$$, radius $$r,$$ and height $$h$$ floats upright in a large vat of fluid of density $$\rho_f.$$ Suppose the cylinder is held down a distance $$x$$ below its equilibrium floating point. What is the buoyant force on the cylinder?

**b)** By thinking of the force you found in part (a) as a restoring force, find the angular frequency of oscillations of the cylinder.

**c)** Explain why, if you were to try this experiment, you would not measure the angular frequency of oscillations you found in part (b). Would the real frequency be faster or slower?

**d)** What does your answer to part (c) say about the limitations of the equations you know for the buoyant force?

lesson: PW107: Fluid Statics: Buoyancy and Surface Tension
label: PW107
name: The surface tension of cell or vesicle membranes has many important biophysical…
desc: The surface tension of cell or vesicle membranes has many important biophysical consequences. For example, a loss of membrane elasticity in red blood cells leads to painful and frequently-lethal disease sickle-cell anemia. One technique to measure the surface tension of a…
statement:
The surface tension of cell or vesicle membranes has many important biophysical consequences. For example, a loss of membrane elasticity in red blood cells leads to painful and frequently-lethal disease sickle-cell anemia.

One technique to measure the surface tension of a **lipid bilayer** (the membrane surrounding a cell) is **micropipette aspiration**. In this technique, a small pipette is placed next to a vesicle. The pressure inside the pipette is reduced, causing the vesicle to deform and to be pushed into the pipette by its own higher pressure. A schematic view looks like this:

credit: Phillips, Rob, et al. Physical biology of the cell. Garland Science, 2012.

Scientists can directly measure the pressure $$P_0$$ outside the vesicle and the pressure $$P_m$$ inside the micropipette. Using microscopy, they can also measure $$R_v,$$ $$R_l,$$ and $$l,$$ and $$d.$$

**a)** Find the surface tension $$\gamma$$ of the cell in terms of the measurable variables.

**b)** Estimate the surface tension of the vesicle shown below, which shows micropipette aspiration in progress.

credit: T. Ursell, reproduced in Phillips, Rob, et al. Physical biology of the cell. Garland Science, 2012.

The pressure outside the cell was atmospheric pressure, $$10^5 \;\mathrm{Pa},$$ and the pressure in the micropipette was smaller than atmospheric pressure by about $$4000\;\mathrm{Pa}.$$

desc: Ignore gravity in this problem. A tube of length $$l$$ is filled with an ideal gas, then spun around one end at angular frequency $$\omega.$$ Find the density of the gas as a function of $$x,$$ the distance from the axis of spin. You can assume the gas remains a constant…
statement:
Ignore gravity in this problem.

A tube of length $$l$$ is filled with an ideal gas, then spun around one end at angular frequency $$\omega.$$ Find the density of the gas as a function of $$x,$$ the distance from the axis of spin. You can assume the gas remains a constant temperature $$T$$ everywhere and give your answer in terms of the density of gas at the spin axis and $$m,$$ the mass of an individual gas molecule.

lesson: PW107: Fluid Statics: Buoyancy and Surface Tension
label: PW107
name: In this problem, we will use the surface tension and heat of vaporization of carbon…
desc: In this problem, we will use the surface tension and heat of vaporization of carbon tetrachloride to estimate the size of an atom. The surface tension of carbon tetrachloride is $$\gamma = 0.027 \;\mathrm{N/m}$$ and its heat of vaporization (the energy that must be put in to get…
statement:
In this problem, we will use the surface tension and heat of vaporization of carbon tetrachloride to estimate the size of an atom. The surface tension of carbon tetrachloride is $$\gamma = 0.027 \;\mathrm{N/m}$$ and its heat of vaporization (the energy that must be put in to get it to boil) is $$\epsilon = 3.1\times 10^8 \;\mathrm{J/m^3}.$$

**a)** Use dimensional analysis to find a length from $$\gamma$$ and $$\epsilon$$ and evaluate that length.

**b)** Suppose a molecule in the center of a fluid has six neighbors - one above, one below, one in front, one in back, one to the left, and one to the right. It bonds with each neighbor (via Van der Waals interactions.) How many bonds would you expect a molecule on the surface of a fluid to make?

**c)** Suppose that boiling a fluid is equivalent to breaking all the inter-atomic bonds between all the molecules in the fluid. Find $$\epsilon$$ in terms of the strength of an individual bond (energy needed to break it) and the size of a molecule.

**d)** Suppose that creating new surface on the fluid is equivalent to breaking the bonds that are lost due to the molecule having fewer neighbors when on the surface. Find $$\gamma$$ in terms of the strength of a bond and the size of a molecule.

**e)** Combine your answers to parts (c) and (d) along with the given data on carbon tetrachloride to estimate the size of a carbon tetrachloride molecule.
tags: fluid statics: buoyancy and surface tension

lesson: PW107: Fluid Statics: Buoyancy and Surface Tension
label: PW107
name: **a)** A flat cylinder (shaped like a coin or DVD) will float with a circular face…
desc: **a)** A flat cylinder (shaped like a coin or DVD) will float with a circular face pointing upwards, but a long cylinder (shaped like a pencil or a AAA battery) will float lying on its side. Both are cylinders; why do they float in different positions? You can answer this…
statement:
**a)** A flat cylinder (shaped like a coin or DVD) will float with a circular face pointing upwards, but a long cylinder (shaped like a pencil or a AAA battery) will float lying on its side. Both are cylinders; why do they float in different positions? You can answer this qualitatively.

**b)** How could you modify a long, thin cylinder so that it floats upright? You cannot change its shape, but you can change the distribution of mass in the cylinder.

**c)** A long rectangular prism has a square cross-section. Like the long cylinder, it will float lying on its side. Unlike the cylinder, its angle of rotation on its side matters. If it is half as dense as water, does it float flat, or tilted like a diamond?

lesson: PW107: Fluid Statics: Buoyancy and Surface Tension

name: When a bubble pops, it doesn't pop all at once. Instead, the pop starts somewhere and…
desc: When a bubble pops, it doesn't pop all at once. Instead, the pop starts somewhere and propagates across the bubble. Let's call the speed of propagation the "popping speed". **a)** Estimate the popping speed using this GIF: credit: The Slow Down Show, YouTube **b)** Develop your…
statement:
When a bubble pops, it doesn't pop all at once. Instead, the pop starts somewhere and propagates across the bubble. Let's call the speed of propagation the "popping speed".

**a)** Estimate the popping speed using this GIF:

credit: The Slow Down Show, YouTube

**b)** Develop your own theory (it doesn't have to be exact; you can use heuristics and estimation) of the popping speed in terms of the surface tension, density, and thickness of a bubble.

**c)** Test your theory from part (b) against the observations you made in part (a). Is your theory plausible (within about an order of magnitude of the observations)? You can use $$\gamma = 0.03\;\mathrm{N/m}.$$

The bubble in this GIF has very little iridescence, indicating that its walls are likely thin enough that they don't cause constructive interference for any wavelength of light, so they may be about $$100 \;\mathrm{nm}$$ thick.

name: A water drop falls in air with a uniform velocity.
desc: A water drop falls in air with a uniform velocity. **a)** Show that for a drop with average radius of $$1\; \mathrm{mm},$$ the difference in pressure from the top to the bottom of the drop is about an order of magnitude smaller than the difference in pressure from inside to…
statement:
A water drop falls in air with a uniform velocity.

**a)** Show that for a drop with average radius of $$1\; \mathrm{mm},$$ the difference in pressure from the top to the bottom of the drop is about an order of magnitude smaller than the difference in pressure from inside to outside the drop. You may use $$\gamma = 0.07 \;\mathrm{N/m}.$$ This shows that the drop is close to spherical, but not exactly so.

**b)** Find the difference between the curvature radii of the drop's surface at the upper and lower points of the drop, which are separated by the distance $$h.$$ You can assume the air pressure $$P_0$$ is constant outside the drop.

name: Two soap bubbles of radii $$a$$ and $$b$$ coalesce to form a soap bubble of radius $$c.$$
desc: Two soap bubbles of radii $$a$$ and $$b$$ coalesce to form a soap bubble of radius $$c.$$ **a)** If the external pressure is $$P,$$ find an expression for the surface tension $$S$$ in terms of $$P, a, b,$$ and $$c.$$ **b)** You might watch two soap bubbles with…
statement:
Two soap bubbles of radii $$a$$ and $$b$$ coalesce to form a soap bubble of radius $$c.$$

**a)** If the external pressure is $$P,$$ find an expression for the surface tension $$S$$ in terms of $$P, a, b,$$ and $$c.$$

**b)** You might watch two soap bubbles with $$a=b=1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ merge. Do you think that measuring the radius of the resulting bubble and measuring the atmospheric pressure would be a good way to determine the surface tension? Why or why not?
