name: This problem extends the applications of complex exponentials begun in the homework last…
desc: This problem extends the applications of complex exponentials begun in the homework last week. **a)** This part gives practice with a mathematical step that will be useful later in the problem. First, let's try re-writing the sum $$1 + e^{i\phi}$$ in terms of the product of a…
statement:
This problem extends the applications of complex exponentials begun in the homework last week.

**a)** This part gives practice with a mathematical step that will be useful later in the problem. First, let's try re-writing the sum $$1 + e^{i\phi}$$ in terms of the product of a complex exponent and a real trigonometric function. Try factoring out $$e^{i\phi/2}.$$

This representation separates the complex phase of $$1 + e^{i\phi}$$ from its magnitude. IE it lets us write $$1 + e^{i\phi} = R(\phi) e^{i\theta(\phi)}$$ for some functions $$R(\phi)$$ and $$\theta(\phi).$$

**b)** Next, we'll re-derive the two-slit interference pattern, $$I \propto \cos^2\left(\dfrac{kd\theta}{2}\right),$$ using the above result. We'll work in the far field limit for small $$\theta,$$ where $$\theta$$ is the angle from the slits to the screen. Let light coming from the lower slit of a two-slit pattern have amplitude $$A\cos(\omega t)$$ at the screen. Then light coming from the second slit has amplitude $$A\cos(\omega t + kd\theta),$$ with $$\theta$$ the angle to the screen and $$k$$ the wavenumber. Write each of these as the real part of a complex amplitude $$Ae^{i(\omega t + \phi)}$$, where $$\phi$$ is different between the two slits. Factor out any common factor and write the result as a complex exponential multiplied to a trigonometric function. Find the time-average of the square of the real part of this expression. This is the two-slit interference pattern.

**c)** Next we'll investigate the $$N$$-slit interference pattern. This is the interference pattern from $$N$$ thin slits, each separated by a distance $$d.$$ Set the top slit to have amplitude $$A\cos(\omega t)$$ at the screen, and the next slit down to have amplitude $$A\cos(\omega t + kd\theta)$$ at the screen. Find the amplitude from each of the remaining slits. Write each amplitude as the real part of a complex exponential. Write the total amplitude at the screen as the real part of a sum of complex exponentials, and factor out any common factor. Evaluate the remaining sum (this problem has hints for this step). Write the resulting amplitude as a complex exponential multiplied to a real function made of trigonometric functions. Finally, find the intensity at the screen as a function of $$\theta, k, d,$$ and $$N.$$

**d)** A single finite slit of width $$w$$ might be thought of as infinitely-many infinitely thin slits. However, simply taking $$N\to\infty$$ in the $$N$$-slit pattern you found in part (a) will not give the diffraction pattern for a single finite slit. Why not? What is the appropriate limit to take to recover the finite slit pattern from the $$N$$-slit pattern?

**e)** Calculate the limit you discussed in part (c) and show that it does in fact reproduce the single-slit pattern as a limit of the $$N$$-slit pattern.

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: This problem is from IPhO 1990 (The Netherlands)
desc: This problem is from IPhO 1990 (The Netherlands) We wish to study X-ray diffraction by a cubic crystal lattice. To do this we start with the diffraction of a plane, monochromatic wave of wavelength $$\lambda$$ that falls perpendicularly on a 2-dimensional grid that consists of…
statement:
This problem is from IPhO 1990 (The Netherlands)

We wish to study X-ray diffraction by a cubic crystal lattice. To do this we start with the diffraction of a plane, monochromatic wave of wavelength $$\lambda$$ that falls perpendicularly on a 2-dimensional grid that consists of $$N_1 \times N_2$$ slits with separations $$d_1$$ and $$d_2.$$ The diffraction pattern is observed on a screen at a distance $$L$$ from the grid. The screen is parallel to the grid and $$L$$ is much larger than $$d_1$$ and $$d_2.$$

**a)** Determine the positions and widths of the principal maximum on the screen. The width is defined as the distance between the minima on either side of the maximum.

**b)** Next, we consider a cubic crystal with lattice spacing $$a$$ and size $$N_0 a \times N_0 a \times N_1 a.$$ Assume $$N_1 \ll N_0.$$ The crystal is placed in a parallel $$X$$-ray beam along the $$z$$-axis at an angle $$\Theta.$$

The diffraction pattern is again observed on a screen at a great distance from the crystal. Calculate the position and width of the maxima as a function of the angle $$\Theta$$ for small $$\Theta.$$ What in particular are the consequences of the fact that $$N_1 \ll N_0?$$

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: An anemometer is a device for measuring the flow speed of a fluid. In this problem, we'll…
desc: An anemometer is a device for measuring the flow speed of a fluid. In this problem, we'll examine a simple laser-anemometer. A fluid flows through a rectangular pipe with thin glass walls with index of refraction $$n = 1.3.$$ The index of refraction of the fluid is the same. The…
statement:
An anemometer is a device for measuring the flow speed of a fluid. In this problem, we'll examine a simple laser-anemometer.

A fluid flows through a rectangular pipe with thin glass walls with index of refraction $$n = 1.3.$$ The index of refraction of the fluid is the same. The fluid contains particles which scatter light in all directions. Two coherent plane waves with wavelength $$\lambda = 515 \;\mathrm{nm}$$ and angle $$\alpha = 4^\circ$$ between their wave vectors are incident on a glass wall.

The angle bisector of the angle between the wave vectors is normal to one wall of the pipe. The pipe is parallel to the plane defined by the wave vectors.

Behind the pipe is a photodetector. The photodetector measures the frequency of changes in dissipated light intensity.

**a)** How long is the spatial period $$\lambda_x$$ of the interference pattern created along the $$x$$-axis?

**b)** Suppose the oscillation frequency detected at the photodetector is $$50 \; \mathrm{KHz}.$$ What is the fluid speed $$v?$$

**c)** Now suppose that the wavelengths of the plane waves differ by $$\delta \lambda = 4.4 \times 10^{-15}\;\mathrm{m}.$$ What is frequency of signal observations observed by the photodetector? Is it possible to determine the flow direction?

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: From Newton's Second Law to the Wave Equation — The __wave equation__ is $$\dfrac{\partial^2 f(x,t)}{\partial…
desc: The __wave equation__ is $$\dfrac{\partial^2 f(x,t)}{\partial t^2} = v^2\,\dfrac{\partial^2 f(x,t)}{\partial x^2}.$$ Any system that obeys it supports traveling waves, and the constant $$v$$ turns out to be the speed of those waves. This problem tests that claim against history…
statement:
The __wave equation__ is $$\dfrac{\partial^2 f(x,t)}{\partial t^2} = v^2\,\dfrac{\partial^2 f(x,t)}{\partial x^2}.$$ Any system that obeys it supports traveling waves, and the constant $$v$$ turns out to be the speed of those waves. This problem tests that claim against history, then derives the wave equation for a stretched string.

__(a)__ In 1865, James Clerk Maxwell discovered that electric fields in free space obey $$\dfrac{\partial^2 E}{\partial t^2} - \dfrac{1}{\mu_0\epsilon_0}\,\dfrac{\partial^2 E}{\partial x^2} = 0,$$ and that magnetic fields obey the same equation with $$B$$ in place of $$E.$$ Taking it as given that the constant $$v$$ in the wave equation is the wave speed, what was Maxwell's prediction for the speed of electromagnetic waves? What did he conclude when he plugged in the measured values of $$\mu_0$$ and $$\epsilon_0?$$

Now consider a long string under uniform tension $$T$$ with mass per unit length $$\lambda.$$ Let $$f(x,t)$$ be the transverse (vertical) displacement of the string from equilibrium at position $$x$$ and time $$t.$$ Ignore gravity, and assume the oscillations are small: the tension magnitude is then the same everywhere along the string, and the angle between the string and the horizontal is everywhere small. The picture below shows such a string from a PhET simulation (the beads just make the string easy to see, and the vertical displacements are greatly exaggerated).

__(b)__ Draw a free-body diagram for a short piece of the string, like the one below. The tension $$T$$ pulls along the string at each end of the piece, at angles $$\theta_L$$ and $$\theta_R$$ above the horizontal at the left and right ends. Using the small-angle approximations $$\cos\theta \approx 1 - \dfrac{\theta^2}{2}$$ and $$\sin\theta \approx \theta,$$ show that the net horizontal force on the piece is second order in the small angles, while the net vertical force is first order: $$F_y \approx T(\theta_R - \theta_L).$$ (This is why we keep only the vertical motion.)

__(c)__ The slope of the string is $$\tan\theta \approx \theta,$$ so $$\theta = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$$ at each end of the piece. If the piece spans a horizontal length $$\Delta x,$$ show that the net vertical force can be written $$F_y \approx T\,\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\,\Delta x.$$

__(d)__ Apply Newton's second law to the piece (its mass is $$\lambda\,\Delta x$$) to show that the string obeys the wave equation, and find the speed of waves on the string. Your answer for $$v$$ comes with a $$\pm$$ sign — what does the sign mean physically?

__(e)__ A __half-Atwood machine__ consists of a block resting on a frictionless horizontal table, connected by a string that runs over a pulley at the table's edge to a second block hanging from the string's free end. The two blocks have equal mass. While the block on the table is held in place, the speed of small transverse waves in the connecting string is $$v_0.$$ The block is then released and the system begins to accelerate. What is the speed of waves in the string now?

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: Any Shape, Either Direction: the General Solution — The wave equation, $$\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial t^2} =…
desc: The wave equation, $$\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial t^2} = v^2\,\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2},$$ has a remarkably broad __general solution__: rather than letting you choose a parameter or two (the way the general solution $$y = A\sin(x+\phi)$$ of $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2…
statement:
The wave equation, $$\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial t^2} = v^2\,\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2},$$ has a remarkably broad __general solution__: rather than letting you choose a parameter or two (the way the general solution $$y = A\sin(x+\phi)$$ of $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = -y$$ lets you pick $$A$$ and $$\phi$$), it lets you choose entire __functions__.

__(a)__ Let $$\tilde{f}$$ be any twice-differentiable function of a single variable, and consider $$f(x,t) = \tilde{f}(ax - bt)$$ for constants $$a$$ and $$b.$$ Substitute into the wave equation (use the chain rule, writing $$u = ax - bt$$ so that $$\tilde{f}$$ is differentiated with respect to its single argument $$u$$) and find the condition on $$a$$ and $$b$$ for this to be a solution.

__(b)__ In the online class PhysicsPOOT — where they teach you physics, but they get it wrong an awful lot — they claim that the most general solution of the wave equation is $$f(x,t) = \tilde{f}(x - vt).$$ What is missing from their claim? Write down a correct general solution, and explain why no extra constant is needed inside the argument, even though part (a) seems to allow solutions like $$\tilde{f}(a(x - vt))$$ for any $$a.$$ Also describe in words what a solution $$\tilde{f}(x - vt)$$ looks like as $$t$$ increases. (Hint for the last part: if you have some function $$g(x),$$ what does the graph of $$g(x-3)$$ look like?)

__(c)__ Two wave pulses travel toward each other on a stretched string, as in the animation below. They overlap, momentarily nearly cancel, then continue on unchanged, as if the other pulse never existed.

Prove that this must happen for any system obeying the wave equation: show that if $$f(x,t)$$ and $$g(x,t)$$ are both solutions, then $$h = f + g$$ is also a solution. (This property is called __linearity__.) Explain why linearity means each pulse propagates exactly as if it were alone.

__(d)__ Suppose the two pulses are mirror images, one upward and one inverted, so that at one instant their displacements cancel and the string is momentarily __flat__. A flat string with no waves on it stays flat forever — yet this string immediately re-forms both pulses and sends them on their way. What information does the string carry at that instant that distinguishes it from a quiet string? Finally, explain why superposition would fail if the wave equation contained a term like $$\left(\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}\right)^2.$$

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: No Radiation Along the Line — Two small sources of radio waves each emit waves of wavelength $$\lambda$$ in…
desc: Two small sources of radio waves each emit waves of wavelength $$\lambda$$ in all directions. The sources oscillate __in phase__ with each other: whenever one source is generating the crest of a wave, so is the other. The sources are separated by a distance $$d.$$ An observer…
statement:
Two small sources of radio waves each emit waves of wavelength $$\lambda$$ in all directions. The sources oscillate __in phase__ with each other: whenever one source is generating the crest of a wave, so is the other. The sources are separated by a distance $$d.$$ An observer finds that there is __no__ radiation along the dashed rays shown below — the line through the two sources, extended outward in both directions. (Treat the sources as identical and ignore the small difference in wave amplitudes arriving from the two sources.)

__(a)__ For the waves to cancel along the dashed rays, they must arrive there exactly out of phase — a phase difference of $$\pi.$$ But the problem says the sources oscillate in phase. Where does the phase difference come from?

__(b)__ Find the smallest possible separation $$d.$$

__(c)__ Find all possible values of $$d.$$

__(d)__ The __wavenumber__ of a wave is $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$$ — the phase the wave accumulates per unit distance traveled. Restate your answer to part (c) as a condition on $$kd.$$

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: Young's Double Slit and the Phasor Method — In 1801, Thomas Young illuminated two thin slits, separated by a…
desc: In 1801, Thomas Young illuminated two thin slits, separated by a distance $$d,$$ with __coherent__, __monochromatic__ light of wavelength $$\lambda.$$ (Monochromatic: a single wavelength. Coherent: the light at the two slits oscillates in phase — when one slit is producing a…
statement:
In 1801, Thomas Young illuminated two thin slits, separated by a distance $$d,$$ with __coherent__, __monochromatic__ light of wavelength $$\lambda.$$ (Monochromatic: a single wavelength. Coherent: the light at the two slits oscillates in phase — when one slit is producing a peak of the electric field, so is the other.) The light falls on a screen a distance $$L$$ away, with $$L \gg d > \lambda$$ — the __far-field__ or __Fraunhofer__ regime. Let $$y$$ measure position on the screen from the point $$O$$ directly opposite the slits, and let $$\theta \approx \dfrac{y}{L}$$ be the (small) angle from the slits to the screen point $$P$$ at height $$y.$$ Find the pattern of light on the screen.

__(a)__ Show that the light from the two slits travels distances that differ by $$\Delta\ell = d\sin\theta \approx d\,\theta$$ to reach the point at angle $$\theta.$$ (Hint: because the screen is effectively very far away, the two paths to the same screen point are nearly parallel near the slits. Draw a circular arc centered on the screen point passing through the nearer slit; near the slits the arc looks like a straight line, and the leftover segment of the longer path is the extra distance.)

__(b)__ Find all screen positions $$y$$ where the light from the two slits arrives exactly in phase — the bright fringes, or __constructive interference__ — and describe what appears on the screen halfway between two adjacent bright fringes.

__(c)__ Suppose light from the nearer slit produces a field $$A\sin(\omega t)$$ at the screen point. With $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$$ the wavenumber, the light from the other slit arrives with phase lag $$kd\theta,$$ so its field is $$A\sin(\omega t - kd\theta).$$ Represent each wave by a __phasor__: an arrow of length $$A$$ rotating at angular frequency $$\omega,$$ whose vertical component is the wave; the second arrow trails the first by the fixed angle $$kd\theta,$$ as in the animation below. Add the two arrows as vectors to show that the total field has amplitude $$2A\cos\left(\dfrac{kd\theta}{2}\right).$$ (Hint: the length of the sum never changes, so freeze the picture at the symmetric moment when the two arrows point equally above and below the horizontal axis.)

__(d)__ The __intensity__ of light is the power delivered per unit area, and it is proportional to the square of the electric field. Find the time-averaged intensity on the screen as a function of $$\theta.$$ (Useful fact: the time average of $$\sin^2(\omega t + \mathrm{const})$$ is $$\dfrac{1}{2}.$$) Check that your formula reproduces the bright and dark fringe locations from part (b).

__(e)__ If the slits are moved farther apart, do the fringes get closer together or farther apart? Show that the angle between adjacent bright fringes is $$\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d}$$ — an inverse relationship between the size of a source and the angular spread of its light that recurs throughout wave optics.

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: Three Slits, Many Slits, and the Diffraction Grating — Coherent, monochromatic light of wavelength…
desc: Coherent, monochromatic light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ (wavenumber $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$$) passes through a row of thin slits, each a distance $$d$$ from the next, and lands on a faraway screen (far-field conditions, small angles). At angle $$\theta$$ from the slits, the…
statement:
Coherent, monochromatic light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ (wavenumber $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$$) passes through a row of thin slits, each a distance $$d$$ from the next, and lands on a faraway screen (far-field conditions, small angles). At angle $$\theta$$ from the slits, the wave from each slit arrives with a phase lag $$kd\theta$$ relative to the wave from the slit before it. The waves can therefore be drawn as __phasors__: arrows of equal length $$A,$$ with angle $$kd\theta$$ between successive arrows, as shown below for three slits. The total amplitude at the screen is the length of the vector sum of the arrows, and the intensity is proportional to the square of that amplitude.

__(a)__ For __three__ slits, the brightest spots (__principal maxima__) occur where all three phasors point the same way. As $$kd\theta$$ grows from $$0$$ to $$2\pi,$$ the sum shrinks, passes through zero twice, and in between reaches a smaller __secondary maximum__. Find the phasor configuration at the secondary maximum, and determine how many times more power per unit area is delivered at a principal maximum than at the secondary maximum.

__(b)__ A __diffraction grating__ is an enormous number $$N$$ of equally spaced slits. For a generic angle $$\theta,$$ the $$N$$ phasors point in directions spread nearly uniformly around a circle, as in the 100-slit diagram below. Explain why the intensity is essentially zero at a generic angle, and find the condition on $$\theta$$ for the bright principal maxima that survive.

__(c)__ Now __white light__ — a mixture of all visible wavelengths, roughly $$400\;\mathrm{nm}$$ to $$700\;\mathrm{nm}$$ — illuminates the grating. Describe what appears on the screen. Within each bright band, which color lies closest to the center of the pattern? (This is why a CD or DVD, whose closely spaced grooves act as a reflective diffraction grating, flashes rainbow colors in white light.)

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: How Wide Is the Slit? — Coherent light of wavelength $$500\;\mathrm{nm}$$ illuminates a single slit whose…
desc: Coherent light of wavelength $$500\;\mathrm{nm}$$ illuminates a single slit whose width $$d$$ is __not__ small compared to the wavelength. On a screen $$3\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the slit, there is a central bright fringe of width $$2\;\mathrm{cm},$$ meaning that the first intensity…
statement:
Coherent light of wavelength $$500\;\mathrm{nm}$$ illuminates a single slit whose width $$d$$ is __not__ small compared to the wavelength. On a screen $$3\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the slit, there is a central bright fringe of width $$2\;\mathrm{cm},$$ meaning that the first intensity zeros lie $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ to either side of the center of the pattern. Find the width $$d$$ of the slit.

__(a)__ First, estimate. Light passing through an aperture of size $$d$$ spreads out through an angle of roughly $$\theta \approx \dfrac{\lambda}{d}.$$ Use this heuristic to estimate the slit width.

__(b)__ Now compute exactly. Let $$u$$ be a coordinate across the slit, running from $$-\dfrac{d}{2}$$ at one edge to $$+\dfrac{d}{2}$$ at the other, with $$u = 0$$ at the center. The slit is illuminated coherently, so every point of the slit oscillates in phase; but light from position $$u$$ reaches the screen point at small angle $$\theta$$ with a phase lag $$ku\theta$$ relative to light from the center, where $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$$ (this is the same far-field geometry as in the double-slit problem, with $$u$$ in place of $$d$$). The slit is continuous rather than a discrete set of thin slits, so instead of adding a finite number of sine waves, integrate: each piece of the slit contributes an amplitude proportional to $$\sin(\omega t - ku\theta)\,\mathrm{d}u.$$ Write the total amplitude at angle $$\theta$$ as an integral over the slit and evaluate it.

__(c)__ Your result mixes the time and the angle. Use the identity $$\cos(a+b) = \cos a\cos b - \sin a\sin b$$ to separate it into the form (function of $$t$$) $$\times$$ (function of $$\theta$$), and show that the amplitude is proportional to $$d\,\sin(\omega t)\,\mathrm{sinc}\left(\dfrac{kd\theta}{2}\right),$$ where $$\mathrm{sinc}(x) = \dfrac{\sin x}{x}.$$

__(d)__ The intensity is proportional to the time average of the squared amplitude (the time average of $$\sin^2 \omega t$$ is $$\dfrac{1}{2}$$). Describe the intensity pattern on the screen, find the angle $$\theta_{\mathrm{dark}}$$ of the first intensity zero, and solve for the slit width $$d.$$ How close was the estimate from part (a)?

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: Babinet's Principle: Measuring a Hair with a Laser — You pluck out a hair and desperately want to measure its…
desc: You pluck out a hair and desperately want to measure its width, so you shine a laser pointer at it and look at the pattern cast on a distant wall. The photographs below show such a setup — a hair taped across a window cut out of a piece of paper — and the streak of bright…
statement:
You pluck out a hair and desperately want to measure its width, so you shine a laser pointer at it and look at the pattern cast on a distant wall. The photographs below show such a setup — a hair taped across a window cut out of a piece of paper — and the streak of bright diffraction spots that appears whenever the laser hits the hair and disappears when it misses.

How is the diffraction pattern of a hair related to that of a __slit__ of the same width? Work through the following argument.

__(a)__ First consider a slit of width $$w$$ in an opaque barrier, illuminated by coherent light. The illumination is in phase across the slit, so in the plane of the barrier the field oscillates as $$\sin(\omega t)$$ everywhere in the opening and is zero on the barrier. Now imagine adding a second plane wave that fills the entire plane and oscillates exactly out of phase with the slit: $$\sin(\omega t + \pi)$$ everywhere. After the addition, what is the total field in the opening? Describe the field across the whole plane — what physical arrangement does it now resemble?

__(b)__ Adding the plane wave changed the field at the aperture plane. Using __linearity__ (the field produced downstream by a sum of sources is the sum of the fields each source produces alone), explain why the diffraction pattern on the distant wall is unchanged by the added plane wave — except at the exact center, $$\theta = 0.$$

__(c)__ Conclude __Babinet's principle__: complementary screens — an opening of some shape in an opaque barrier, and an opaque object of the same shape with everything else open — produce the same far-field diffraction pattern, apart from the bright forward spot. The hair of width $$w$$ therefore diffracts like a slit of width $$w,$$ whose intensity zeros fall at angles $$\theta_n = \dfrac{n\lambda}{w}.$$ If the laser has wavelength $$650\;\mathrm{nm},$$ the wall is $$2.0\;\mathrm{m}$$ away, and the dark gaps between the bright spots are spaced $$1.3\;\mathrm{cm}$$ apart, how wide is the hair?

lesson: PW112: Waves: Interference and Diffraction
label: PW112
name: The Airy Pattern and a Scaling Check — Coherent light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ (wavenumber $$k =…
desc: Coherent light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ (wavenumber $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$$) illuminates a circular hole of radius $$r,$$ and the far-field diffraction pattern is observed on a distant screen. By the symmetry of the hole, the pattern is a central bright disk surrounded by…
statement:
Coherent light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ (wavenumber $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$$) illuminates a circular hole of radius $$r,$$ and the far-field diffraction pattern is observed on a distant screen. By the symmetry of the hole, the pattern is a central bright disk surrounded by concentric rings, called an __Airy pattern__:

__(a)__ For a single slit of width $$d,$$ the far-field amplitude at small angle $$\theta$$ is proportional to $$\int_{-d/2}^{d/2} \sin(\omega t - ku\theta)\,\mathrm{d}u,$$ where $$u$$ runs across the slit and $$ku\theta$$ is the phase lag of light from position $$u$$ relative to the center. Adapt this integral to the circular hole: let $$u$$ run horizontally across the circle (the phase-lag geometry, viewed from above, is unchanged), and account for the fact that the hole admits more light near its center than near its edges, as shown by the red chord below. Set up the integral; do not evaluate it.

__(b)__ The integral is not elementary: its value involves a __Bessel function__, and the resulting amplitude is proportional to $$r^2\,\dfrac{J_1(rk\theta)}{rk\theta}.$$ Plotted against $$\theta,$$ this looks much like the single slit's $$\mathrm{sinc}$$ pattern, with the zeros slightly shifted. The online class PhysicsPOOT — where they teach you physics, but they get it wrong an awful lot — claims instead that the amplitude is proportional to $$r^2\,\dfrac{J_1\left(\dfrac{\theta}{rk}\right)}{rk\theta}.$$ Can dimensional analysis alone determine who is right?

__(c)__ Settle the question with a scaling argument: if the radius of the hole is doubled, what happens to the angular size of the diffraction pattern according to each formula? Which behavior is physically correct? (Recall the aperture heuristic: light passing through an aperture of size $$d$$ spreads through an angle $$\theta \approx \dfrac{\lambda}{d}.$$)

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: Answer the following conceptual questions:
desc: Answer the following conceptual questions: **a)** Suppose you have a convex lens imaging an object. You block the top half of the lens. What does the resulting image look like? (Hint: go ahead and try it! There's probably a lens somewhere in your house. A light bulb is easy to…
statement:
Answer the following conceptual questions:

**a)** Suppose you have a convex lens imaging an object.

You block the top half of the lens. What does the resulting image look like? (Hint: go ahead and try it! There's probably a lens somewhere in your house. A light bulb is easy to image with a lens. Use a piece of paper to block half the lens and see what happens.)

**b)** A coin is under water. You are above the water looking at it. Does the coin appear closer than it really is, farther than it really is, or does it look like it's its real distance from you?

**c)** Suppose you hold a magnifying glass underwater. What happens to its magnifying power?

**d)** When a person is **nearsighted** they can focus sharply on objects that are near their eyes, but cannot focus on objects that are far from their eyes. Does a nearsighted person need convex or concave lenses to focus on things that are far away?

**e)** Why does a mirror flip left and right but not up and down? That is, when you look in the mirror and raise your right hand, it looks like your reflection raises its right hand. Why?

**f)** **Chromatic aberration** is the name for when focusing an image's red light makes the blue light slightly out of focus and vice versa. Between lenses and mirrors, one tends to suffer from chromatic aberration while the other does not. Which is which and why?

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: Do the following calculations:
desc: Do the following calculations: **a)** A concave shaving mirror has a radius of curvature of $$35\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ It is positioned so that the image of a man's face is $$2.7$$ times the size of his face. How far is the mirror from the man's face? **b)** A biconvex thin spherical…
statement:
Do the following calculations:

**a)** A concave shaving mirror has a radius of curvature of $$35\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ It is positioned so that the image of a man's face is $$2.7$$ times the size of his face. How far is the mirror from the man's face?

**b)** A biconvex thin spherical lens has radii of $$100\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and $$20.0\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ The lens is made of glass with an index of refraction of $$1.54$$ and is immersed in air (index of refraction $$1$$). If an object is placed $$70.0 \; \mathrm{cm}$$ in front of the $$100\;\mathrm{cm}$$ surface, locate the resulting image. Is it real or virtual? Inverted or upright? Determine the magnification of the image.

**c)** A fiber optic cable has index of refraction $$n.$$ It is desired that when a ray of light bounces off the edge of the cable, no light is transmitted. Find the maximum angle with the normal to the edge of the cable at which a light ray can approach the edge of the cable and reflect back into the cable with zero transmission. You may assume the material surrounding the cable has index of refraction $$1.$$

**d)** A **corner reflector** is three plane mirrors meeting at right angles. Describe how light bounces off a corner reflector, and explain why a corner reflector is also called a **retroreflector**.

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: Make the following estimations:
desc: Make the following estimations: **a)** You stand at the beach and your height is $$h$$. Estimate the distance between you and the horizon, assuming light travels in straight lines. **b)** People can sometimes see things on the surface of the ocean much further away than the…
statement:
Make the following estimations:

**a)** You stand at the beach and your height is $$h$$. Estimate the distance between you and the horizon, assuming light travels in straight lines.

**b)** People can sometimes see things on the surface of the ocean much further away than the limit you calculated in part (a). Estimate the gradient in the index of refraction of the air needed for this phenomenon to occur. Your answer should be in $$\mathrm{m}^{-1}$$ and should indicate the derivative of the index of refraction with respect to height.

**c)** Given that the index of refraction of air is about 1.0003, estimate the temperature gradient needed over of ocean to observe the effect you studied in part (b). State the assumptions you're making.

Explain why this phenomenon is fairly rare compared to the more common mirages you might see above hot asphalt on a summer day.

**d)** How small must the hole of a pinhole camera made with a shoebox be if you want to be able to recognize people's faces in photos it takes, assuming the people are $$5\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the camera when a photo is taken?

**e)** You're standing at the top of the shadow of a tall skyscraper in the mid-afternoon. How fast does the shadow travel, in $$\mathrm{m/s}?$$

__Melikamp, Parts of a Parabola, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Parts_of_Parabola.svg__

__By IkamusumeFan - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=37254596__

**c)** Suppose that a mirror has a focal length of $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ and the radius of the mirror (horizontal distance from the axis of the mirror to the edge of the mirror, when the mirror's axis is vertical) is $$1\;\mathrm{m}.$$ If the mirror is spherical, not parabolic, light hitting the edges of the mirror will not focus directly at the focus, a defect called **spherical aberration**. lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: Inside a Pinhole Camera — In __geometric optics__ we assume that light travels in straight lines. (This is a…
desc: In __geometric optics__ we assume that light travels in straight lines. (This is a good approximation when every hole and obstacle is much larger than the wavelength of the light, so that diffraction is negligible.) Light leaves every point of an object traveling in straight…
statement:
In __geometric optics__ we assume that light travels in straight lines. (This is a good approximation when every hole and obstacle is much larger than the wavelength of the light, so that diffraction is negligible.) Light leaves every point of an object traveling in straight lines in all directions. A little distance away is a closed box with a small hole — a __pinhole__ — in its front face. The object, drawn as an arrow so it has a clear top and bottom, is $$3\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the pinhole; the box is $$30\;\mathrm{cm}$$ deep; and the object is $$10\;\mathrm{cm}$$ tall.

__(a)__ The only light that reaches the back panel of the box is the light that passes through the pinhole; the box blocks everything else. By tracing rays from the top and from the bottom of the object through the hole, describe what appears on the back panel. Is it __upright__ (right-side up) or __inverted__ (upside down)?

__(b)__ How tall is the pattern on the back panel? (Hint: look for similar triangles.)

__(c)__ The __magnification__ of an image is defined as $$M = -\dfrac{i}{o},$$ where $$o$$ is the distance from the pinhole to the object and $$i$$ is the distance from the pinhole to the image. Compute $$M$$ for this camera, and explain what the sign and the magnitude of your answer each say about the image.

__(d)__ What could you change about the setup to make the magnitude of the magnification larger than $$1?$$

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: Sunlight Through a Triangular Hole — You cut a __triangular__ hole in the center of a large piece of paper…
desc: You cut a __triangular__ hole in the center of a large piece of paper and take the paper outside on a sunny day, with the sun directly overhead. You hold the paper parallel to the sidewalk and vary how high you hold it. Light streams through the hole and makes a bright pattern…
statement:
You cut a __triangular__ hole in the center of a large piece of paper and take the paper outside on a sunny day, with the sun directly overhead. You hold the paper parallel to the sidewalk and vary how high you hold it. Light streams through the hole and makes a bright pattern on the ground. In this problem you will explain why the __shape__ (not just the size) of the pattern changes as you change the height of the paper. Treat light as traveling in straight lines, and recall that a pinhole forms an image with magnification $$M = -\dfrac{i}{o},$$ where $$o$$ is the distance from the pinhole to the source and $$i$$ is the distance from the pinhole to the image.

__(a)__ First, forget the triangle: suppose the paper has only a tiny round pinhole, so a bright dot appears on the sidewalk. For the dot to be round, what needs to be round — the sun, the pinhole, both, or neither? What happens to the dot as you raise the paper higher?

__(b)__ During a partial solar eclipse the sun is not round — it looks like the photograph below. Predict what the dots of light beneath a kitchen colander (or a leafy tree) look like during a partial eclipse.

__(c)__ Now back to normal, round-sun sunlight. Instead of one pinhole, imagine __three__ pinholes located at the vertices of an equilateral triangle with $$1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ sides. Describe the pattern on the ground (i) when the paper is held low, so that each image of the sun is only $$0.2\;\mathrm{cm}$$ in radius, and (ii) when the paper is held high, so that each image of the sun is much larger than $$1\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ As the paper rises, do the centers of the images move?

__(d)__ Finally, consider the actual triangular hole: every point of the hole acts as a pinhole. Explain why the bright patch is triangular when the paper is near the ground but becomes a single large, round blob when the paper is held high.

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: The Focal Length of a Parabolic Mirror — The __law of reflection__ says that when a ray of light strikes a…
desc: The __law of reflection__ says that when a ray of light strikes a mirror at an angle $$\theta$$ to the __normal__ (the perpendicular to the mirror's surface), it bounces off at the same angle $$\theta$$ on the other side of the normal. When the mirror is curved, the law still…
statement:
The __law of reflection__ says that when a ray of light strikes a mirror at an angle $$\theta$$ to the __normal__ (the perpendicular to the mirror's surface), it bounces off at the same angle $$\theta$$ on the other side of the normal. When the mirror is curved, the law still applies point by point: the ray reflects as if off the __tangent line__ to the mirror at the point where it strikes.

A mirror has the shape of the parabola $$y = ax^2$$ (with $$x$$ and $$y$$ measured in the same units of length). Rays of light come straight down, parallel to the parabola's axis of symmetry. All such rays reflect to a single point on the axis, called the __focal point__ — this is what makes parabolic mirrors useful in telescopes. The distance from the vertex of the parabola to the focal point is the __focal length__ $$f.$$

__(a)__ Before calculating, use dimensional analysis. The focal length $$f$$ has dimensions of length and can depend only on the parameter $$a$$ (note that $$x$$ is a variable describing position along the mirror, not a parameter of its shape). What are the dimensions of $$a,$$ and what form must the formula for $$f$$ take? Does a steeper parabola (larger $$a$$) have a longer or a shorter focal length?

__(b)__ What is the slope of the parabola at the point $$(x, ax^2)?$$

__(c)__ Consider the special incoming ray that reflects off the mirror and then travels exactly __horizontally__, as in the figure below. What must the slope of the parabola be at the point where this ray strikes? Find the coordinates of that point in terms of $$a.$$

__(d)__ The reflected horizontal ray passes through the focal point, which lies on the axis of symmetry $$x = 0.$$ Use this to find the focal length $$f,$$ and check the result against part (a).

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: The Law of Reflection from Wave Interference — If you shine a laser straight down at a CD, some of the light…
desc: If you shine a laser straight down at a CD, some of the light bounces straight back up — but some reflects off at completely different angles, in violation of the law of reflection. The reason is interference: light leaves the CD's closely spaced grooves at the angles where…
statement:
If you shine a laser straight down at a CD, some of the light bounces straight back up — but some reflects off at completely different angles, in violation of the law of reflection. The reason is interference: light leaves the CD's closely spaced grooves at the angles where waves from adjacent grooves __constructively interfere__ (line up in phase). In this problem you will apply the same idea to a smooth, flat mirror and show that constructive interference happens only along the path that obeys the law of reflection — so the law of reflection is a consequence of the wave nature of light.

Light starts at point $$A$$ and reaches point $$B$$ after bouncing off a plane mirror. Imagine light from $$A$$ reflecting toward $$B$$ off __every__ point along the mirror, as in the figure (the heavy path is the one obeying the law of reflection). Recall that the __wavenumber__ $$k$$ of the light is the phase the wave picks up per unit distance traveled.

__(a)__ Focus on two nearby paths that strike the mirror at points a small horizontal distance $$d$$ apart. Both incoming legs descend toward the mirror at very nearly the same angle $$\theta$$ to the normal, as in the zoomed-in figure below. In terms of $$k,$$ $$d,$$ and $$\theta,$$ what is the phase difference between the two paths at the moment they reach the mirror? (Do not use a small-angle approximation.)

__(b)__ After reflecting, both paths travel on to $$B,$$ leaving the mirror at very nearly the same angle $$\phi$$ to the normal, as in the figure below. The path that was shorter on the way in is longer on the way out — be careful with signs. What is the __total__ phase difference between the two complete paths from $$A$$ to $$B?$$

__(c)__ For most reflection points on the mirror, the phase difference between nearby paths is not a multiple of $$2\pi,$$ and adding up the waves from many nearby reflection points averages to nearly zero amplitude. What condition on $$\theta$$ and $$\phi$$ makes nearby paths constructively interfere for __all__ small $$d?$$ Interpret your result.

__(d)__ Light of a fixed frequency picks up phase at a constant rate in time, so paths with equal phase are paths with equal travel time. Restate your result from part (c) as a general principle about the time light takes. This principle is called __Fermat's principle__, or the principle of stationary time.

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: Snell's Law from Fermat's Principle — Light travels at speed $$c$$ in vacuum and at the slower speed…
desc: Light travels at speed $$c$$ in vacuum and at the slower speed $$\dfrac{c}{n}$$ inside a transparent material, where $$n$$ is the material's __index of refraction__ (or __refractive index__). Air has $$n_{\mathrm{air}} \approx 1.0003,$$ while a typical glass has $$n \approx…
statement:
Light travels at speed $$c$$ in vacuum and at the slower speed $$\dfrac{c}{n}$$ inside a transparent material, where $$n$$ is the material's __index of refraction__ (or __refractive index__). Air has $$n_{\mathrm{air}} \approx 1.0003,$$ while a typical glass has $$n \approx 1.5.$$ For any wave, the speed, frequency, and wavelength are related by $$v = f\lambda.$$

__(a)__ A beam of light passes from air into glass. Which of the following properties of the light change: the speed, the frequency, the wavelength, the direction of travel? For the frequency, use this argument: peaks of the wave do not appear or disappear at the surface, so if a source emits $$N$$ wave peaks over a long time $$T,$$ all $$N$$ peaks must also pass any point inside the glass during that time.

__(b)__ __Fermat's principle__ says that light travels between two points along a path such that nearby paths take the same amount of time — for the refraction paths in this problem, the path of least time. Point $$A$$ is in the air and point $$B$$ is in the glass, as in the figure. Explain, using Fermat's principle, why light does __not__ travel from $$A$$ to $$B$$ in a straight line, and say which way the actual path bends.

__(c)__ Consider the actual path and a nearby path that crosses the air-glass surface a small distance $$d$$ away, as in the figures below. Let $$\theta_{\mathrm{air}}$$ and $$\theta_{\mathrm{glass}}$$ be the angles the two legs make with the normal to the surface. One of the two paths is longer in the air by a distance $$d\sin\theta_{\mathrm{air}};$$ the other is longer in the glass by $$d\sin\theta_{\mathrm{glass}}.$$ Convert these extra distances into extra travel __times__ (keep the indices of refraction $$n_{\mathrm{air}}$$ and $$n_{\mathrm{glass}}$$ in your expressions), then set the two extra times equal, as Fermat's principle requires, and simplify. The equation you find is called __Snell's law__.

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: A Plate with a Varying Index of Refraction (IPhO 1984) — This problem appeared at the 1984 International…
desc: This problem appeared at the 1984 International Physics Olympiad (Sweden). A transparent plate has an index of refraction $$n(z)$$ that varies continuously with the depth $$z$$ inside the plate. Light arrives from a medium with index $$n_A$$ at an angle $$\alpha$$ to the normal…
statement:
This problem appeared at the 1984 International Physics Olympiad (Sweden). A transparent plate has an index of refraction $$n(z)$$ that varies continuously with the depth $$z$$ inside the plate. Light arrives from a medium with index $$n_A$$ at an angle $$\alpha$$ to the normal, passes through the plate, and exits into a medium with index $$n_B$$ at an angle $$\beta$$ to the normal, as shown.

You may use __Snell's law__: when light crosses the interface between media with indices $$n_1$$ and $$n_2,$$ the angles to the normal obey $$n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2.$$ Show that $$n_A\sin\alpha = n_B\sin\beta,$$ no matter how $$n(z)$$ varies inside the plate.

__(a)__ Warm up with the simplest case: $$n(z) = n_0,$$ a constant. Apply Snell's law at the top and bottom surfaces and verify the claim.

__(b)__ Next suppose the plate has two layers with constant indices $$n_0$$ and $$n_1.$$ Verify the claim again.

__(c)__ Explain why the claim holds for any continuously varying $$n(z).$$

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: Building a Lens with Fermat's Principle — A __lens__ bends the light that passes through it. A…
desc: A __lens__ bends the light that passes through it. A __plano-convex__ lens is flat on one side; the other side is a piece of a sphere of radius $$R.$$ The lens is made of material with index of refraction $$n,$$ so light inside it travels at speed $$\dfrac{c}{n}$$ instead of…
statement:
A __lens__ bends the light that passes through it. A __plano-convex__ lens is flat on one side; the other side is a piece of a sphere of radius $$R.$$ The lens is made of material with index of refraction $$n,$$ so light inside it travels at speed $$\dfrac{c}{n}$$ instead of $$c.$$ Rays arriving parallel to the axis, perpendicular to the flat side, all converge to a single __focal point__ $$F$$ a distance $$f$$ — the __focal length__ — past the lens.

By __Fermat's principle__, light takes paths such that nearby paths take equal time. The light really does take __all__ of the drawn paths (running them from the focus outward or from outside to the focus takes the same time either way), and since they are all neighbors of one another, all of them must take the __same total time__. The outer paths travel farther, but the central paths pass through more of the slow lens material, and the two effects balance exactly. In this problem you will use that balance to find the lens's thickness profile, its focal length, and the lens equation. Let $$\tau(y)$$ be the thickness of the lens at height $$y$$ above the axis, and $$\tau_0 = \tau(0)$$ the thickness at the center. Assume the lens is thin and the rays are close to the axis: $$\tau_0 \ll R,$$ $$y \ll f,$$ and $$y \ll R.$$

__(a)__ First, a geometry result to be reused several times — call it the __lag theorem__. A ray travels from the focal point to the plane of the lens, arriving at height $$y$$ above the axis; compared with the ray along the axis, it covers an extra distance $$\delta.$$ Using the Pythagorean theorem, show that $$\delta \approx \dfrac{y^2}{2f}$$ when $$y \ll f.$$

__(b)__ A ray passes through a thickness $$\tau$$ of lens material. How much __extra time__ does this take, compared with covering the same distance $$\tau$$ in vacuum? Express your answer in terms of $$n,$$ $$\tau,$$ and $$c.$$

__(c)__ Fermat's principle requires the total time lag — the lag from the extra distance plus the lag inside the glass — to be the same for every ray, independent of $$y.$$ Use this to find the thickness profile $$\tau(y)$$ in terms of $$\tau_0,$$ $$y,$$ $$f,$$ and $$n.$$ Then interpret: why must the lens thin out away from its center, and why does a larger $$n$$ allow a thinner, flatter lens?

__(d)__ Now bring in the spherical shape of the curved surface. The amount by which the curved surface recedes at height $$y$$ — the difference $$\tau_0 - \tau(y)$$ — is given by the same lag-theorem geometry applied to the sphere of radius $$R:$$ $$\tau_0 - \tau \approx \dfrac{y^2}{2R}$$ (using $$\tau_0 \ll R$$). Combine this with part (c) to find the focal length $$f$$ in terms of $$R$$ and $$n.$$ The result is called the __lensmaker's equation__.

__(e)__ Finally, derive the __lens equation__. Light leaves an object on the axis a distance $$o$$ from the lens and converges to an image a distance $$i$$ past the lens. Apply the lag theorem on both the object side and the image side to find the total extra distance traveled by the ray crossing the lens at height $$y,$$ compared with the axial ray. The thickness profile from part (c) compensates an extra distance of exactly $$\dfrac{y^2}{2f}$$ — and it is the same lens, so it must be compensating this ray's extra distance too. Conclude a relation among $$o,$$ $$i,$$ and $$f.$$

lesson: PW113: Lenses and Mirrors
label: PW113
name: Two Lenses on a Cylinder — Two thin converging lenses are mounted on the ends of a hollow cylinder of length…
desc: Two thin converging lenses are mounted on the ends of a hollow cylinder of length $$L = 20\;\mathrm{cm},$$ one at each end, sharing the cylinder's axis as their common optical axis. You are given two facts about the system. Fact 1: if a point source of light is placed a distance…
statement:
Two thin converging lenses are mounted on the ends of a hollow cylinder of length $$L = 20\;\mathrm{cm},$$ one at each end, sharing the cylinder's axis as their common optical axis. You are given two facts about the system.

Fact 1: if a point source of light is placed a distance $$l_1 = 5\;\mathrm{cm}$$ to the left of the left lens, the light emerges from the right end of the cylinder as a parallel beam.

Fact 2: if a beam of light enters the left end of the cylinder parallel to the axis, the light emerging from the right end converges to a point on the axis a distance $$l_2 = 10\;\mathrm{cm}$$ to the right of the right lens.

Find the focal lengths $$f_1$$ (left lens) and $$f_2$$ (right lens). You may use the __lens equation__ $$\dfrac{1}{i} + \dfrac{1}{o} = \dfrac{1}{f}$$ for each thin lens, where $$o$$ is the object distance and $$i$$ the image distance, together with two standard facts: light emerges from a lens parallel to the axis exactly when its source (or an intermediate image acting as the source) sits at the lens's focal point, and a parallel beam entering a lens converges toward the lens's focal point.

__(a)__ Use Fact 1. The left lens forms an image of the point source; that image acts as the source for the right lens. For the final beam to be parallel, where must that intermediate image sit? Turn your answer into an equation relating $$l_1,$$ $$f_1,$$ $$f_2,$$ and $$L.$$

__(b)__ Use Fact 2. After the parallel beam passes the left lens, the light heads toward (or appears to come from) the left lens's focal point. Write the lens equation for the right lens in terms of $$l_2,$$ $$f_1,$$ $$f_2,$$ and $$L.$$

__(c)__ Solve the two equations. Each focal length satisfies a quadratic, so you should find __two__ solutions — show numerically that both are physically meaningful, and describe what the light does inside the cylinder in each case.

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Answer the following conceptual questions:
desc: Answer the following conceptual questions: **a)** Suppose it's a very hot day. Which would feel hotter to the touch - a metal sheet, or a piece of styrofoam? If both are sitting in the shade, which is actually hotter? Suppose it's a very cold day. Which would feel colder to the…
statement:
Answer the following conceptual questions:

**a)** Suppose it's a very hot day. Which would feel hotter to the touch - a metal sheet, or a piece of styrofoam? If both are sitting in the shade, which is actually hotter? Suppose it's a very cold day. Which would feel colder to the touch? Which is actually colder? If there's anything counterintuitive about these answers, explain how that could occur.

**b)** Many devices need to control how hot they get. A circuit that controls the temperature of a system is called a **thermostat**. A simple type of thermostat consists of a **bimetallic strip**, two pieces of different metals bolted together.

Explain what happens when the temperature of this strip changes. How could this be used to turn a circuit off once the temperature reached a certain point that was the hottest desired temperature?

**c)** Even if air pressure stays constant, the density of air changes from day to day. What are some reasons why?

**d)** A fever of $$105^\circ \mathrm{F}$$ will likely kill a human. However, a human can survive for long periods in $$105^\circ \mathrm{F}$$ heat without their body temperature increasing beyond normal. If heat always moves from hot (the air) to cool (the human), how is this possible?

**e)** Certain ants that live in the Sahara desert can also maintain body temperatures cooler than the surrounding air and sand. Given that they lack all the physiological mechanisms relevant for humans, how might they possibly do this? (Hint: it involves the way the ants' bodies interact with light.)
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Perform the following calculations:
desc: Perform the following calculations: **a)** The linear expansion coefficient of a material is defined as $$a_L = \dfrac{1}{L} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} L}{\mathrm{d} T}$$ where $$L$$ is the length of some object made of the material. The volumetric expansion coefficient is defined as…
statement:
Perform the following calculations:

**a)** The linear expansion coefficient of a material is defined as

$$a_L = \dfrac{1}{L} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} L}{\mathrm{d} T}$$

where $$L$$ is the length of some object made of the material.

The volumetric expansion coefficient is defined as

$$a_V = \dfrac{1}{V} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} T} $$

where $$V$$ is the volume of the object. How are these two expansion coefficients related, assuming the material expands isotropically (the same way in all directions)?

**b)** $$3$$ moles of an ideal gas expand isothermally from $$5\;\mathrm{atm}$$ to $$3\;\mathrm{atm}$$ at temperature $$0\;^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$ How much heat does the gas absorb?

**c)** One mole of a monatomic gas performs a Carnot cycle between $$400 \;\mathrm{K}$$ and $$300\;\mathrm{K}.$$ On the upper isothermal transformation, the initial volume is $$1\;\mathrm{L}$$ and the final volume is $$5\;\mathrm{L}.$$ Find the work performed during a cycle and the amount of heat exchanged with each heat reservoir.

**d)** You heat $$1\;\mathrm{L}$$ of water from $$0^\circ\;\mathrm{C}$$ to $$100^\circ\;\mathrm{C}.$$ How much does the entropy of the water increase? Ignore any expansion of the water or variation in the heat capacity.
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Make the following estimations:
desc: Make the following estimations: **a)** Consider two ways of heating a cold house in winter: A "space heater" is a device that runs current through a resistor. The power dissipated in the resistor is released as heat. By contrast, a "heat pump" is a device which also uses…
statement:
Make the following estimations:

**a)** Consider two ways of heating a cold house in winter:

A "space heater" is a device that runs current through a resistor. The power dissipated in the resistor is released as heat.

By contrast, a "heat pump" is a device which also uses electric current to heat an area, but in a very different way. The heat pump takes heat from outside (where it is cold) and moves the heat to inside (where it is warm).

Suppose both devices are as efficient as possible, given their designs described above. Which one is more efficient at warming up a house? Estimate how many times more efficient it is.

**b)** There is a theoretical limit for the efficiency of solar cells, called the "Shockley-Queisser" limit, of approximately $$33.7\%.$$ Does this limit derive from the second law of thermodynamics alone, or are the physical details of the solar cell involved? How do you know?

**c)** Suppose you were to climb Mount Everest. The amount of oxygen in the air would be reduced compared to sea level. By what fraction?

**d)** At sea level, the air is about $$20\%$$ oxygen, and you can consider the rest to be nitrogen. About what percentage would be oxygen at the top of Mount Everest if we model the air as isothermal and at equilibrium? In fact, the percentage of oxygen in the air at the top of Mount Everest is almost exactly the same as at sea level. Why might that be?

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: A Carnot cycle of an ideal gas consists of four steps. Each step is reversible.
desc: A Carnot cycle of an ideal gas consists of four steps. Each step is reversible. 1. Isothermal expansion at temperature $$T_H$$ 2. Adiabatic expansion until the temperature reaches $$T_C.$$ 3. Isothermal compression at temperature $$T_C.$$ 4. Adiabatic compression to return to…
statement:
A Carnot cycle of an ideal gas consists of four steps. Each step is reversible.

1. Isothermal expansion at temperature $$T_H$$ 2. Adiabatic expansion until the temperature reaches $$T_C.$$ 3. Isothermal compression at temperature $$T_C.$$ 4. Adiabatic compression to return to the original state of the system.

**a)** Draw a Carnot cycle on a PV diagram and a TS diagram.

**b)** Suppose that during step 1, the volume of the system expands from $$V_1$$ to $$V_2.$$ Find $$V_3,$$ the volume at the end of the adiabatic expansion, in terms of $$V_2.$$ Then find $$V_4,$$ the volume at the end of the isothermal compression.

**c)** Find net work done during the cycle.

**d)** Find the net heat absorbed during the cycle.

**e)** Compute the efficiency of the Carnot cycle, defined as the net work performed divided by the heat input during the isothermal expansion.

**f)** Show that a Carnot cycle from $$T_H$$ to $$T_C$$ has the same efficiency as two Carnot cycles, one from $$T_H$$ to $$T_M$$ and the second from $$T_M$$ to $$T_C,$$ where the second cycle takes in all the heat from the first cycle.

**g)** Suppose some cycle from $$T_H$$ to $$T_C$$ existed which was more efficient than the Carnot cycle. Remembering that the Carnot cycle is reversible (so it can take in work and move heat from $$T_C$$ to $$T_H$$ instead of taking in heat and outputting work as described earlier in this problem), show that it would be possible to construct a thermodynamic cycle with $$\Delta S_{\text{universe}} < 0,$$ and discuss what this means for the efficiency of a Carnot cycle.
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: **a)** A human metabolism is about $$2000\;\mathrm{Calories}$$ per day…
desc: **a)** A human metabolism is about $$2000\;\mathrm{Calories}$$ per day. $$1\;\mathrm{Calorie} = 4200\;\mathrm{J}.$$ What is the human metabolism in watts? **b)** Suppose a $$70\;\mathrm{kg}$$ person climbs a mountain, gaining $$1000\;\mathrm{m}$$ of elevation. If they did this…
statement:
**a)** A human metabolism is about $$2000\;\mathrm{Calories}$$ per day. $$1\;\mathrm{Calorie} = 4200\;\mathrm{J}.$$ What is the human metabolism in watts?

**b)** Suppose a $$70\;\mathrm{kg}$$ person climbs a mountain, gaining $$1000\;\mathrm{m}$$ of elevation. If they did this perfectly efficiently, by what fraction would their metabolism increase for the day?

**c)** Suppose an adult's body begins to generate a fever. (A fever is a defense mechanism engaged in by the body - the body deliberately increases its own temperature as an attempt to fight off an infection.) If all of their metabolism were directed into increasing their own temperature, how long would it take the person's body temperature to rise $$2\;\mathrm{K}?$$

**d)** When you breathe, moisture in your lungs gets turned into vapor in the air, which you then breathe out. It takes $$2500\;\mathrm{J}$$ to turn $$1\;\mathrm{g}$$ of room-temperature water into water-vapor. How much water per day would an adult (without a fever) need to lose via breathing if this were their only heat-loss mechanism?

**e)** Another way to lose heat is via radiation. We lose heat via radiation according to the equation

$$J = \epsilon \sigma T^4$$

where $$J$$ is the heat lost per unit time per unit surface area, $$\sigma$$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann Constant and is approximately $$\sigma = 5.7 \times 10^{-8} \dfrac{\mathrm{W}}{\mathrm{m^2K^4}},$$ and $$\epsilon$$ is the emissivity, which we take to be a number between zero and one.

Suppose $$\epsilon = 1$$ for humans. Then how many Calories of heat would a human lose via radiation each day. Your answer should pose a certain dilemma - how might you resolve that dilemma?

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Suppose the only use for energy when driving a car is overcoming air drag,
desc: Suppose the only use for energy when driving a car is overcoming air drag, $$ F_D = \dfrac12 C_D \rho_{\rm air} A v^2 $$ You can assume $$C_D = 0.25$$ and $$\rho_{\rm air} = 1.2 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ Estimate the best-possible gas mileage for a car driving $$60\;\mathrm{mph}$$…
statement:
Suppose the only use for energy when driving a car is overcoming air drag,

$$ F_D = \dfrac12 C_D \rho_{\rm air} A v^2 $$

You can assume $$C_D = 0.25$$ and $$\rho_{\rm air} = 1.2 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$

Estimate the best-possible gas mileage for a car driving $$60\;\mathrm{mph}$$ under such conditions. How much does this gas mileage change in cold weather versus hot weather?

You can assume that the energy stored in gasoline is $$46.4 \;\mathrm{MJ\cdot kg^{-1}}$$ (megajoules per kilogram) and one gallon of gasoline has a mass of $$2.9\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ The latent heat of vaporization of gasoline is around $$250\;\mathrm{kJ \cdot kg^{-1}}.$$ You can assume that the gas is a hydrocarbon which chemical formula $$\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}$$ for some $$n.$$ It is combined with oxygen in the air, and burns to create carbon dioxide and water.

For carbon dioxide, $$C_V = 54 \;\mathrm{J/(mol\;K)}$$. For water vapor, $$C_V = 44 \;\mathrm{J/(mol \; K)}.$$

Given the uncertainties and rough nature of your estimations, does the Carnot efficiency matter for your estimates? Real cars are around 20 - 25% efficient; does the second law explain that?

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Suppose a piston has a spring in it, pushing on its head. The spring constant is $$k.$$…
desc: Suppose a piston has a spring in it, pushing on its head. The spring constant is $$k.$$ The rest length of the spring is equal to the length of the piston, so that there is zero tension in the spring when the piston head is at the end of the piston. Some gas is inserted into the…
statement:
Suppose a piston has a spring in it, pushing on its head. The spring constant is $$k.$$ The rest length of the spring is equal to the length of the piston, so that there is zero tension in the spring when the piston head is at the end of the piston.

Some gas is inserted into the piston from the left. The pressure from the gas compresses the spring a distance $$x.$$

Suppose the gas is held at constant temperature by contact with the environment. (This means heat can transfer freely through the walls of the piston.)

**a)** Suppose the piston moves slightly to the right, so $$x$$ increases. What happens to the entropy of the gas?

**b)** Suppose the piston moves slightly to the right, so $$x$$ increases. What happens to the entropy of the surroundings?

**c)** In thermodynamics, a process will be **spontaneous** if it leads to higher total entropy. Find $$x$$ such that neither movement to the right nor movement to the left is spontaneous. This is the equilibrium position of the piston.

**d)** Interpret your answer to part (c) in terms of forces.

**e)** We found the equilibrium in (c) by considering entropy changes to the whole universe. It is often easier to consider only the system of interest, but this requires new ideas. Define the **Helmholtz free energy** of the piston by

$$ F = U - TS $$

where $$U$$ is the internal energy of the piston (including the spring) and $$S$$ is the entropy of the gas. Find $$x$$ such that the Helmholtz free energy is minimized.

**f)** Explain why, in general, for systems at constant temperature and which cannot do work on the environment we can maximize the entropy of the universe by minimizing the Helmholtz free energy of the system.
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Humans release about $$29 \;\mathrm{GT}$$ (gigatons) of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ gas per year…
desc: Humans release about $$29 \;\mathrm{GT}$$ (gigatons) of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ gas per year. ($$1\;\mathrm{GT} = 10^{12}\;\mathrm{kg}$$). The atmosphere of Earth contains about $$750\;\mathrm{GT}$$ of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ total. One idea to prevent atmospheric $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ from…
statement:
Humans release about $$29 \;\mathrm{GT}$$ (gigatons) of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ gas per year. ($$1\;\mathrm{GT} = 10^{12}\;\mathrm{kg}$$). The atmosphere of Earth contains about $$750\;\mathrm{GT}$$ of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ total.

One idea to prevent atmospheric $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ from increasing is to create machines which extract $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ directly from the air. What is the minimum power that must be used to extract $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ from the air at the same rate that humanity currently releases it?

For simplicity, you can assume the machine aims to keep the $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ as a gas at atmospheric pressure, but separate it from the rest of the gas in the atmosphere. That is, you can ignore any energy needed to compress the gas into a solid, or combine it with other materials in chemical reactions, etc.

Atmospheric pressure is about $$10^5 \;\mathrm{Pa}$$ and the radius of Earth is about $$6400\;\mathrm{km}.$$

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: A U-shaped tube contains a semi-permeable membrane - one through which water can pass…
desc: A U-shaped tube contains a semi-permeable membrane - one through which water can pass, but salt cannot. The membrane is fixed in place at the bottom of the tube. On the left side of the tube, there is salt water, in which the number of ions per unit volume is $$n.$$ On the right…
statement:
A U-shaped tube contains a semi-permeable membrane - one through which water can pass, but salt cannot. The membrane is fixed in place at the bottom of the tube.

On the left side of the tube, there is salt water, in which the number of ions per unit volume is $$n.$$ On the right hand side, there is fresh water. There is an equal amount of water on either side. The tube is held at constant temperature $$T.$$

**a)** Qualitatively describe what happens and why.

**b)** Calculate the parameters of the final equilibrium position of the system. You will need to invent variables and choose which variable to solve for.

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: A certain cyclic process with one mole of an ideal polyatomic gas can appear as a circle…
desc: A certain cyclic process with one mole of an ideal polyatomic gas can appear as a circle on the $$PV$$ diagram (with a suitable scaling of the axes). Coordinates of the circle center are $$(P_0,V_0).$$ The diameter along the pressure axis is $$2\Delta P,$$ and the diameter along…
statement:
A certain cyclic process with one mole of an ideal polyatomic gas can appear as a circle on the $$PV$$ diagram (with a suitable scaling of the axes). Coordinates of the circle center are $$(P_0,V_0).$$ The diameter along the pressure axis is $$2\Delta P,$$ and the diameter along the volume axis is $$2\Delta V.$$

Find all pairs of points on opposite sides of the circle (separated by 180 degrees) with equal heat capacities, $$\left.\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}T}\right|_{\text{cycle}}.$$ (This means neither a heat capacity at constant volume nor at constant pressure, but instead a heat capacity while staying on the circular path in the PV diagram.) Calculate these heat capacities.

Note: Assume that the heat capacity of a gas at constant volume, $$C_V,$$ is independent of $$T.$$ You may use $$C_V$$ and $$C_P$$ in your answers.

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: The Sonoluminescing Bubble (USAPhO 2011) — __Single-bubble sonoluminescence__ occurs when sound waves cause a…
desc: __Single-bubble sonoluminescence__ occurs when sound waves cause a bubble suspended in a fluid to collapse so that the gas trapped inside increases in temperature enough to emit light. The bubble actually undergoes a series of expansions and collapses caused by the sound-wave…
statement:
__Single-bubble sonoluminescence__ occurs when sound waves cause a bubble suspended in a fluid to collapse so that the gas trapped inside increases in temperature enough to emit light. The bubble actually undergoes a series of expansions and collapses caused by the sound-wave pressure variations. This problem, from __USAPhO 2011__, considers a simplified model of a bubble undergoing sonoluminescence.

Assume the bubble is originally at atmospheric pressure $$P_0 = 101\;\mathrm{kPa}.$$ When the pressure in the fluid surrounding the bubble is decreased, the bubble expands __isothermally__ (at constant temperature) to a radius of $$36.0\;\mathrm{\mu m}.$$ When the pressure increases again, the bubble collapses to a radius of $$4.50\;\mathrm{\mu m}$$ so quickly that no heat can escape. Between the collapse and the subsequent expansion, the bubble undergoes __isochoric__ (constant-volume) cooling back to its original pressure and temperature. The bubble contains a monatomic gas and is suspended in water at $$T = 293\;\mathrm{K}.$$

The cycle is sketched on the __pressure-volume (PV) diagram__ below: $$A\to B$$ is the isothermal expansion (it follows an __isotherm__, the hyperbola $$PV=\text{constant}$$), $$B\to C$$ is the rapid collapse (it follows an __adiabat__), and $$C\to A$$ is the isochoric cooling, a vertical drop back to the start.

You may find the following useful. The __ideal gas law__: $$PV = nRT,$$ where $$n$$ is the number of moles and $$R = 8.31\;\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}$$ is the gas constant. The __first law of thermodynamics__: $$\Delta U = Q - W,$$ where $$U$$ is the internal energy of the gas, $$Q$$ is the heat added to it, and $$W$$ is the work done __by__ it. For a monatomic ideal gas, $$U = \tfrac32 nRT,$$ the molar heat capacity at constant volume is $$C_V = \tfrac32 R,$$ and the adiabatic index is $$\gamma = C_P/C_V = \tfrac53.$$ A reversible adiabatic process obeys $$PV^\gamma = \text{constant},$$ and the work done by an ideal gas expanding isothermally from $$V_1$$ to $$V_2$$ is $$W = nRT\,\ln(V_2/V_1).$$

__(a)__ Find the number of moles of gas in the bubble. (Careful: the problem mentions two radii. Decide which one describes the bubble while it is at atmospheric pressure and at the temperature of the water.)

__(b)__ Find the pressure after the expansion. (A shortcut: if the radius of a gas bubble grows by a factor $$\alpha$$ at constant temperature, by what factor does its pressure change?)

__(c)__ Find the pressure after the collapse.

__(d)__ Find the temperature after the collapse.

__(e)__ Find the total work done __on__ the bubble during the whole cycle.
