lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Heat or Work? — In thermodynamics, energy can enter or leave a system in exactly two ways: as __heat__ or…
desc: In thermodynamics, energy can enter or leave a system in exactly two ways: as __heat__ or as __work__. Roughly speaking, energy is transferred as __work__ when the transfer is macroscopic — a single coordinated force acting through a distance, or a single electric current…
statement:
In thermodynamics, energy can enter or leave a system in exactly two ways: as __heat__ or as __work__. Roughly speaking, energy is transferred as __work__ when the transfer is macroscopic — a single coordinated force acting through a distance, or a single electric current charging a capacitor. Energy is transferred as __heat__ when the transfer is microscopic — billions of tiny, random, uncoordinated pushes, like air molecules from a fire colliding with an object, or electrons rattling the nuclei of a resistor.

Importantly, heat and work describe __how energy is transferred__, not types of energy stored in an object. We never say a body "contains heat" or "contains work"; after the transfer the energy is stored as thermal energy, elastic energy, kinetic energy, and so on. The __first law of thermodynamics__ expresses energy conservation: $$\Delta U = Q - W,$$ where $$U$$ is the system's internal energy, $$Q$$ is the energy that enters as heat, and $$W$$ is the work done __by__ the system. (Some books define $$W$$ as work done __on__ the system, flipping its sign; both conventions are valid, so always check.)

__(a)__ You give a toy car a single large push to set it moving. Did you transfer energy to the car as heat or as work?

__(b)__ You light a fire near the car, and hot gas from the fire strikes it, warming it up. Heat or work?

__(c)__ Energy is transferred into a car and, as a result, the car gets hotter. Can you conclude the energy was transferred as heat? If not, give a counterexample.

__(d)__ Energy is transferred into a car and, as a result, the car starts to move. Can you conclude the energy was transferred as work? If not, devise a mechanism (however inefficient) by which energy entering as heat could set the car moving. What is the general name for a device that does this?

__(e)__ The gas in a bubble is compressed so quickly that no heat is exchanged, and its temperature rises. Using the first law, determine the sign of $$W$$ for the gas during the compression, and interpret the sign physically.
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Free Expansion — In a __free expansion__, a gas in a thermally insulated container is allowed to rush out…
desc: In a __free expansion__, a gas in a thermally insulated container is allowed to rush out into a vacuum — for example, a partition is removed so the gas suddenly has a larger volume available, with nothing on the other side to push against. The figure below shows the gas before…
statement:
In a __free expansion__, a gas in a thermally insulated container is allowed to rush out into a vacuum — for example, a partition is removed so the gas suddenly has a larger volume available, with nothing on the other side to push against. The figure below shows the gas before, during, and after.

Background you may use: the first law of thermodynamics is $$\Delta U = Q - W,$$ where $$W$$ is the work done by the gas and a gas does work $$\mathrm{d}W = P\,\mathrm{d}V$$ only by pushing something as it expands. An __ideal gas__ is one whose intermolecular potential energy is negligible, so its internal energy is purely the kinetic energy of its molecules and depends only on temperature: $$U = C_V nT.$$

__(a)__ During a free expansion of an ideal gas, how much heat is exchanged, and how much work does the gas do? What happens to its temperature?

__(b)__ A real gas usually cools slightly during a free expansion. Explain why, using the potential energy of the molecules. (Real gas molecules weakly attract one another.)

__(c)__ A PV diagram tracks a system's pressure and volume as it undergoes a process. Why can a free expansion not be drawn as a curve on a PV diagram, even though its start and end points can be plotted?
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Two Heat Capacities — Consider this question: "Suppose you add $$2\;\mathrm{J}$$ of energy as heat to one…
desc: Consider this question: "Suppose you add $$2\;\mathrm{J}$$ of energy as heat to one mole of an ideal gas. How much does its temperature rise?" Background you may use: the first law of thermodynamics is $$\mathrm{d}U = \mathrm{d}Q - \mathrm{d}W,$$ with $$W$$ the work done by the…
statement:
Consider this question: "Suppose you add $$2\;\mathrm{J}$$ of energy as heat to one mole of an ideal gas. How much does its temperature rise?"

Background you may use: the first law of thermodynamics is $$\mathrm{d}U = \mathrm{d}Q - \mathrm{d}W,$$ with $$W$$ the work done by the gas. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, $$U = C_V nT,$$ where the constant $$C_V$$ (the __molar heat capacity at constant volume__) depends on the gas: $$C_V = \tfrac32 R$$ for a monatomic gas and $$C_V = \tfrac52 R$$ for a diatomic gas like $$\mathrm{O_2}.$$ The ideal gas law is $$PV = nRT$$ with $$R = 8.31\;\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}.$$ In mechanics, work is $$\mathrm{d}W = \vec F\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec x.$$

__(a)__ Explain why the question, exactly as posed above, cannot be answered. There are at least two separate reasons.

__(b)__ Suppose a gas at pressure $$P$$ pushes a plate of area $$A$$ outward by a small distance $$\mathrm{d}x,$$ perpendicular to the plate, as shown. Show that the work the gas does can be written $$\mathrm{d}W = P\,\mathrm{d}V,$$ where $$\mathrm{d}V$$ is the increase in the gas's volume. Conclude that a gas held at constant volume (an __isochoric__ process) does no work.

__(c)__ Now answer the repaired question: $$2\;\mathrm{J}$$ of heat is added to one mole of a __monatomic__ ideal gas __at constant volume__. How much does the temperature rise?

__(d)__ Suppose instead the heat is added while the gas is held at constant __pressure__. To achieve the same temperature rise as in part (c), will more, less, or the same amount of heat be needed? Explain physically before calculating anything.

__(e)__ Define the __molar heat capacity at constant pressure__ as $$C_P = \dfrac1n\left.\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}T}\right|_P$$ (the bar means pressure is held constant). By writing $$\mathrm{d}Q = \mathrm{d}U + P\,\mathrm{d}V$$ and using the differential of the ideal gas law, prove that $$C_P = C_V + R.$$
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: The Shape of an Adiabat — An __adiabatic__ process is one in which no heat is exchanged: $$\mathrm{d}Q = 0.$$…
desc: An __adiabatic__ process is one in which no heat is exchanged: $$\mathrm{d}Q = 0.$$ A process can be adiabatic because the system is well insulated (like a thermos) or simply because it happens too fast for significant heat to flow — sound waves compressing air and a rapidly…
statement:
An __adiabatic__ process is one in which no heat is exchanged: $$\mathrm{d}Q = 0.$$ A process can be adiabatic because the system is well insulated (like a thermos) or simply because it happens too fast for significant heat to flow — sound waves compressing air and a rapidly collapsing bubble are both adiabatic for this reason. On a PV diagram, the curve traced by a reversible adiabatic process is called an __adiabat__. This problem derives its equation for an ideal gas.

Everything you need is in these four equations: the ideal gas law $$PV = nRT;$$ the first law of thermodynamics $$\mathrm{d}U = \mathrm{d}Q - \mathrm{d}W;$$ the work done by a gas $$\mathrm{d}W = P\,\mathrm{d}V;$$ and the internal energy of an ideal gas $$U = C_V nT.$$ You may also use the fact that the molar heat capacities satisfy $$C_P = C_V + R.$$

__(a)__ Set $$\mathrm{d}Q = 0,$$ take differentials where needed, and reduce the four equations to the pair $$P\,\mathrm{d}V + V\,\mathrm{d}P = nR\,\mathrm{d}T$$ and $$C_V n\,\mathrm{d}T = -P\,\mathrm{d}V.$$

__(b)__ We want a curve on the PV plane, so eliminate $$\mathrm{d}T$$ between the two equations. Show that the result can be written $$\dfrac{C_P}{C_V}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{V} + \dfrac{\mathrm{d}P}{P} = 0.$$

__(c)__ Integrate to show that along an adiabat $$PV^\gamma = \text{constant},$$ where $$\gamma = \dfrac{C_P}{C_V}$$ is called the __adiabatic index__ or __heat capacity ratio__ ($$\gamma = \tfrac53$$ for a monatomic gas, $$\tfrac75$$ for a diatomic gas).

__(d)__ Combine your result with the ideal gas law to show that an adiabatic process also satisfies $$TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}.$$

__(e)__ An adiabat and an isotherm ($$PV = \text{constant}$$) pass through the same point $$(V, P)$$ of a PV diagram, as shown below. Compare their slopes at that point, and explain physically why the adiabat is the steeper curve.

(The class first met $$PV^\gamma = \text{constant}$$ when analyzing the oscillations of a thermally insulated piston; this derivation shows where it comes from.)
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Sliding Weights and the Meaning of Reversibility — In classical thermodynamics, entropy $$S$$ is defined by…
desc: In classical thermodynamics, entropy $$S$$ is defined by $$\mathrm{d}S = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q_{\text{reversible}}}{T}.$$ The subscript matters: the formula applies only to __reversible__ processes — ones that stay arbitrarily close to equilibrium at every moment. Equivalently, a…
statement:
In classical thermodynamics, entropy $$S$$ is defined by $$\mathrm{d}S = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q_{\text{reversible}}}{T}.$$ The subscript matters: the formula applies only to __reversible__ processes — ones that stay arbitrarily close to equilibrium at every moment. Equivalently, a process is reversible if the system could be returned to its initial state __without any external work being done on it__. (The definition is not "is it possible to undo this process?" — almost anything can be undone if you are willing to do work.) This problem builds intuition for what reversibility means.

A vertical piston contains gas. Heat passes freely through the piston walls, so the gas stays at the surrounding temperature whenever it is in equilibrium. A weight sits on top of the piston head, compressing the gas. Beside the piston is a shelf at exactly the height of the bottom of the weight; the weight can be slid horizontally and frictionlessly between the piston head and the shelf, which takes no work as long as the two are at the same level.

__(a)__ The weight is slid off onto the shelf. Describe what the piston does before settling into its new equilibrium, noticeably higher than before. To return the system to its initial state, what would have to be done? Is the expansion reversible?

__(b)__ Start over with the single weight replaced by two weights, each half as heavy, with shelves available at whatever heights are needed. The weights are slid off one at a time, the piston settling between slides. Explain how the system can now be returned to its initial state with __less__ external work than in part (a). (Hint: after the piston rises, which weight should be lifted, and onto what?)

__(c)__ Now replace the weights with a pile of sand. One grain at a time is slid off onto a shelf at exactly that grain's height. How much external work does it take to restore the system this time? Is the process reversible?

__(d)__ While the piston oscillates and settles after each slide, its motion is damped out by __dissipative forces__ — friction and air drag, i.e. complicated randomized molecular interactions that turn coordinated motion into heat. Combine your observations into a general statement about reversible processes in the real world, and about the price paid for getting close to reversibility. How is this statement expressed in terms of the entropy of the universe?
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Which Way Does Heat Flow? — When a small amount of heat $$\mathrm{d}Q$$ enters a body reversibly at…
desc: When a small amount of heat $$\mathrm{d}Q$$ enters a body reversibly at temperature $$T,$$ the body's entropy changes by $$\mathrm{d}S = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{T}$$ (with $$\mathrm{d}Q$$ negative if heat leaves). The __second law of thermodynamics__ says the total entropy of the…
statement:
When a small amount of heat $$\mathrm{d}Q$$ enters a body reversibly at temperature $$T,$$ the body's entropy changes by $$\mathrm{d}S = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{T}$$ (with $$\mathrm{d}Q$$ negative if heat leaves). The __second law of thermodynamics__ says the total entropy of the universe never decreases: $$\mathrm{d}S_{\text{universe}} \ge 0,$$ with equality only in the idealized reversible limit.

A hot block of metal at temperature $$T_H$$ and a cold block at temperature $$T_C < T_H$$ are placed in contact. You know from experience which way heat flows — this problem shows the second law demanding it. Suppose, for contradiction, that a small amount of heat $$\mathrm{d}Q > 0$$ flows out of the cold block and into the hot block.

__(a)__ What is the entropy change of the hot block?

__(b)__ What is the entropy change of the cold block?

__(c)__ Find the total entropy change of the universe (the two blocks are the only things involved), determine its sign, and state what the second law concludes about heat flowing from cold to hot. Check that heat flowing the other way — hot to cold — is consistent with the second law.

__(d)__ A __heat pump__ is a device that keeps a house warm in winter by moving energy as heat from the cold outdoors to the warm indoors — apparently exactly the forbidden direction. Heat pumps run on electricity. Explain why a working heat pump does not violate the second law, and what would be special about an ideal, reversible heat pump.
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: The Entropy of an Isothermal Expansion — "Find the entropy of an ideal gas." That is vague, so make it…
desc: "Find the entropy of an ideal gas." That is vague, so make it concrete: compute the entropy __change__ of $$n$$ moles of an ideal gas that expands reversibly and isothermally from volume $$V_1$$ to volume $$V_2.$$ Background you may use: entropy is defined for reversible…
statement:
"Find the entropy of an ideal gas." That is vague, so make it concrete: compute the entropy __change__ of $$n$$ moles of an ideal gas that expands reversibly and isothermally from volume $$V_1$$ to volume $$V_2.$$

Background you may use: entropy is defined for reversible processes by $$\mathrm{d}S = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q_{\text{reversible}}}{T};$$ the first law is $$\mathrm{d}U = \mathrm{d}Q - \mathrm{d}W$$ with $$\mathrm{d}W = P\,\mathrm{d}V$$ the work done by the gas; the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature; and the ideal gas law is $$PV = nRT.$$

__(a)__ In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, what is $$\mathrm{d}Q$$ in terms of $$P$$ and $$\mathrm{d}V?$$ (Watch out: isothermal is not the same as adiabatic — the gas here is in contact with its surroundings and absorbs heat as it expands.)

__(b)__ Use the ideal gas law to eliminate $$P$$ and $$T,$$ then integrate to find $$\Delta S$$ for the expansion from $$V_1$$ to $$V_2.$$

__(c)__ Classical thermodynamics can only ever give entropy __changes__. Quantum statistical mechanics goes further: for a monatomic ideal gas the absolute entropy is given by the __Sackur-Tetrode equation__, $$S = Nk_B\left(\ln\left(\dfrac{V}{N}\left(\dfrac{4\pi m}{3h^2}\,\dfrac{U}{N}\right)^{3/2}\right) + \dfrac52\right),$$ where $$N$$ is the number of atoms, $$m$$ is the mass per atom, $$h$$ is Planck's constant, and $$U$$ is the internal energy. You do not need to derive or memorize this — but show that for an isothermal expansion it reproduces your answer to part (b). (Recall $$Nk_B = nR,$$ and $$\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b.$$)
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: Answer the following conceptual questions:
desc: Answer the following conceptual questions: **a)** Consider two ways people have thought about making something go faster than the speed of light: 1 - You shine a laser pointer on the moon. You shake the laser pointer back and forth very quickly, so the dot the laser pointer…
statement:
Answer the following conceptual questions:

**a)** Consider two ways people have thought about making something go faster than the speed of light:

1 - You shine a laser pointer on the moon. You shake the laser pointer back and forth very quickly, so the dot the laser pointer makes on the moon moves faster than the speed of light.

2 - You have a very long pair of scissors. As you cut with the scissors, at the moment shortly before the scissors close completely, the point where the blades meet moves with a speed faster than the speed of light.

Both of these scenarios are indeed possible in theory (although engineering the appropriate laser point and scissors would be difficult, it isn't disallowed by relativity). So why can we say that "nothing move faster than light" in relativity?

**b)** Suppose Ursula and Vernor live a far way apart from each other, but stationary with respect to each other. They are capable of communicating much faster than light via an ansible (a hypothetical type of phone).

Every morning, Ursula flips a coin. If the coin comes up heads, she calls Vernor and says "Good morning, Vernor!" Then Vernor replies, "Good morning, Ursula!" If the coin comes up tails, Ursula calls Vernor and says "How are you?" to which Vernor replies "I'm fine, thanks." Assume that the time between Ursula flipping the coin and making the call is small, and so is the time between Vernor hearing Ursula's message and responding.

Consider the following events:

1 - Ursula flips a coin 2 - Ursula speaks into ansible 3 - Vernor hears what Ursula said 4 - Vernor replies to Ursula 5 - Ursula hears what Vernor said

In the reference from where Ursula and Vernor are at rest, these events are in chronological order 1-2-3-4-5.

In the frame of an observer moving from Ursula to Vernor at an appreciable fraction of light speed, what is the order of the events? How about in the frame of an observer moving from Vernor to Ursula?

**c)** Suppose there is a block of wood that is $$5 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ thick in its own rest frame. It moves at relativistic speed toward a stationary drill that is $$4\;\mathrm{cm}$$ long. However, due to length contraction, the block is only $$3\;\mathrm{cm}$$ thick in the frame of the drill. So in the frame of the drill, the drill is long enough to drill a hole all the way through the block. However, in the block's frame, the block is $$5\;\mathrm{cm}$$ thick, but the drill is only $$\dfrac{12}{5}\;\mathrm{cm}$$ long. So in the block's frame, the drill is not long enough to drill through the block. Imagine the block continues towards the drill until the front of the block reaches the back of the drill bit. Then the block instantaneously turns around. Does the drill go through the block or not?

**d)** In a recent problem of the day, we considered riding a bike on a treadmill, asking whether it was as difficult to ride up an inclined treadmill as to ride up a hill of the same incline outdoors (neglecting wind, etc.) Answer that question again not by considering the work done, but purely from the relativity principle.
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: Perform the following computations:
desc: Perform the following computations: **a)** An object emits light at a constant frequency in its own frame. When it moves toward you at speed $$v,$$ you observe the frequency to be $$f.$$ When it moves away from you at speed $$v,$$ you observe the frequency to be $$f'.$$ Find…
statement:
Perform the following computations:

**a)** An object emits light at a constant frequency in its own frame. When it moves toward you at speed $$v,$$ you observe the frequency to be $$f.$$ When it moves away from you at speed $$v,$$ you observe the frequency to be $$f'.$$ Find $$v.$$

**b)** In some frame, Ursula and Vernor have a relative velocity of $$1.2 c.$$ Is this enough to determine Ursula's velocity in Vernor's frame? If so, what is it? If not, give the range of possible velocities of Ursula in Vernor's frame.

**c)** Suppose you want to go from a speed $$0$$ to a speed $$v$$ relative to Earth. You want to do this in two jumps of velocity, each the same size as measured in whatever your rest frame is at the beginning of the jump. How large should each jump be?

**d)** Consider the following problem:

"$$A$$ and $$B$$ are rockets moving toward each other. $$C$$ is in between them, and in $$C$$'s frame, the distance between them is $$d_C.$$ According to $$C,$$ the speeds of $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$v_A$$ and $$v_B$$ (both approaching $$C$$, but from opposite sides.) In $$A$$'s reference frame, how long will it be until the rockets meet?"

Ursula solves this problem by first finding the time $$t_C$$ for the rockets to meet in $$C$$'s reference frame, $$t_C = \dfrac{d_C}{v_A + v_B}$$. Then, she uses the Lorentz factor $$\gamma_A.$$ From $$A$$'s perspective, $$C$$'s clock is running slow by a factor $$\gamma_A,$$ so $$\begin{aligned} t_A &= \gamma_A t_C. \\[6pt] &= \gamma_A \dfrac{d_C}{v_A + v_B}. \end{aligned}$$

Vernor finds $$\gamma_A$$ and uses length contraction to find $$d_A = \dfrac{d_C}{\gamma_A}$$ to be the distance between $$A$$ and $$B$$ in $$A$$'s frame. Next, he uses velocity addition to find that $$v_{B;A} = \dfrac{v_A + v_B}{1 + v_Av_B/c^2}$$ is the speed of $$B$$ in the frame of $$A.$$ With a distance and a speed, he divides to find $$\begin{aligned} t_A &= \dfrac{d_A}{v_{B;a}} \\[8pt] &= \dfrac{d_C\left(1 + \dfrac{v_Av_B}{c^2}\right)}{\gamma_A (v_A + v_B)} \end{aligned}$$

These answers aren't the same, though. Who is right - Ursula, Vernor, or neither? And why?
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: Make the following estimations:
desc: Make the following estimations: **a)** Estimate the Lorentz factor $$\gamma$$ when $$\dfrac{v}{c} = 0.01$$ without using a calculator. **b)** Estimate the Lorentz factor $$\gamma$$ when $$\dfrac{v}{c} = 0.99$$ without using a calculator. **c)** Suppose you take drive across the…
statement:
Make the following estimations:

**a)** Estimate the Lorentz factor $$\gamma$$ when $$\dfrac{v}{c} = 0.01$$ without using a calculator.

**b)** Estimate the Lorentz factor $$\gamma$$ when $$\dfrac{v}{c} = 0.99$$ without using a calculator.

**c)** Suppose you take drive across the country, then drive back. If you had a very-accurate clock that you left and home and another that you took with you, and they were synchronized before you left, estimate how different their times would be when you got back. (Ignore the general relativistic-effect of time dilation that occurs because the airplane is at high elevation.) What if you had flown instead?

**d)** A mathematical model for Brownian motion starts with a random walk.

In a simple random walk, once per unit of time $$\tau$$, an object moves either left or right with equal probability, always a distance $$L$$.

In Brownian motion, we take the limit of a random walk such that $$\tau \to 0$$ holding the diffusion constant, $$D = \dfrac{L^2}{2\tau}$$ fixed.

Brownian motion is a good model to use when watching a particle diffusing over a long time. Use special relativity to argue that it cannot be a perfect model over very short times. Find a time $$t_m(D)$$ such that the Brownian motion model can't work at times shorter than $$t_m.$$
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: The famous ``twin paradox'' begins with a pair of twins, call them Ursula and Vernor, who…
desc: The famous ``twin paradox'' begins with a pair of twins, call them Ursula and Vernor, who live on Earth. Ursula takes a spaceship ride at a $$v = \dfrac35 c$$ to a distant star $$3\;\mathrm{ly}$$ away, then turns around and comes back at the same speed. When she returns, Vernor…
statement:
The famous ``twin paradox'' begins with a pair of twins, call them Ursula and Vernor, who live on Earth. Ursula takes a spaceship ride at a $$v = \dfrac35 c$$ to a distant star $$3\;\mathrm{ly}$$ away, then turns around and comes back at the same speed. When she returns, Vernor has aged many more years than Ursula has.

This is often called a paradox because, if we consider Ursula's perspective, it sounds as if Ursula stayed in place and Vernor went away and turned around again, so that Vernor should be younger.

**a)** Why is Ursula the younger twin when they rejoin, not Vernor?

Below is a spacetime diagram showing the worldline of Ursula.

**b)** How much does Ursula age during the outbound trip?

**c)** When Ursula returns to Earth, how much older is Vernor than Ursula?

**d)** Once per year (of time experience by Vernor), Vernor sends out a radio message to Ursula saying "Happy Birthday!". Copy the spacetime diagram and draw in worldlines of these messages.

**e)** During Ursula's outbound journey, what is the time experienced by Ursula between receipt of birthday messages from Vernor?

**f)** During Ursula's return journey, what is the time experience by Ursula between receipt of birthday messages from Vernor?

**g)** How many total birthday messages does Ursula receive?

**h)** Ursula also sends a birthday message to Vernor, once per year of time as experienced by Ursula. What is the time between receipt of these messages for Vernor? How many of them are there?
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: Laboratory observers measure the length of a moving rod lying along its direction of…
desc: Laboratory observers measure the length of a moving rod lying along its direction of motion in the laboratory frame. Then the rod speeds up a little. Again laboratory observers measure its length, which they find to be a little shorter than before. They call this shortening of…
statement:
Laboratory observers measure the length of a moving rod lying along its direction of motion in the laboratory frame. Then the rod speeds up a little. Again laboratory observers measure its length, which they find to be a little shorter than before. They call this shortening of length Lorentz contraction. How did this shortening of length come about? As happens so often in relativity, the answer lies in the relativity of simultaneity .

First, how much shortening takes place when the rod changes from speed v to speed $$v + \mathrm{d}v?$$ Let $$L_0$$ be the proper length of the rod when measured at rest. At speed $$v$$ its laboratory-measured length $$L$$ will be shorter than this by the Lorentz contraction factor:

$$ L = \dfrac{L_0}{\gamma} $$

**a)** Find the change in length $$\mathrm{d}L$$ of the rod when it speeds up from $$v$$ to a slightly greater speed $$v + \mathrm{d}v.$$

**b)** We would like to understand the kinematics of the shortening of the rod you analyzed in part (a).

Imagine the front of the rod and the back of the rod both have little rockets attached to them. In order for the rod to speed up, these rockets fire at the same time in the rod's frame.

Which rocket fires first in the lab frame, and by how much?

**c)** Show that the delay you calculated in (b) explains the shortening of the rod you calculated in (a).
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: A rectangular prism piece of glass with index of refraction $$n = 1.5$$ moves to the…
desc: A rectangular prism piece of glass with index of refraction $$n = 1.5$$ moves to the right at speed $$v = \dfrac{12}{13}c$$. A light beam is incident on the piece of glass at an angle $$\theta_1 = 45^\circ$$ to the normal to the glass, with the light moving both toward the glass…
statement:
A rectangular prism piece of glass with index of refraction $$n = 1.5$$ moves to the right at speed $$v = \dfrac{12}{13}c$$. A light beam is incident on the piece of glass at an angle $$\theta_1 = 45^\circ$$ to the normal to the glass, with the light moving both toward the glass and to the right. (So the glass and light are moving partially in the same direction.)

Find $$\theta_2,$$ the angle of the light with respect to the normal inside the glass, and $$\theta_3,$$ the angle of the light with respect to the normal on leaving the glass.
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: Electrons and positrons can be combined to create photons (a process called…
desc: Electrons and positrons can be combined to create photons (a process called **annihilation**), and photons can be destroyed to create electrons and positrons (called **pair production**). Imagine two boxes, $$A$$ and $$B$$, with equipment to facilitate annihilation and pair…
statement:
Electrons and positrons can be combined to create photons (a process called **annihilation**), and photons can be destroyed to create electrons and positrons (called **pair production**).

Imagine two boxes, $$A$$ and $$B$$, with equipment to facilitate annihilation and pair production. $$A$$ begins with some electrons and positrons (collectively called its matter) while $$B$$ is empty.

$$A$$ annihilates its matter and sends the resulting photons to $$B$$, which is to its right. Then $$B$$ uses pair production to create matter. In this way, matter is passed from $$A$$ to $$B$$ without being lost.

Next, imagine the same process, but with $$A$$ on the ground and $$B$$ up on a platform above $$A.$$ Matter moves from $$A$$ to $$B$$.

**a)** Argue that in the vertical experiment $$B$$ cannot receive the same amount of matter that $$A$$ sent, or else a fundamental law of physics would be violated. (In the horizontal experiment, $$B$$ can receive the same amount of matter $$A$$ sent.)

**b)** Suppose the mass of the matter originally in $$A$$ was $$m,$$ the height between $$A$$ and $$B$$ is $$h,$$ and local gravitational acceleration is $$g$$ (assumed uniform). Assuming no matter is lost going from $$A$$ to $$B,$$ quantify the size of the violation of the physical law you described in part (a).

**c)** General relativity predicts a phenomena called **gravitational redshift**. Argue that if this phenomena works the same way as the Doppler shift, shifting photons to a lower frequency as they travel through a gravitational field, it can explain the results of the above experiment.

**d)** Suppose one photon of $$\lambda = 600\;\mathrm{nm}$$ is generated at the ground and another is generated $$20\;\mathrm{m}$$ above the ground. Find the beat frequency between these two photons when they are brought together.
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: **a)** Suppose a spaceship begins at rest relative to Earth. The ship accelerates in a…
desc: **a)** Suppose a spaceship begins at rest relative to Earth. The ship accelerates in a straight line at $$a.$$ Using Newtonian physics, find the time it would take the spaceship to reach $$c,$$ the speed of light. This is the time scale on which relativistic corrections become…
statement:
**a)** Suppose a spaceship begins at rest relative to Earth. The ship accelerates in a straight line at $$a.$$ Using Newtonian physics, find the time it would take the spaceship to reach $$c,$$ the speed of light. This is the time scale on which relativistic corrections become important for finding the trajectory of the ship.

**b)** In one dimension, the relativistic velocity addition law is

$$ v' = \dfrac{u+v}{1 + \dfrac{uv}{c^2}} $$

where $$v$$ is the velocity of an object in some frame $$S,$$ $$u$$ is the velocity of some other frame $$S'$$ relative to $$S,$$ and $$v'$$ is the velocity of the object in $$S'.$$

Suppose $$u$$ is very small and denote it $$\mathrm{d}u.$$ Find $$v' - v \equiv \mathrm{d}v$$ to first order in $$\mathrm{d}u$$.

**c)** Now suppose a spaceship experiences __proper acceleration__ $$a.$$ This means that, at any event, if we transform into a reference frame where the ship's velocity is momentarily $$0,$$ the ship's acceleration is $$a$$ in that frame.

Extending your answer from part (b), find a differential equation for the velocity of the ship in the Earth's frame as a function of time in the Earth's frame. Separate variables in the differential equation.

**d)** Recall the hyperbolic trigonometric functions,

\begin{aligned} \sinh(\phi) & = \dfrac{e^\phi - e^{-\phi}}{2} \\ \cosh(\phi) & = \dfrac{e^\phi + e^{-\phi}}{2} \\ \tanh(\phi) & = \dfrac{\sinh\phi}{\cosh\phi} \end{aligned}

(You may wish to verify that for these functions, $$\mathrm{cosh}^2\phi - \mathrm{sinh}^2\phi - 1.$$)

Let $$\dfrac{v}{c} = \tanh\phi$$ and use this substitution to solve the differential equation from part (c). Solve for $$v$$ as a function of $$t.$$

Accelerating at $$g,$$ how long would it take a spaceship to reach $$0.1c$$ in the Earth frame? How long to reach $$0.5c?$$ How long to reach $$0.99c?$$
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: In the previous problem, we solved a differential equation for velocity addition using…
desc: In the previous problem, we solved a differential equation for velocity addition using the substitution $$\dfrac{v}{c} = \mathrm{tanh}\phi.$$ The quantity $$\phi$$ is called the **rapidity**. This and the next problem, we rebuild a number of the basic results in special…
statement:
In the previous problem, we solved a differential equation for velocity addition using the substitution $$\dfrac{v}{c} = \mathrm{tanh}\phi.$$ The quantity $$\phi$$ is called the **rapidity**. This and the next problem, we rebuild a number of the basic results in special relativity using this quantity.

**a)** Consider two points in space, separated in the horizontal direction by $$\Delta x$$ and in the vertical direction by $$\Delta y.$$ The distance $$d$$ between the points can be found with the Pythagorean theorem, $$d^2 = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2$$.

Suppose we introduce a coordinate system rotated relative to the first one by an angle $$\theta.$$

Find $$\Delta x'$$ and $$\Delta y'$$ in terms of $$\Delta x, \Delta y,$$ and $$\theta.$$

**b)** Show by explicit calculation (using your equation from part (a)) that $$d^2 = \Delta x'^2 + \Delta y'^2.$$

We say that $$d$$ is **invariant** under rotations of coordinates.

**c)** We've seen that in relativity, there is a quantity that is invariant with respect to boosts (or Lorentz transformations). This quantity is the interval between two events,

$$ (\Delta s)^2 = (\Delta x)^2 - (c \Delta t)^2 $$

The interval is not invariant with respect to rotations (as you may optionally check).

However, in showing that distance is invariant with respect to rotations, you used the fact $$\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1.$$ In hyperbolic geometry, the equivalent identity is

$$ \mathrm{\cosh^2\phi} - \mathrm{\sinh^2\phi} = 1 $$

Define equations for a "hyperbolic rotation" by making an analogy to the equations for a rotation you found in part (a).

Show that the interval is invariant with respect to the hyperbolic rotation you defined.

**d)** The interval is invariant with respect to the Lorentz transformation,

\begin{aligned} x' &= \gamma (x - vt)\\ t' &= \gamma \left( t - \dfrac{vx}{c^2}\right) \end{aligned}

Suppose this is because the hyperbolic rotation is a Lorentz transformation. In that case, find $$\mathrm{sinh}\phi$$ and $$\mathrm{cosh}\phi$$ in terms of $$v.$$

Explain the origin of the substitution $$\dfrac{v}{c} = \mathrm{tanh}\phi$$
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: This problem extends the previous problem on hyperbolic rotations.
desc: This problem extends the previous problem on hyperbolic rotations. **a)** Going back to ordinary rotations, suppose we rotate coordinates by $$\alpha,$$ then rotate the rotated coordinates by $$\beta.$$ What is the overall effect? Answer intuitively, and use your answer to…
statement:
This problem extends the previous problem on hyperbolic rotations.

**a)** Going back to ordinary rotations, suppose we rotate coordinates by $$\alpha,$$ then rotate the rotated coordinates by $$\beta.$$ What is the overall effect? Answer intuitively, and use your answer to derive the angle addition formulas

\begin{aligned} \cos(\alpha + \beta) & = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta \\ \sin(\alpha + \beta) & = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\beta\cos\alpha \end{aligned}

**b)** By analogy with your work in part (e), find formulas for $$\sinh(\phi + \rho)$$ and $$\cos(\phi + \rho).$$

**c)** Extend your work in part (b) to find a formula for $$\tanh(\phi + \rho)$$ and use this to derive the velocity addition formula in special relativity.
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: Galileo's Ship and the Relativistic Baseball — Galileo imagined doing experiments inside the cabin of a ship…
desc: Galileo imagined doing experiments inside the cabin of a ship sailing at a perfectly steady velocity: jumping, playing catch, watching insects fly around. He claimed that __no matter what experiment you try__, you cannot tell the difference between the cabin of a smoothly…
statement:
Galileo imagined doing experiments inside the cabin of a ship sailing at a perfectly steady velocity: jumping, playing catch, watching insects fly around. He claimed that __no matter what experiment you try__, you cannot tell the difference between the cabin of a smoothly sailing ship and the same cabin on land. In modern language: the laws of physics are exactly the same in every __inertial reference frame__ (every non-accelerating frame). This is the __principle of relativity__. Throughout these problems, "frame" means an inertial frame, and "the baseball's frame" means the frame in which the baseball is at rest.

__(a)__ Standing on the ground, you can jump forward $$2.2\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Now you are in a cabin on a boat sailing at a constant $$5\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ and you jump forward, in the direction the boat moves. How far forward do you land, __relative to the boat__? (Assume the boat is much more massive than you, so it is not pushed backward appreciably when you jump.)

__(b)__ The principle of relativity applies only to ideal inertial frames. Give at least two distinct reasons why the cabin of a real ship, even one sailing at constant speed relative to the water, is not a perfectly inertial reference frame.

__(c)__ A baseball has mass $$145\;\mathrm{g}$$ and volume $$220\;\mathrm{cm}^3.$$ It moves to the right at a constant speed $$v$$ just below the speed of light. The baseball is then highly length-contracted, so its volume is very small and its density is enormous. Black holes are regions of spacetime with very high density — so if the baseball moves fast enough, does it become a black hole? Answer using only the principle of relativity.

__(d)__ A quantity that has the same value in every inertial frame is called an __invariant__. (This is different from a __constant__ or conserved quantity, which is something that does not change over time within one frame.) For each of the following, decide whether it is invariant: an object's energy, its electric charge, its mass, the distance between two objects, the time between two events, and the property of two events "happening at the same time."
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: The Interval Along a Light Beam — In relativity, the primitive object is the __event__ — a single point in…
desc: In relativity, the primitive object is the __event__ — a single point in space and time, like the snap of your fingers. Different frames disagree about where and when an event happened, but they all agree that it happened. In a given frame an event has coordinates $$(x,y,z,t).$$…
statement:
In relativity, the primitive object is the __event__ — a single point in space and time, like the snap of your fingers. Different frames disagree about where and when an event happened, but they all agree that it happened. In a given frame an event has coordinates $$(x,y,z,t).$$ Coordinates are frame-dependent, but the __invariant interval__ $$\Delta s$$ between two events, defined by $$(\Delta s)^2 = (\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2 + (\Delta z)^2 - (c\Delta t)^2,$$ has the same value in every inertial frame. (We take this invariance as the founding postulate of special relativity; everything else follows from it.)

__(a)__ A flash of light travels in a straight line (in vacuum, with no reflections) from event $$A$$ to event $$B.$$ No coordinates are given — invent your own. What is the interval between $$A$$ and $$B?$$

__(b)__ Use part (a) and the invariance of the interval to prove that the speed of light is the same, $$c,$$ in every inertial reference frame.

__(c)__ You send a flash of light from your flashlight off into outer space. Zap the lightning dog chases after it at $$99.9$$ percent of the speed of light (as measured in your frame). In Zap's frame, how fast does the flash recede from her?
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: The Twins and the Invariant Interval — Ursula and Vernor are twins, both $$18$$ years old. Vernor boards a…
desc: Ursula and Vernor are twins, both $$18$$ years old. Vernor boards a spaceship and travels to a distant star — $$6\;\mathrm{ly}$$ away in Ursula's frame — arriving after $$10\;\mathrm{y}$$ of Ursula's time. He turns around immediately and returns at the same speed. Recall the…
statement:
Ursula and Vernor are twins, both $$18$$ years old. Vernor boards a spaceship and travels to a distant star — $$6\;\mathrm{ly}$$ away in Ursula's frame — arriving after $$10\;\mathrm{y}$$ of Ursula's time. He turns around immediately and returns at the same speed.

Recall the __invariant interval__: $$(\Delta s)^2 = (\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2 + (\Delta z)^2 - (c\Delta t)^2$$ has the same value in every inertial frame. For events along a slower-than-light path, $$(\Delta s)^2$$ is negative, and it is convenient to use the __proper time__ $$\tau,$$ defined by $$(\Delta s)^2 = -c^2\tau^2,$$ or equivalently $$\tau^2 = (\Delta t)^2 - \dfrac{1}{c^2}\left((\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2 + (\Delta z)^2\right).$$ The proper time is invariant, and it equals the time between two events in the frame where they happen at the same place.

__(a)__ Identify three natural events in this story. How old is Ursula when Vernor returns?

__(b)__ Compute the proper time $$\tau$$ between Vernor's departure and his turnaround. How much time passes __in Vernor's frame__ during the outbound trip? (In Vernor's frame, what are $$\Delta x,$$ $$\Delta y,$$ and $$\Delta z$$ between those two events?)

__(c)__ How old is Vernor when he returns? Twins, yet different ages — this is the famous "twin paradox."

__(d)__ In Vernor's frame, how far away is Earth just as he arrives at the star (before he turns around)? Hint: in Vernor's frame you know both the speed at which Earth recedes and how long it has been receding. Compare your answer with the $$6\;\mathrm{ly}$$ Ursula would quote — this is __length contraction__.
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: The Ultrarelativistic Oscillator (IPhO 1994) — In special relativity, the energy $$E$$ and momentum $$p$$ of…
desc: In special relativity, the energy $$E$$ and momentum $$p$$ of a free particle with rest mass $$m$$ are related by $$E = \sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2c^4}.$$ When such a particle is subject to a conservative force, the total energy — the sum of $$\sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2c^4}$$ and the potential…
statement:
In special relativity, the energy $$E$$ and momentum $$p$$ of a free particle with rest mass $$m$$ are related by $$E = \sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2c^4}.$$ When such a particle is subject to a conservative force, the total energy — the sum of $$\sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2c^4}$$ and the potential energy — is conserved. If the particle's energy is much greater than its rest energy $$mc^2,$$ the rest energy can be neglected; such a particle is called __ultrarelativistic__. The relation $$f = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ between force and momentum remains valid in relativity.

Consider one-dimensional motion of an ultrarelativistic particle subject to an attractive central force of __constant magnitude__ $$f$$ (always pointing toward the origin). At $$t = 0$$ the particle is at the origin with momentum $$p_0 > 0.$$ There may be short intervals of time near the turning points during which the particle is not ultrarelativistic; neglect them. (From IPhO 1994, China.)

__(a)__ On a spacetime diagram with "square" axes (equal scales for $$x$$ and $$ct$$), what does the worldline of an ultrarelativistic particle look like? Plot the particle's position $$x$$ against time $$t$$ for at least one period of the motion.

__(b)__ Plot the particle's momentum $$p$$ against its position $$x$$ for one period, indicating the direction in which the curve is traced.

__(c)__ Find the coordinates of the turning points of the motion in terms of $$p_0,$$ $$f,$$ and $$c.$$

__(d)__ Find the total energy of the particle in terms of $$p_0$$ and $$c.$$ (Use $$\Delta U = f\,\Delta x$$ for the constant-magnitude force, together with energy conservation.)
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: Deriving the Lorentz Transformation — Inertial frames move at constant velocity relative to one another, so…
desc: Inertial frames move at constant velocity relative to one another, so it is reasonable to assume the transformation between their coordinates is __linear__. Let frame $$S'$$ move to the right at speed $$v$$ relative to frame $$S,$$ with origins arranged so that the event $$(x,t)…
statement:
Inertial frames move at constant velocity relative to one another, so it is reasonable to assume the transformation between their coordinates is __linear__. Let frame $$S'$$ move to the right at speed $$v$$ relative to frame $$S,$$ with origins arranged so that the event $$(x,t) = (0,0)$$ in $$S$$ is also $$(x',t') = (0,0)$$ in $$S'.$$ Write $$x' = a_{xx}x + a_{xt}t$$ and $$t' = a_{tx}x + a_{tt}t$$ for constant coefficients (which may depend on $$v$$). Postulate that the spacetime interval is invariant; pairing each event with the common origin, this reads $$x'^2 - (ct')^2 = x^2 - (ct)^2.$$

__(a)__ Substitute the linear transformation into the invariance equation. By matching the coefficients of $$x^2,$$ $$t^2,$$ and $$xt$$ on the two sides, derive three independent equations relating the four coefficients.

__(b)__ Three equations cannot determine four unknowns — and they shouldn't, since we have not yet used the relative speed of the frames. The worldline $$x = 0$$ (the spatial origin of $$S$$) moves at velocity $$-v$$ through $$S',$$ i.e. it satisfies $$x' = -vt'.$$ Use this to derive a fourth equation: $$-v = \dfrac{a_{xt}}{a_{tt}}.$$

__(c)__ Solve your four equations for $$a_{tt}.$$ The result is called the __Lorentz factor__ $$\gamma.$$

__(d)__ Find the remaining coefficients and write out the full transformation, including the transverse coordinates $$y'$$ and $$z'.$$
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: A Rod Passes Through a Cylinder (USAPhO) — A rod travels at a constant speed $$v = \dfrac{4}{5}c$$ to the…
desc: A rod travels at a constant speed $$v = \dfrac{4}{5}c$$ to the right relative to a hollow cylinder, passing through it and out the other side. In the cylinder's frame the cylinder is $$15\;\mathrm{m}$$ long, and the left end of the rod aligns with the left end of the cylinder…
statement:
A rod travels at a constant speed $$v = \dfrac{4}{5}c$$ to the right relative to a hollow cylinder, passing through it and out the other side. In the cylinder's frame the cylinder is $$15\;\mathrm{m}$$ long, and the left end of the rod aligns with the left end of the cylinder (call this event $$A$$) __at the same time__ as the right end of the rod aligns with the right end of the cylinder (event $$B$$). (Adapted from a USAPhO problem.)

You will need the __Lorentz transformation__: if frame $$S'$$ moves to the right at speed $$v$$ relative to $$S,$$ an event with coordinates $$(x,t)$$ in $$S$$ has coordinates $$x' = \gamma(x - vt)$$ and $$t' = \gamma\left(t - \dfrac{vx}{c^2}\right)$$ in $$S',$$ where $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}}.$$ For $$v = \dfrac{4}{5}c,$$ $$\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}.$$ Also recall the interval $$(\Delta s)^2 = (\Delta x)^2 - (c\Delta t)^2$$: events with $$(\Delta s)^2 > 0$$ are __spacelike-separated__, and $$\Delta s$$ is then their __proper length__ — the distance between them in the frame where they are simultaneous.

__(a)__ Sketch, on a spacetime diagram in the cylinder's frame with "square" axes (equal scales for $$x$$ and $$ct$$), the worldlines of the left end of the rod (RL), the right end of the rod (RR), the left end of the cylinder (CL), and the right end of the cylinder (CR). What are the slopes of the four worldlines?

__(b)__ Explain why the rod is exactly $$15\;\mathrm{m}$$ long in the cylinder's frame. Then place the cylinder's left end at $$x = 0$$ and the rod's left end at $$x = -15\;\mathrm{m}$$ at $$t = 0,$$ and find the cylinder-frame coordinates of events $$A$$ and $$B$$ and the interval between them.

__(c)__ Lorentz-transform $$A$$ and $$B$$ into the rod's frame.

__(d)__ How long are the rod and the cylinder in the rod's frame? In the cylinder's frame the rod fits entirely inside the cylinder for one instant; is the rod ever entirely inside the cylinder in the rod's frame? Resolve the apparent contradiction.
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: Bell's Spaceships and the Breaking Rope — Ursula and Vernor sit in spaceships that are at rest in the Earth's…
desc: Ursula and Vernor sit in spaceships that are at rest in the Earth's frame, separated by $$1\;\mathrm{ly}$$ along the line joining them, with Vernor in front. A rope is tied taut between the two ships; the rope cannot stretch by any appreciable amount. At the same instant (in the…
statement:
Ursula and Vernor sit in spaceships that are at rest in the Earth's frame, separated by $$1\;\mathrm{ly}$$ along the line joining them, with Vernor in front. A rope is tied taut between the two ships; the rope cannot stretch by any appreciable amount. At the same instant (in the Earth frame), both ships begin to accelerate in the direction from Ursula toward Vernor, and from then on the two ships always have exactly the same acceleration as each other in the Earth frame, until both are traveling at $$0.99c$$ relative to Earth. Does the rope break? (This famous puzzle is known as Bell's spaceship paradox.) Recall the Lorentz factor $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}},$$ which is about $$7.1$$ at $$v = 0.99c,$$ and the Lorentz transformation $$t' = \gamma\left(t - \dfrac{vx}{c^2}\right)$$ for the time coordinate in a frame moving at speed $$v$$ in the $$+x$$ direction.

__(a)__ Give a plausible-sounding argument that the rope should __not__ break.

__(b)__ Give a plausible-sounding argument, using length contraction, that the rope __must__ break. In particular: once the ships are coasting at $$0.99c,$$ how far apart are they in their own (shared) rest frame?

__(c)__ To resolve the paradox, model the acceleration as a rapid sequence of identical small velocity "bursts," fired by both ships simultaneously in the Earth frame. The first pair of bursts is simultaneous in the ships' frame too — why? Are later pairs of bursts simultaneous in the (now moving) ships' frame? Which ship fires first, as judged in the ships' frame? What happens to the ships' separation in their own frame, and does the rope break?

__(d)__ In the Earth frame, the ships' separation never changes. Yet the rope must break in this frame too, since breaking — like being a black hole — is an invariant. What breaks the rope, as described in the Earth frame?
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW115: Relativity: Length Contraction, Time Dilation, and Relativity of Simultaneity
label: PW115
name: Seeing an Approaching Clock Run Fast: the Doppler Shift — Ursula and Vernor float toward each other in deep…
desc: Ursula and Vernor float toward each other in deep space at relative speed $$v.$$ Vernor holds a large digital clock facing Ursula, who watches it through a telescope. __Time dilation__ (a consequence of the invariance of the interval) says that in Ursula's frame, a clock moving…
statement:
Ursula and Vernor float toward each other in deep space at relative speed $$v.$$ Vernor holds a large digital clock facing Ursula, who watches it through a telescope. __Time dilation__ (a consequence of the invariance of the interval) says that in Ursula's frame, a clock moving at speed $$v$$ ticks slowly by the Lorentz factor $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-(v/c)^2}}$$: between two events on Vernor's worldline separated by time $$\Delta t$$ in Ursula's frame, his clock advances only $$\dfrac{\Delta t}{\gamma}.$$ Surprisingly, Ursula nevertheless __sees__ Vernor's clock running __fast__. This problem works out why, and by how much.

__(a)__ It is tempting to answer "Ursula sees the clock run slow, by the time-dilation factor $$\gamma.$$" Why doesn't time dilation directly answer the question of what Ursula __sees__ through her telescope?

__(b)__ Put Ursula at rest at $$x = 0$$ in her own frame. Let $$A = (x_0,\,0)$$ and $$B = \left(x_0 - d,\,\dfrac{d}{v}\right)$$ be two events at which Vernor's clock face emits light toward Ursula (he covers a distance $$d$$ toward her between them, at speed $$v$$). Find the coordinates of the reception events $$U_A$$ and $$U_B$$ at which that light reaches Ursula, and show that the time between receptions is $$\Delta t_U = d\,\dfrac{c-v}{vc}.$$

__(c)__ By time dilation, between $$A$$ and $$B$$ Vernor's clock advances $$\Delta t_V = \dfrac{d}{\gamma v}.$$ Compute the ratio $$\dfrac{\Delta t_V}{\Delta t_U}$$ — the factor by which Ursula sees Vernor's clock run fast — and simplify.

__(d)__ Vernor's clock display glows green. Light of frequency $$f$$ is a kind of clock that "ticks" $$f$$ times per second. What frequency does Ursula observe, and is the light shifted toward the blue or the red end of the spectrum? What would she observe if Vernor were instead receding at speed $$v?$$
tags: relativity: length contraction, time dilation, and relativity of simultaneity

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: Answer the following conceptual questions:
desc: Answer the following conceptual questions: **a)** When an atom absorbs a photon, it jumps up to an excited state. Simple discussions of quantum mechanics often state that the energy difference between the ground state and excited state is exact, but no photon would ever have…
statement:
Answer the following conceptual questions:

**a)** When an atom absorbs a photon, it jumps up to an excited state. Simple discussions of quantum mechanics often state that the energy difference between the ground state and excited state is exact, but no photon would ever have __exactly__ the right energy to cause a jump to an excited state. In reality, the atom can absorb a range of different photon energies. For some transitions, this range is very narrow, and for others it is rather wide. It is observed that the wider the range of energies of photons that can cause a transition, the shorter the duration of time the atom stays in the excited state before decaying back down to the ground state. Why?

**b)** A proton and a deuteron (a proton and neutron together), each with energy $$3\;\mathrm{MeV}$$, approach a rectangular potential barrier of height $$10\;\mathrm{MeV}.$$ Which particle has a better chance of penetrating the barrier? (You can answer qualitatively; you may want to work the problem on tunnelling later in this problem set before answering this question.)

**c)** Can a hydrogen atom absorb a photon that exceeds its binding energy?

**d)** What are the dimensions of the wavefunction $$\Psi(x)?$$

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: Perform the following computations:
desc: Perform the following computations: **a)** A particle of mass $$m$$ is in an infinite square well of width $$w$$ in the ground state. Find the force on the walls. **b)** Now suppose that there are $$N$$ particles in the well, and its width is $$Nw.$$ Assume that $$N$$ is large…
statement:
Perform the following computations:

**a)** A particle of mass $$m$$ is in an infinite square well of width $$w$$ in the ground state. Find the force on the walls.

**b)** Now suppose that there are $$N$$ particles in the well, and its width is $$Nw.$$ Assume that $$N$$ is large. The first particle is in the ground state. The second particle is in state $$n = 2,$$ etc. Find the approximate force on the walls.

**c)** Singly-charged sodium ions are accelerated through a potential difference of $$325\;\mathrm{V}.$$ What is the momentum acquired by individual ions? What is the de Broglie wavelength?

**d)** A nonrelativistic particle is moving three times as fast as an electron. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelengths, particle to electron, is $$1.813\times 10^{-4}.$$ What type of particle is it?

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: Make the following estimations:
desc: Make the following estimations: **a)** Suppose you want to study the structure of a crystal via diffraction. This requires a wavelength only a few times larger than the spacing between atoms to get larger diffraction angles. Roughly how much energy would a photon need to study…
statement:
Make the following estimations:

**a)** Suppose you want to study the structure of a crystal via diffraction. This requires a wavelength only a few times larger than the spacing between atoms to get larger diffraction angles. Roughly how much energy would a photon need to study most solids in this way? How much energy would an electron need? A neutron?

**b)** Suppose the potential energy a particle would have in some region is $$U$$ and the total energy of the particle (neglecting its rest mass energy) is $$E.$$ Then classically, the particle can only enter the region if $$E \ge U,$$ because otherwise the particle's kinetic energy would be negative.

Quantum mechanically, if the particle moves through the region in a time $$\Delta t,$$ then its energy is uncertain due to the time-energy uncertainty relationship. As a heuristic, we can think of the particle as "borrowing" an energy similar to its energy uncertainty for a time similar to the time to pass through the region. This allows the particle to pass through the region and pop out on the other side, even though classically this is impossible. However, the particle is only likely to do this "borrowing" if, with the borrowed energy, it can pass through the barrier in less than the time uncertainty.

Suppose the length of the region of high potential energy is $$L.$$ Suppose the particle borrows twice the energy it needs to be able to enter the classically-forbidden region. (The reason for using twice as much as the minimum is so that, on entering the forbidden region, the particle has some energy left over as kinetic energy so that it can get through the region.) Estimate $$L$$ in terms of $$U, E,$$ and the mass $$m$$ of the (nonrelativistic) particle such that the particle could have a reasonable chance of passing through the barrier.

**c)** Suppose you wish to balance a pencil on its pointy end as accurately as possible. This is an unstable equilibrium, so that if the pencil were perfectly vertical and stationary, it would balance, but the slightest misalignment will make it topple. Due to quantum uncertainty, the pencil will always be either a little tilted away from the vertical or have a little sideways motion, or both. Estimate the longest duration for which a pencil could theoretically be made to balance.

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: A zinc ball of radius $$R = 1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ is located in a vacuum far away from other…
desc: A zinc ball of radius $$R = 1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ is located in a vacuum far away from other bodies and is charged to a potential $$\phi_0 = -0.5\;\mathrm{V}.$$ (This assumes $$\phi = 0$$ at infinity.) The ball is illuminated by a monochromatic ultraviolet light with wavelength…
statement:
A zinc ball of radius $$R = 1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ is located in a vacuum far away from other bodies and is charged to a potential $$\phi_0 = -0.5\;\mathrm{V}.$$ (This assumes $$\phi = 0$$ at infinity.) The ball is illuminated by a monochromatic ultraviolet light with wavelength $$\lambda = 290\;\mathrm{nm}.$$

**a)** What is the maximum velocity $$v_1$$ of photoelectrons flying out of the ball?

**b)** Consider one of the maximum-velocity electrons from part (a). What is its velocity when far away from the ball?

**c)** Determine the potential $$\phi_1$$ of the ball after prolonged exposure to the UV light.

**d)** Determine the net number $$N$$ of electrons that escape the ball after a prolonged exposure to the UV light.

The maximum wavelength of light that can cause zinc to emit photoelectrons is $$\lambda_0 = 332\;\mathrm{nm}.$$

You may also use the following constants:

\begin{aligned} c &= 3.0 \times 10^8\;\mathrm{m/s} \\ h &= 6.6\times 10^{-34}\;\mathrm{J\;s}\\ \epsilon_0 &= 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \;\mathrm{F/m} \\ e &= 1.6\times 10^{-19}\;\mathrm{C}\\ m_e &=9.1\times 10^{-31}\;\mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: In this problem, you'll find the energy levels in the **Bohr model** of the hydrogen atom.
desc: In this problem, you'll find the energy levels in the **Bohr model** of the hydrogen atom. **a)** Our model of a hydrogen atom consists of an electron of mass $$m_e$$ in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around a proton of mass much larger than $$m_e.$$ You can assume the orbit…
statement:
In this problem, you'll find the energy levels in the **Bohr model** of the hydrogen atom.

**a)** Our model of a hydrogen atom consists of an electron of mass $$m_e$$ in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around a proton of mass much larger than $$m_e.$$ You can assume the orbit is nonrelativistic. What is the energy of the atom as a function of $$L,$$ the angular momentum of the electron about the proton?

**b)** In class, we studied a particle on a ring, finding that regardless of the radius of the ring, the only allowed orbits are those with $$L = n\hbar.$$ This is true for the hydrogen atom as well. What are the energy levels as a function of $$n?$$

**c)** Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, and its spectrum can be observed in a wide variety of astrophysical objects. In these spectra, perhaps the most important feature is the **Lyman-Alpha line**, which is the frequency of light emitted when a hydrogen atom decays from $$n=2$$ to $$n=1.$$ Suppose that in a certain spectrum, the Lyman-Alpha line is observed to have a wavelength of $$176\;\mathrm{nm}.$$ By what factor is the spectrum redshifted?

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: **a)** Think of a hydrogen atom as having some radius, $$r.$$ Think of an electron as…
desc: **a)** Think of a hydrogen atom as having some radius, $$r.$$ Think of an electron as having an uncertainty in position $$\Delta x \approx r$$ and find the kinetic energy of the electron. **b)** Find $$r$$ such that the total energy of the hydrogen atom is minimized. **c)**…
statement:
**a)** Think of a hydrogen atom as having some radius, $$r.$$ Think of an electron as having an uncertainty in position $$\Delta x \approx r$$ and find the kinetic energy of the electron.

**b)** Find $$r$$ such that the total energy of the hydrogen atom is minimized.

**c)** Compare the size $$r$$ that you found in part (b) to the radius of the ground state of the Bohr model.

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: A neutron interferometer splits a monoenergetic beam of neutrons into two parallel beams…
desc: A neutron interferometer splits a monoenergetic beam of neutrons into two parallel beams, a distance $$d$$ apart. These are brought together after each has travelled a path length $$l.$$ It is found that if the two beams are in the same horizontal plane the interference is…
statement:
A neutron interferometer splits a monoenergetic beam of neutrons into two parallel beams, a distance $$d$$ apart. These are brought together after each has travelled a path length $$l.$$ It is found that if the two beams are in the same horizontal plane the interference is constructive, but if the system is rotated so that one beam is vertically above the other the interference gradually changes as the system is rotated, and becomes completely destructive as the system becomes vertical. Explain this result and obtain an expression for the neutron energy in terms of $$d, l,$$ and fundamental constants.

You may assume that change in the gravitational potential energy of the neutrons is small compared to their kinetic energy.

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: In this problem, you'll combine relativity and quantum mechanics to explain **Compton…
desc: In this problem, you'll combine relativity and quantum mechanics to explain **Compton scattering**. Suppose a photon approaches an electron. The photon collides with the electron and moves in a new direction with angle $$\theta.$$ The electron also recoils at relativistic speed…
statement:
In this problem, you'll combine relativity and quantum mechanics to explain **Compton scattering**. Suppose a photon approaches an electron.

The photon collides with the electron and moves in a new direction with angle $$\theta.$$ The electron also recoils at relativistic speed. This process is called "Compton scattering".

We will treat the collision as a classical collision between point particles, but use the quantum mechanical relationships between energy, momentum, wavelength, and frequency to study the effect on the photon. We will work in a frame where the initial velocity of the electron is zero. Define the following variables: \begin{aligned} \lambda &= \text{initial wavelength of photon} \\ \lambda' &= \text{wavelength of scattered photon} \\ K &= \text{frequency of scattered electron} \\ m &= \text{mass of electron}\\ \theta &= \text{angle by which photon is deflected}\\ \phi &= \text{angle of scattered electron's path with the original path of the photon}\\ h &= \text{Planck's constant} \\ c &= \text{speed of light} \end{aligned}

**a)** Find equations for conservation of energy, conservation of momentum in the initial direction of motion of the photon, and conservation of momentum in the transverse direction. You may need to know that in relativity, the energy of a massive particle is $$E = \gamma mc^2$$ and the momentum is $$\vec{p} = \gamma m \vec{v}.$$

**b)** Find the frequency shift $$\Delta \lambda = \lambda' - \lambda$$ of the photon as a function of $$\theta$$ and fundamental constants.

**c)** Explain why the shift in photon wavelength is easier to observe for x-rays, which are high frequency, than for visible light.

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: This problem explores the basics of **quantum tunnelling** for a particle moving in one…
desc: This problem explores the basics of **quantum tunnelling** for a particle moving in one dimension. A particle of mass $$m$$ approaches a "barrier" from the left. By "barrier", we mean that $$U = 0$$ for $$x<0$$ and for $$x > L.$$ In between, $$U = U_0.$$ Note that this is simply…
statement:
This problem explores the basics of **quantum tunnelling** for a particle moving in one dimension. A particle of mass $$m$$ approaches a "barrier" from the left. By "barrier", we mean that $$U = 0$$ for $$x<0$$ and for $$x > L.$$ In between, $$U = U_0.$$ Note that this is simply a region where the potential energy of the particle suddenly increases when it enters; it isn't a wall or physical obstruction. You can imagine that there is simply a very strong force $$f = \dfrac{U_0}{\Delta x}$$ on the particle in some very small region of space from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = \Delta x,$$ and a force of equal magnitude in the opposite direction on the other side of the barrier. When the particle's position is $$x<0$$ or $$x>L$$ it is "outside the well" and when its position is $$0<x<L$$ it is said to be "inside the well". The situation with the particle outside the well is sketched below.

**a)** Classically, what is the condition on the speed of the particle such that it penetrates the barrier?

A quantum particle is capable of penetrating the barrier, with some probability, even when it has less energy than this! The rest of the problem works out roughly how this is possible.

**b)** Suppose the particle has energy $$E.$$ Find its wavenumber $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$$ while outside the well. Then find it while inside the well.

**c)** If the particle classically does not have enough energy to penetrate the barrier, show that the wavenumber you calculated in (b) is imaginary.

**d)** The wavefunction of a particle with wavenumber $$k$$ oscillates sinusoidally. In the complex numbers, this means the wavefunction is proportional to $$e^{ikx}.$$ Let's suppose this continues to be true for the wavefunction inside the barrier, when the particle does not have enough energy to enter the barrier classically. Describe the shape of the wavefunction inside the barrier.

**e)** The particle's chance of penetrating the barrier is small if the wavefunction diminishes significantly from the left of the barrier to the right. Find an approximate condition combining $$m, L, U,$$ and $$E$$ such that the particle has a reasonable chance of penetrating the barrier.

**f)** Compare the condition you found in (e) to the one you estimated based on the time-energy uncertainty principle in problem 3.

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: There are two different velocities often associated with waves: their **phase velocity**…
desc: There are two different velocities often associated with waves: their **phase velocity** and their **group velocity**. In this problem, we define these quantities and explore which is a more apt description of the speed of motion of an object described by a wave. **a)** Imagine…
statement:
There are two different velocities often associated with waves: their **phase velocity** and their **group velocity**. In this problem, we define these quantities and explore which is a more apt description of the speed of motion of an object described by a wave.

**a)** Imagine a pure sine wave traveling to the right. Take one particular peak of the wave and measure its speed. This is the **phase velocity** of the wave. What is the phase velocity for a photon? (You may use the fact that $$E = pc$$ for a photon.) What is the phase velocity for a particle with mass $$m$$ and momentum $$p$$ moving in free space (potential is zero)?

------------

The pure sinusoids we examined in part (a) do not really represent a particle moving. Although the particle has momentum in a given direction, it is equally-likely to be found anywhere, since the square of the wavefunction is constant. (This is of course not precisely true for $$\Psi(x) \propto \sin(kx - \omega t),$$ but it is true for the complex $$\Psi(x) \propto e^{i(kx - \omega t)}$$.) So the probability distribution for the position of the particle doesn't move.

However, consider a superposition of two waves, one with angular frequency and wavenumber $$\omega$$ and $$k,$$ and a second with angular frequency and wavenumbers $$\omega + \mathrm{d}\omega$$ and $$k + \mathrm{d}k.$$ As the notation suggests, consider these two waves to be very similar in frequency and wavelength. We consider a state in which the wavefunction of the particle is a superposition of these two waves, \[\Psi(x,t) \propto e^{i(kx-\omega t)} + e^{i((k+\mathrm{d}k)x - (\omega + \mathrm{d}\omega)t)}\]

**b)** Describe the probability distribution for the location of a particle given by the $$\Psi$$ described above at the time $$t = 0.$$ Specifically, locate a point where the probability is at a peak.

**c)** A time $$t$$ later, where has the same peak moved to?

**d)** Relate your answer to (c) to the definition of the **group velocity**, \

**e)** Find the group velocity for a photon and for a massive particle.

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
label: PW116
name: Photons, Planck's Constant, and Photon Momentum — If a very faint source of light shines on a very sensitive…
desc: If a very faint source of light shines on a very sensitive detector, the image does not build up smoothly and continuously. Instead, the detector registers light in discrete events — "Ping! Ping! Ping!" — one pixel at a time. Light comes in particles called __photons__. Each…
statement:
If a very faint source of light shines on a very sensitive detector, the image does not build up smoothly and continuously. Instead, the detector registers light in discrete events — "Ping! Ping! Ping!" — one pixel at a time. Light comes in particles called __photons__. Each photon propagates like a wave, traveling at the speed of light $$c$$ and obeying the usual wave relations, but it carries a definite amount of energy that is delivered all at once when the photon is detected. The energy of a photon is $$E = hf,$$ where $$f$$ is the frequency of the photon's wave and $$h$$ is a fundamental physical constant called __Planck's constant__.

__(a)__ Suppose the wavefunction of a photon has wavelength $$\lambda.$$ What is its frequency in terms of $$\lambda$$ and $$c?$$

__(b)__ What are the __dimensions__ of Planck's constant? (Dimensions, not units: a quantity can be measured in many different units, but it always has the same dimensions. Write them in terms of mass $$\mathrm{M},$$ length $$\mathrm{L},$$ and time $$\mathrm{T}.$$)

__(c)__ Name a familiar physical quantity with the same dimensions as Planck's constant. (For reference, $$h \approx 6.626\times 10^{-34}\;\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}},$$ a value that is supplied on the USAPhO. The smallness of $$h$$ is a rough indication that quantum mechanics differs from classical mechanics only at very small scales.)

__(d)__ Which has higher energy — a blue photon or a red photon?

__(e)__ The __reduced Planck's constant__ is $$\hbar = \dfrac{h}{2\pi}$$ (pronounced "h bar"). Rewrite the photon energy $$E = hf$$ in terms of $$\hbar$$ and the angular frequency $$\omega = 2\pi f.$$

__(f)__ The momentum of a photon is $$p = \dfrac{E}{c}.$$ Find the photon's wavelength $$\lambda$$ in terms of its momentum $$p.$$ Then rewrite the momentum in terms of $$\hbar$$ and the wavenumber $$k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}.$$ (These momentum relations turn out to hold for massive particles as well — they are the __de Broglie__ relations.)

lesson: PW116: Quantum Mechanics: Photons and Quantization
